items.body: @avagin @ayushr2 let me know if you'd prefer this in separate PRs.
@nixprime could you take a loot at this pr too?
@avagin could you import this so that tests run? I haven't run all the tests yet (still need #12461).

@tamird Have we benchmarked the new ilist or refs implementation compared to their old go_generics one? IIRC, with Go generics, we add interface method calls and these types are on the hot paths for various subsystems.
Thanks very much for the analysis! That makes sense, at least for ilist. How about the second commit that touches refs?

I think the refs case is fine, with some changes:

- The `LoggingPolicy` type argument has the same same-shape problem, resulting in an indirect call to `LoggingPolicy.enabled()` in every `IncRef/TryIncRef/DecRef`:

- An ergonomic complaint: having to explicitly specify `refs.LoggingDisabled` everywhere is a bit obnoxious, since the intended use of the feature is that it's disabled by default, and selectively enabled to debug refcounting problems for specific types. Is it possible to define e.g. `type RefsBase[T any, L LoggingPolicy] struct{...}; type Refs[T any] = RefsBase[T, LoggingDisabled]; type LoggedRefs[T any] = RefsBase[T, LoggingEnabled]`?
Done. Required some more go_stateify surgery, please have a look!
Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

> Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

There's a big ergonomics benefit. Using bazel in editors is not very well supported, so anyone working on gvisor without the benefit of internal tooling can't easily jump to definition on types generated by `go_generics`.
Could I please get a CI run on this?

It looks like it doesn't work in `bpf/input_bytes.go` anymore either... From experimentation, it looks like it works if `bpf.load*()` is inlined into a call site where `endian` is specified explicitly, but when it's inlined into e.g. `bpf.Exec[endian Endianness]()` the type-switch occurs at runtime. I'm asking the Go team if there's anything we can do about this.

Apparently this is https://github.com/golang/go/issues/59591.

I tried inlining `LogRefs()` into `IncRef()` etc. (`var l L; if _, ok := any(l).(loggingEnabled); ok { ... }`), but this didn't help the generated code.

Unlike go_generics, native Go generics only instantiate distinct code for different argument "shapes"; see https://github.com/golang/proposal/blob/master/design/generics-implementation-gcshape.md. prs.title: atomicptr: use atomic.Pointer
prs.head: 3e6c298682bcd2e8c480af2170b7915fb7d594f4

items.body: @ayushr2 could you have a look at this one?

IIUC, we are using `go_generics` package to generate code which is using Go's native generics support. Two levels of generated code. So why not directly replace the `go_generics` atomic pointer with `atomic.Pointer`? Maybe I am missing something. Is there a benefit to doing it this way?

> 

I couldn't agree more, but stateify doesn't yet support generics. That requires the first N-1 commits in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470, so I was planning to send that after that PR (and this one) merge.
Having said that, I could move those commits to this PR, since there is some question about whether https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470 can be merged at all.

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.
> 
> We should probably add native support to stateify for `atomic.Pointer`; such that it should be able to detect `atomic.Pointer` usage and generate code using .Load() and .Store(). I don't know if the AST parser we use is capable to do this.

It's not that the AST parser isn't capable, it's that that state package fundamentally wants to register a `reflect.Type` under a unique name: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/70f9a824dc761638488b988ebd33930569a83c65/pkg/state/types.go#L339

Since there's no `reflect.Type` associated with an uninstantiated generic, we'd need to do string matching on the type's name and its methods to discover that it is an `atomic.Pointer`.

> If not, we can add support for new `stateify` tags like:
> 
> ```
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state: pointer".(int)"`
> ```

We perhaps could, but is that any better? This would make a poor addition to `go_stateify` because it doesn't generalize beyond `atomic.Pointer`.

> 
> If you intend to cleanup `atomicptr` from go_generics, then we could also just use:
> 
> ```
> // +stateify savable
> type S struct {
> 	// descriptorTable holds descriptors.
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state:".(int)"`
> }
> 
> func (s *S) savePtr() int {
> 	return s.ptr.Load()
> }
> 
> func (s *S) loadPtr(_ goContext.Context, ptr int) {
> 	s.ptr.Store(ptr)
> }
> ```

We could, but that feels quite manual, and ergonomically worse than what exists today.

Before the codegen deficiencies were pointed out in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470#pullrequestreview-3645103398 my goal was to remove type parameter support from go_generics, leaving only constants.

Now answering your first point:

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.

Well, I don't disagree, but haven't come up with a cleaner way of supporting generics with stateify. I'm all ears for suggestions!
A friendly reminder that this PR had no activity for 120 days.

> A friendly reminder that this PR had no activity for 120 days.

Yes, I am waiting for guidance from @ayushr2.

Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

I worry that this may no longer inline. These are used in very hot paths, including some `go:nosplit` paths where stack budget matters.

Is there a way to enforce that these continue to inline as they did before?

Go has no force-inline directive. We can guard the hot call sites in CI:
compile them with `-m=2` on amd64 and arm64 and require an `inlining call
to` diagnostic at each site. Checking `can inline` alone would miss a
caller where the compiler decided not to inline. The [Go compiler's
inlining test](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/022c8636110ebac86a9b88724cda168ed713c21f/src/cmd/compile/internal/test/inl_test.go#L339-L359)
distinguishes the two.

I checked the generated code with Go 1.27.2. On both architectures,
`Load`, `Store` and `Swap` produced identical instruction bytes,
relocations and stack-frame sizes before and after the change. The real
`//go:nosplit` `seccompMmapHandler` inlines `Load`; a deliberately
non-inlined control leaves a call that the check detects. I'd cover that
handler and representative `Store` and `Swap` callers. Are there other
stack-sensitive call sites you'd want covered?

[Compiler output and checks](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/0d07a278-4454-4de6-940d-1369a36da3b6).
Both code-generation builds per architecture, the arm64 link, and the
correctness tests passed. The job is red because the qualification-only
probe was missing a package comment.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: checklocks: guard the TCP segment queue
source.body:
The segment queue uses mu for its list and frozen state, but checklocks does not enforce that ownership. Guard both fields and enforce the existing caller-held lock requirement of emptyLocked.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce UDP receive-state ownership
source.body:
Packet delivery reads frozen under rcvMu, but freeze, thaw, and restore write it under mu. Use rcvMu for all accesses and group frozen with the receive state it controls.

Annotate the receive fields and reuse thaw after successful restore so checklocks enforces the same ownership during normal operation and save/restore.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard socket option state
source.body:
SocketOptions documents locking for its error queue and linger option, but checklocks does not enforce those contracts. Add field guards using the mutexes already held by their accessors and replace the redundant locking prose.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: fix fragmentation shutdown locking
source.body:
The post-Release check added in a4fb3b200fdc returns an error while still holding mu, so a later Process or Release blocks indefinitely. Unlock before returning and enforce the existing outer-state and release-helper lock contracts.

Document how marking a reassembler done excludes further processing and gives release exclusive cleanup ownership. Timeout callbacks run with the fragmentation mutex held and cannot reenter the owner.

Cover processing after release followed by another release, and make existing internal-state inspections follow the guarded contract.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard gonet connection state
source.body:
Guard deadline timers and cancellation channels with the deadline mutex, and check the caller-held contract on setDeadline. Guard the TCP read buffer with readMu while preserving the readMu-before-deadline-mutex lock order.

Construct deadline state as a fresh value so initialization is visible to checklocks. Timer callbacks retain their captured cancellation channel, preserving deadline reset behavior without copying a used mutex.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce hostinet lock and atomic rules
source.body:
Require the persistent-event mutex for mask updates and direct waiter-entry operations while allowing lock-free atomic mask reads. Require atomic access to shutdown and backlog state.

Guard the collection of listeners awaiting restore with its collection mutex, retaining detached-list processing after unlocking.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce link endpoint ownership
source.body:

TUN flags remain immutable for an association; readers capture the association under the device mutex before accessing flags without it. Final release remains a file-lifetime boundary.

source.title: checklocks: synchronize plugin readiness
source.body:
Plugin readiness checks read and clear a cache that the notifier updates under its own mutex. Readers do not acquire that mutex, so consuming cached events races with notification updates and other readiness checks. The unsynchronized cache dates to 079c1a937be.

Make the cache atomic and consume requested IN/OUT bits with a snapshot CAS. Preserve unrelated events and the existing fallback when not all requested I/O events are cached. Avoid acquiring the notifier mutex in Readiness, since notification callbacks can re-enter it.

Add a concurrent-readiness regression using disjoint cached I/O bits, retaining error, hangup, and high bits without invoking the plugin C implementation. Annotate the atomic cache and notifier registration contracts, and document the external owner of the remaining event state.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: fix proc network sysctl ownership
source.body:
Proc file descriptions share sysctl sources, so per-FD locks do not protect cached state. Read the port range and TCP SACK setting from the synchronized stack instead of retaining unsynchronized duplicate caches. Rejected SACK writes no longer change the value read back. The old netstack replacement path was removed by f4da28bc0a623.

Enforce the mutex protecting PortManager's authoritative ephemeral range with checklocks. Keep the synchronous reservation callback's caller-held lock contract explicit where it cannot yet be annotated.

Forwarding intentionally retains the last-written value introduced by 600d14f83e1d. Give that source its own mutex and serialize the cache update with SetForwarding. Cover cross-source readback and rejected SACK writes.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: lock queue-discipline test accounting
source.body:
Guard FIFO and token-bucket test accounting with each fixture's existing mutex. Snapshot the FIFO packet count under that mutex before reporting a timeout, since dispatcher writes may still be in progress.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard the stack random source
source.body:
Require lockedRandomSource.mu when accessing the underlying random source, making its existing concurrency contract statically checked.

source.title: checklocks: fix TCP atomic state access
source.body:
Two TCP state paths use atomic storage without preserving its synchronization contract.

The send-buffer option callback atomically disables autotuning without the endpoint or send-queue mutex, but endpoint probes copy the flag with RacyLoad. The first commit uses atomic snapshot accesses, declares the flag and queue-lock contracts, and extends the endpoint-probe regression with a concurrent option callback. The unsynchronized snapshot dates to 96459f55984 and was retained by ef9e8d91318.

Readiness and shutdown also update connection-direction bits under different mutexes. The load-then-swap added in 89b6a474c62 can lose a concurrent send-closed or receive-closed update. The second commit uses atomic OR and declares the field's atomic contract; passing the zero-valued open state remains a no-op.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: publish initialized TCP endpoint IDs
source.body:
TCP ICMP errors read endpoint addresses and ports without taking the endpoint mutex since 62b4c2f5173. An active connection previously published its selected ephemeral tuple before assigning it to the endpoint, so an incoming error could race with that assignment or report a zero local port.

Assign the selected port before registering the endpoint and restore the old ID if registration fails. Taking the endpoint mutex in the ICMP reader would deadlock synchronous loopback errors during writes.

Extend the existing connect-error test to deliver a matching ICMP error as soon as the endpoint is registered. Pause the handshake clock before SYN allocation so later synchronization cannot hide the publication race.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce UDP endpoint lock contracts
source.body:
Require the error mutex for the last error, and the endpoint mutex for read shutdown and binding. Exclude endpoint locks while writing: a synchronous loopback ICMP error can reacquire the read lock and deadlock behind a waiting writer.

Document the endpoint lock held through synchronous registration callbacks, which checklocks cannot currently follow.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce Unix socket ownership
source.body:
Enforce mutex ownership of Unix transport queues, receive buffers, endpoint state, and the abstract socket namespace. Require the endpoint lock in helpers that assume it and take the existing rights-transfer test's queue snapshot under the queue lock.

Construct the abstract namespace as a fresh value so initialization does not require locking an unpublished object. Preserve weak socket ownership and document the callback, teardown, and save/restore phases that cannot be expressed as unconditional field guards.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Check existing task and signal locking contracts
source.body:
Require callers of the locked stop, ptrace, exit and wait helpers to
hold the signal-handler or TaskSet mutex that the helper uses. Check
that accesses to group-stop state and the termination signal use the
same locks as their writers.

A task and its thread group share a TaskSet. Declare that relationship
for checklocks, and document the synchronous callbacks and list members
whose owning lock the analyzer cannot infer.

prs.title: Keep metric field lookup nosplit
prs.head: f5f0270289147db0614fd2eadc1ed15dcb652f81

items.body: @EtiennePerot could you please TAL as the author of the commits mentioned in the description? I discovered this while investigating failures in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/14502.
@konstantin-s-bogom mind having a look here?
@EtiennePerot could you please take a look? once this lands I will put up another PR to fix the gap in checkescape that admitted this use of maps under nosplit.

> For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

no, things are getting *slower*. the implementation is going from using maps to using open-coded binary search, but that is what's needed here to preserve `nosplit`.
Great, ty! Once this lands I'll send the checkescape fixes that catch the map use in nosplit.

Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

The commit message now explicitly states that the original paired ARM64 measurement showed lookup slowing from about 6.7 ns/op with a map to 12.5 ns/op with binary search, to preserve nosplit behavior.

Field lookup tests pass normally and with the race detector; Nogo and formatting also pass. The full ARM64 metric suite still hits the duration-bucketer failure covered by #14359, which I reproduced on current master as well. All builds and tests ran in Docker.

Assisted-by: Codex

Thanks for finding this out. I still think we can do better here, especially for large-cardinality metrics (e.g. syscall counters). Will work on that on my own, but approving anyway here though this might race.
Any idea why 48?

48 comes from [79b38029d](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/79b38029d), whose commit message reports that linear search was faster than both map and binary search through 48 values. Added that direct citation to the comment in 13e28b4f1. This preserves the existing cutoff; I haven't remeasured the crossover with the current toolchain.

Assisted-by: Codex

Hoisted `targetAddr` before the binary-search loop in 13e28b4f1.

Assisted-by: Codex

Changed in 13e28b4f1: allocate `valuesSorted` at its final length, fill it with the original declaration indices, and sort in place with `slices.SortFunc`. The uniqueness check now uses `map[string]struct{}`.

Assisted-by: Codex

Minor nit on this comment: `valueIndices` is local to `NewField` and does not escape `NewField`. What ensures `v` escapes to the heap is that `allowedValues` (and `valuesSorted`) are stored into the returned `Field` struct, which callers assign to package-level vars or long-lived metric objects. For small fields ($\le 48$), `valuesSorted` is not constructed and `valueIndices` is dropped, but `v` is still retained in `Field.values`.

Changed construction to retain the pointers in the preallocated sorted slice and updated the comment in 13e28b4f1. One subtlety: a map can remain local while pointer values stored in it escape; Go 1.26.3's [map0 test](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_map.go#L13-L22) demonstrates this. Indexed slice stores likewise make the pointees escape ([slice6](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_slice.go#L62-L68)), preserving stable heap addresses here. Small fields only use pointer equality.

Assisted-by: Codex

prs.title: tcp: forward SYN in TIME_WAIT to the protocol handler
prs.head: e503a89e87b363812834ccaa96eb503446490faa

items.body:
Thanks for the fix — I verified it against the reproducer from #15013: with this change applied to the `go` branch
  (v0.0.0-20260925204757-f6e2c02e9739), all three tests pass under -race, and our own netstack tests pass with the default 60
  s TIME_WAIT.

  One small note: the default handler's return value is ignored in the reuseTW path. In the normal delivery path, a default
  handler that returns false leads to a RST (unknown destination); here such a SYN would be dropped silently. tcp.Forwarder
  always returns true, so it doesn't affect the forwarder case, but it may be worth either honouring the result (e.g.
  replying with RST when it returns false) or noting in a comment why it's safe to ignore.

Thanks, you were right. The reuseTW closure dropped the handler result, and Forwarder.HandlePacket returns false for anything that is not a bare SYN, so a SYN-ACK with a higher sequence number in TIME_WAIT was dropped without a reply. I pushed a follow-up commit that sends a RST in that case, as nic.DeliverTransportPacket does, plus an e2e test for it. The test fails without the change and the //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/... tests pass with it.

I ran into this issue in Lima and tested the fix together with different workarounds, but nothing really comes close to this so really hope someone from Google can review and merge!

Claude's writeup below:

---

A downstream data point for this change, measured. gvisor-tap-vsock accepts all TCP through `tcp.Forwarder`, and Lima runs it in-process for every `vmType: vz` VM on macOS (the default network), so a guest that makes short connections to a host service that closes first hits #15013 within seconds: the guest reuses the source port, and `connect()` hangs until gVisor's 60 s TIME_WAIT runs out (7–68 s, by how much is left).

I backported both commits of this PR onto the gVisor that Lima 2.1.3 vendors (`a174eb65023f`, through gvisor-tap-vsock v0.8.9). The PR's non-test diff (the `stack.go` getter and the `connect.go` hunk, 36 lines) applies there with `patch -p1` at line offsets only. Then I built Lima v2.1.3 with and without it (`replace gvisor.dev/gvisor`) and ran both on the same VM (Fedora 44 guest, kernel 6.19, default sysctls; macOS host). The reproducer from #15013 fails on stock `a174eb65023f` and passes with the backport under `-race`.

| guest→host, host closes first | without | with this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 workers × 500 connections, three runs | 8, 10, 8 stalls of ~68 s | 0 connects over 1 s, max 7 ms |
| 4 workers × 5,000, unthrottled | 48.6 conn/s, 24 stalls of ~68 s, 412 s | 8,032 conn/s, 0 over 1 s, max 10 ms, 2.5 s |
| 1 worker at 10 conn/s, 5 min | 12 stalls (three of ~68 s) | 0 over 1 s, max 15 ms |
| SYNs that reopened a 4-tuple still in TIME_WAIT | 62, every one stalled | 9,506, every one answered |

`TCP.ForwardMaxInFlightDrop` stayed 0 in every run. With the patch, `CurrentConnected` still reached 22,784 (TIME_WAIT endpoints), so TIME_WAIT is kept and only the reopen changes. The client saw no errors, and `ResetsSent` didn't move.

For contrast, the workaround from the issue (a 1 s `TCPTimeWaitTimeoutOption`, set in gvisor-tap-vsock's `createStack`) on the same workloads: 8 stalls per 8 × 500 run and 24 in the 4 × 5,000 run, each ~1.04 s, which is the guest's first SYN retransmission. It shortens the stall but doesn't remove it. This PR removes it.

Earlier, unpatched, on the same setup: one worker at only 2 conn/s stalled ~68 s four times in 15 minutes, and aborting from the guest (`SO_LINGER {1,0}`, so gVisor never enters TIME_WAIT) gave 0 stalls in 20,000 connections. Full record: https://github.com/twistco/foldyard/blob/07a824b680482e727f3c41e3b4212dcd6c0ec1b1/docs/lima-usernet-freeze.md

AI disclosure: Claude (Claude Code) did the backport, the builds, the runs and this write-up.

source.title: test: skip agent tool call tests until the netstack TIME_WAIT fix
source.body:
Skip `TestAgent_ToolCall` and `TestEditMessageCancelsToolCallsOnAgent` until #30471 lands.

The agent's gVisor netstack accepts connections through `tcp.Forwarder` and has no listening endpoint, so it drops a SYN that reuses a source port it still holds in TIME_WAIT (google/gvisor#15013). Agent API requests open a new connection each and the agent closes first, so a client that reuses a port within 60s hangs for about 63s. Both tests make enough requests to one agent to hit it (CODAGT-1336, CODAGT-1331). The same stall was reproduced against a production agent on dogfood, so this is a product bug, tracked in PLAT-717.

#30471 removes these skips. It pins coder/gvisor to a cherry-pick of google/gvisor#15019, an open PR from an outside contributor that no gVisor maintainer has reviewed, and adds a deterministic regression test.

source.title: fix: forward TIME_WAIT reopen SYNs to the agent netstack's forwarder
source.body:
The workspace agent's tailnet netstack accepts TCP through `tcp.Forwarder` and has no gVisor listening endpoint. gVisor only delivers a SYN that reopens a 4-tuple in TIME_WAIT to a listening endpoint, so it dropped the SYN and every retransmit until TIME_WAIT expired, and the client's dial hung for up to about 63s (google/gvisor#15013). The agent holds TIME_WAIT whenever it closes first, which is every agent API request, and any forwarded port whose server closes first.

This bumps the gVisor fork to coder/gvisor@e31c917bd99f, the head of draft coder/gvisor#4. That branch is based on google/gvisor#15019, an open PR from an outside contributor that no gVisor maintainer has reviewed, plus our fixes for a duplicate or stale SYN queued behind the reopening SYN and for a SYN-ACK that ended TIME_WAIT. This PR also adds a tailnet test that reopens a connection from the same source port after the agent closed it, a test of those fork-only behaviors (`tailnet/timewait_test.go`) so a pin bump that drops them fails CI, and re-enables the two tests that #30465 skips.

This covers the reopen RFC 1122 allows, a SYN above the old connection's `RcvNxt`. A reopening SYN at or below it still waits out TIME_WAIT, with or without this change. PLAT-717 tracks that.

The fix only takes effect on upgraded agents.

**Merge order:** this PR pins `e31c917bd99f`, the unmerged head of coder/gvisor#4. coder/gvisor only allows squash merges, so re-bump `go.mod` to the squash commit of coder/gvisor#4 before merging this PR, as main does for coder/gvisor#3 (`7a658db7b714`).

Fixes CODAGT-1331, CODAGT-1336
Part of PLAT-717

<details>
<summary>Evidence and decisions</summary>

**Reproduction**
- `TestConn_ReusedSourcePortAfterServerClose` fails 3 of 3 on the old pin, with the reused-port dial timing out, and passes 50 of 50 with the bump. A control using a fresh source port passes on the old pin.
- 3000 sequential `ListProcesses` calls through `AgentConn` against agenttest: 29 stalls of about 63s on the old pin, 0 with the bump. Every stall reused a source port the agent held in TIME_WAIT.

**Production (dogfood, one real agent)**

Test scenarios against an agent without the fix. The fix has only run in the test suite and CI, not on dogfood.

- coderd `listening-ports`, which the dashboard polls every 5s: 5 of 2617 requests failed with a 500 after the handler's 30s timeout.
- The app proxy, with a backend that closes every connection: 1 of 3000 requests hung 63.6s.
- `coder port-forward` to a server that closes first: 0.7% to 1.0% of connections stalled for 7, 15, 31 or 63s, the SYN retransmit times. With the client closing first there were 0 stalls in 6000.
- `coder ssh` is not exposed: one connection per process, from a new tailnet IP.
- Details are on PLAT-717.

**Alternatives considered**
- *Retry agent requests that get no connection, in tests:* rejected. It masks the bug, and chatd's own agent requests stay exposed.
- *Make the SDK client close agent API connections first:* not needed. It only helps against old agents, and not for apps or port forwarding.
- *Shorten the netstack TIME_WAIT:* rejected. It needs a tailscale fork change, and it shortens the stall without removing it.
- *Skip the tests only:* rejected as the fix, because this is a production bug. #30465 skips them until this lands.

**Not included:** gVisor's own tests. The fork is built from gVisor's test-free `go` branch; coder/gvisor#4 lists the results of running them against the pinned branch.

</details>

> 🤖 This PR was created with the help of Coder Agents, and _will be_ reviewed by a human. 🏂🏻

source.title: tcp: deliver TIME_WAIT reopen SYNs to the default handler
source.body:
Delivers a SYN that reopens a 4-tuple in TIME_WAIT to the stack's default handler when no listening endpoint matches it. Tailscale's netstack, which Coder workspace agents use, accepts TCP through a `tcp.Forwarder` and has no listening endpoint, so the SYN and every retransmit were dropped until TIME_WAIT expired, and the client's dial hung for up to about 63s (google/gvisor#15013). This covers the reopen RFC 1122 allows, a SYN above the old connection's `RcvNxt`. Other reopening SYNs still wait out TIME_WAIT; PLAT-717 tracks that.

The first commit imports upstream's forwarder e2e test and the three helper packages it imports, unchanged from `a5b10b7dd`, the source this branch is built from. `go test` allows one package per directory, so the test is in `e2e/forwarder_test/`, where upstream's bazel build keeps it in `e2e/`.

The next two commits cherry-pick google/gvisor#15019, an open PR from an outside contributor that no gVisor maintainer has reviewed, with its tests. The other commits are ours, each with the test for its change:
- When an endpoint closes, a segment still in its queue that matches no other endpoint is now delivered to the default handler, as in `nic.DeliverTransportPacket`. It gets a RST only if there is no default handler or the handler returns false. Before, a duplicate of the reopening SYN queued behind it got a RST, and the client's dial failed with "connection refused".
- The TIME_WAIT fallback redelivers the SYN through that path instead of calling the handler and sending the RST itself.
- The fallback only redelivers a SYN without ACK, as Linux only reopens TIME_WAIT for one. With #15019 alone, a SYN-ACK above `RcvNxt` ended TIME_WAIT for its 4-tuple and got a RST. Now it is dropped and TIME_WAIT continues.
- `handleTimeWait` delivers the reopening SYN before draining the endpoint's queue. Before, a stale SYN queued behind it reached the handler first and got the SYN-ACK, so the client reset it and connected only on its 1s retransmit. The listener path and upstream master have the same order.
- `TransportProtocolDefaultHandler` is renamed `TransportProtocolHandler`, so it pairs with `SetTransportProtocolHandler` as `TransportProtocolOption` pairs with `SetTransportProtocolOption`.

<details>
<summary>Testing</summary>

Nothing in this repository runs tests, so run them by hand. Every commit builds and passes its tests:

```
go test -count=1 ./pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/test/e2e/forwarder_test/
```

- `TestForwarderReopenAfterTimeWait` (from #15019) fails on the base and passes here.
- `TestForwarderReopenAfterTimeWaitDuplicateSYN` fails at the #15019 cherry-pick and passes here.
- `TestForwarderTimeWaitSynAckKeepsTimeWait` replaces #15019's `TestForwarderTimeWaitRejectedGetsReset` in the commit that drops the SYN-ACK, since that test expects the RST this branch no longer sends.
- `TestForwarderTimeWaitDeclinedSYNGetsReset` covers a default handler that returns false for the reopening SYN.
- `TestForwarderReopenAfterTimeWaitStaleSYN` fails without the `handleTimeWait` reorder and passes here.
- All of `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` and `pkg/tcpip/stack/...` from upstream `a5b10b7dd` pass against this branch in a scratch copy, including the existing TIME_WAIT tests, and the `-race` run is clean.

coder/coder#30471 pins this branch's head and runs the same cases in its CI in `tailnet/timewait_test.go`, plus a tailnet test that reopens a connection from the same source port after the agent closed it.

</details>

**When squash-merging**, use this message instead of the default list of commit messages:

```
tcp: deliver TIME_WAIT reopen SYNs to the default handler

A SYN that reopens a 4-tuple in TIME_WAIT was only delivered to a
listening endpoint, so a stack that accepts connections through a
tcp.Forwarder dropped it until TIME_WAIT expired (google/gvisor#15013).
Deliver such a SYN without ACK to the protocol's default handler when no
listening endpoint matches it.

When an endpoint closes, a segment still in its queue that matches no
other endpoint is also delivered to the default handler, and gets a RST
only if there is no handler or the handler returns false. handleTimeWait
delivers the reopening SYN before it drains the queue.

Based on the unmerged google/gvisor#15019, with these differences: the
SYN is delivered through tryDeliverSegmentFromClosedEndpoint, a SYN-ACK
above RcvNxt is dropped and TIME_WAIT continues where #15019 replies with
RST, queued segments go to the default handler before any RST, the
reopening SYN is delivered before the queue is drained, and the getter is
named TransportProtocolHandler. Upstream's forwarder e2e test and the
helpers it imports are copied from a5b10b7dd, with #15019's tests and
the tests for these differences added.
```

> 🤖 This PR was created with the help of Coder Agents, and _will be_ reviewed by a human. 🏂🏻

source.title: docs: the Lima user-mode network freeze — a gVisor TIME_WAIT bug, measured
source.body:
**Update 2026-10-23:** gVisor #15019 has been measured downstream: Lima 2.1.3 with it backported had 0 stalls in 35,000 connections (Finding 12). Reported on [google/gvisor#15019](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15019#issuecomment-6362902795) and [containers/gvisor-tap-vsock#757](https://github.com/containers/gvisor-tap-vsock/issues/757). foldyard's own workaround is in #130 (attribution users only).

**Draft: not for merging as is.** Kept here so the investigation isn't lost. The plan is to merge it alongside a workaround or an upstream fix.

New connections from a \`vz\` guest to your computer freeze for 7–68 s, in bursts that catch every caller of one destination at once. gVisor's netstack, which Lima's hostagent runs through gvisor-tap-vsock, drops a SYN that reopens one of its TIME_WAIT endpoints when nothing is listening ([google/gvisor#15013](https://github.com/google/gvisor/issues/15013); fix [#15019](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15019), unmerged). This only happens when the host side closed first.

- \`docs/lima-usernet-freeze.md\`: the capture, gVisor's own counters, the duration rule, thresholds (no safe rate), containers through pasta, the separate \`maxInFlight\` freeze (fixed in Lima 2.3.0), alternatives (QEMU slirp: 0 in 133,200), guest settings measured, and ranked mitigations.
- \`docs/lima-freeze-kit/\`: the scripts to re-run it.

Updated to match the compiler's [ASCII-space split](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/noder/noder.go#L334-L339) and [single terminal CR removal](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/syntax/parser.go#L169-L181). prs.title: Allocate process_vm test buffers per case
prs.head: e0f75c3ea08d7b74e1c757e9034285142c551309

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

> Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

In response to [your review](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15061#pullrequestreview-5399663055):

The original run was OOM-killed while enumerating tests, before any syscall case ran. It used a 300 MB scheduling estimate; I don't have evidence of the worker's hard memory limit. There are five parameterized tests, and [GoogleTest retains a parameter copy for each](https://github.com/google/googletest/blob/52eb8108c/googletest/include/gtest/internal/gtest-param-util.h#L402-L410). With two 32 MiB strings per parameter, that is at least 320 MiB of payload for registration alone, plus temporary copies.

After this change, all 50 cases passed in native and each of the two systrap variants with the same worker estimate. The actual 32 MiB syscall buffers are unchanged. The noncopying comparison also avoids duplicating and concatenating those large buffers while a case runs.

[Original run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/980d63fa-55b9-49d3-81d5-46ff7ca7cedb) · [After-fix run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/a20482e5-86cd-4bce-aa3c-1906c0a66d4a)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

items.body:
Could you weigh in on whether the added test is worth keeping? It exercises the public CLI with a controlled clang-tidy executable to cover nonzero exits and stderr diagnostics, but adds considerably more setup than the production fix.

source.title: Propagate failures from source lint tools
source.body:
Propagate failures from source lint tools

e362ccc8a added a lint summary that continues after individual checks fail. Calling each check in a conditional disables Bash errexit inside its helpers, so unsuccessful formatters, file selection, or installation can fall through to a successful result. Empty output from a failed formatter can be reported as clean, and --fix ignores formatter failures.

Run each check in an unconditional shell that stops on failures, including inside command substitutions, then collect its status for the summary. Preserve captured formatter status and diagnostics. Exercise these failure boundaries and continued reporting through the public lint entrypoint.

source.title: Recognize complete dependency license texts
source.body:
Replace phrase-based classification with complete license-text matching
to avoid combining independent notices. The old matcher combined Arrow's
BSD terms and OpenSSL's advertising clause into BSD-4-Clause [1].

Delegate text matching and identifier ownership to google/licensecheck
[2], configured with the complete LLVM exception [3]. References alone
do not establish a license grant. Keep the scanner's identifiers literal
so policy review sees the distinctions the detector can establish.

Regenerate the catalog for the new classifier dependency and the legacy
University of Illinois/NCSA grants in LLVM [3] and Kythe [4], previously
reported as MIT. Scope the corresponding policy exceptions to these two
dependencies and record their redistribution conditions, retaining the
existing source versions and archive hashes.

[1]: https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/e03105efc/go/LICENSE.txt
[2]: https://github.com/google/licensecheck/blob/16aaea366/scan.go
[3]: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/cb2f0d0a5/LICENSE.TXT
[4]: https://github.com/kythe/kythe/blob/a182743b6/LICENSE#L205-L251

prs.title: Declare the TLDK plugin build inputs
prs.head: 675d49b1c7a1b43ac0d2a5cbe4ab5d897ff44afa

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
/gemini review

## Code Review

This pull request replaces the implicit external source downloads of the TLDK/DPDK plugin stack with pinned Bazel inputs built via `rules_foreign_cc`. It introduces several patches to support musl libc compatibility, replaces glibc's backtrace with `libbacktrace`, and adds a test for stack unwinding. The review feedback highlights three key issues: a thread-safety race condition in `capture_stack` due to concurrent redirection of the global DPDK log stream, a potential out-of-bounds write in the backtrace patch's `trace_frame` callback, and a build compatibility issue in `toolchain.bzl` where standard environments might fail the strict compiler check.

This adapter is compiled only into `backtrace_test`. Its only caller is
`TestDumpStack`, which calls it twice serially; neither call starts DPDK
workers or runs in parallel. Production stack dumping does not use this
capture adapter. A mutex here would therefore add no protection needed by
the current callers, and would not serialize unrelated DPDK log writers.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

The bound follows from the pinned library's callback contract:
[`backtrace_simple` stops when the callback returns nonzero](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/backtrace.h#L125-L131),
and its [implementation stops unwinding immediately](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/simple.c#L83-L86).
Each dump starts with size zero. The callback writes indices 0 through
255, then returns 1, so it cannot enter again with size 256. I'll keep the
existing bound without a redundant precheck.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The strict check `toolchain.compiler not in ["gcc", "clang"]` can fail on standard environments (such as Linux with Bazel's autoconfigured toolchain) where `toolchain.compiler` is set to `"compiler"`. Since DPDK's makefiles and `rules_foreign_cc` already handle compiler compatibility and detection, this strict check is unnecessary and can be safely removed to avoid breaking the build on standard setups.

```suggestion
    toolchain = find_cc_toolchain(ctx)
```

The pinned rules_cc detector [returns `gcc` or `clang` for those compilers;
`compiler` is its fallback](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_cc/blob/21e14308c/cc/private/toolchain/unix_cc_configure.bzl#L290-L295).
Here the compiler identifier also selects DPDK's configuration through
`RTE_TARGET = x86_64-native-linuxapp-$(C_COMPILER)`. Removing this check
would pass the unsupported `compiler` configuration to DPDK rather than
make that toolchain work. I'll retain the explicit GCC/Clang requirement.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: Return ENOENT for missing original destinations
source.body:
Return ENOENT for missing original destinations

Match Linux's SO_ORIGINAL_DST result when conntrack has no matching connection [1]. Both the uninitialized-table guard and an initialized conntrack lookup returned ENOTCONN. The guard and syscall expectation introduced in b3ff31d04 prevented a panic but used the wrong errno.

Return the existing ENOENT error from both lookup paths. Extend the NAT reaping test to verify the original destination while tracked and the missing-connection error after reaping. Correct the syscall expectation, close its socket through FileDescriptor, and remove the unrelated raw socket capability requirement from this TCP query.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_proto.c#L254-L307

source.title: Bound TUN and TAP interface MTUs
source.body:
Bound TUN and TAP interface MTUs

The rtnetlink MTU setter added in 6dd4ef415 accepted any uint32 value for TUN and TAP devices. This also let callers enlarge the MTU used by the allocation guard in f51097051. Linux instead requires a minimum of 68 and a maximum of 65535 minus the device's link header length, returning EINVAL outside that range [1][2].

Give TUN-created NICs these bounds and check them before changing the endpoint MTU. Preserve the bounds when moving the NIC to another stack. Zero-valued NIC options remain unrestricted, preserving the policies of other link endpoints.

Exercise both rtnetlink setters for TUN and TAP at the valid boundaries and immediately outside them, including a high-bit value. Check that rejected requests preserve the MTU and that NIC moves preserve the bounds. These are interface configuration limits; the oversized-write allocation contract is unchanged.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/drivers/net/tun.c#L1372
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/core/dev.c#L8637

prs.title: Honor committed memory allocation requests
prs.head: 36900f03504f22a8a89271d95f9beaa172f9d233

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
/gemini review

## Code Review

This pull request updates the memory allocation logic in `pkg/sentry/pgalloc` to support committing allocated memory ranges under `AllocateAndCommit` mode. It replaces manual zeroing and huge page touching with a unified chunk-based iteration using `safemem.Zero`, handles bus errors by translating them to `linuxerr.ENOMEM`, and adds a comprehensive unit test `TestAllocateAndCommit` to verify these behaviors. I have no feedback to provide as there are no review comments.

[🤖] 1 issue found:

- **[minor · performance]** Zeroing recycled pages via safemem.Zero slows Allocate up to 14% (`pkg/sentry/pgalloc/pgalloc.go:708`, inline)

[🤖] Review agent has no findings.

Thanks for adding the `REP; STOSQ` ERMS path in `pkg/safecopy/memclr_amd64.s` and the multi-page fault test. That resolves the performance issue from the previous review.

I reran `BenchmarkAllocateRecycled` on the Intel Xeon @ 2.80 GHz (16 alternating pinned runs per side, `-c opt`, Mann-Whitney U test) comparing the merge-base (`fc82ffe54827`) against `9b469b192862`:

| Case | Base | Head | Delta | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4K/hot | 319.1 ns | 327.8 ns | +2.73% | <0.001 |
| 64K/hot | 2.63 µs | 2.64 µs | +0.51% | 0.007 |
| 2M/hot | 105.1 µs | 105.9 µs | +0.81% | 0.17 |
| 4K/cold | 1029.5 ns | 1039.5 ns | +0.97% | 0.008 |
| 64K/cold | 8.46 µs | 8.42 µs | -0.51% | 0.21 |
| 2M/cold | 236.2 µs | 238.0 µs | +0.77% | 0.12 |

The cold 64 KiB and 2 MiB slowdowns on the Xeon are completely gone.

---
<sub>automated review agent</sub>

Thanks for measuring the allocator itself. The 14.3% regression for cold 2 MiB allocations is worth fixing. Recycled pages can lack backing, so replacing `safemem.Zero` with `clear` unconditionally would bring back the fatal SIGBUS this PR fixes. I’ll compare the base, this head, and a fault-safe fast path using your hot and cold cases, and post the benchstat results here. I’ll also check that a fault partway through zeroing still returns an allocation error.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

I used your first suggestion in 9b469b1928: safecopy now uses
`REP STOSQ` for ranges of at least 2 KiB on amd64 CPUs with ERMS.
The stores remain inside the fault handler's protected range. The
allocator now returns ENOMEM even when the first page clears and the
second faults; a separate test checks an unaligned clear with a tail.

I ran [your benchmark on one pinned AMD EPYC core][1], 16 times per
version. Hot 64 KiB went from 1.638 µs with `clear()` to 2.298 µs
with the SSE loop and 1.625 µs with this change. Hot 2 MiB is back
at baseline too. The 4 KiB cases still cost 1.72% hot and 2.92% cold.
The PR description has all six benchstat rows.

The AMD worker didn't reproduce your cold 2 MiB slowdown on the SSE
version. If the Xeon is still available, could you rerun the cold
64 KiB and 2 MiB cases against this head?

[1]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/892b217c-14c4-48ce-b3db-e414c9ba4777

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

The revision uses `GetKernelVersion()` to skip the short-length assertion on native kernels below Linux 5.16, following `EventfdTest.BigWriteFails`. The focused case passes on native Linux and both systrap configurations; the older-kernel skip is source-reviewed only.

The only public-tree reference I found to `IPV6_CHECKSUM_SETSOCKOPT_SHORT_EXCEPTION` is this test. It was introduced in b488df0a2 with a TODO referring to b/212585236. Is the variable set by an internal test configuration, and should removing it here be accompanied by cleanup there?

source.title: Preserve moved TUN devices across restore
source.body:
Preserve moved TUN devices across restore

The TUN save/restore support in 8bf3dc484 classified preserved NICs by
kind, but moving a NIC to another network namespace discarded that kind.
A moved TUN device was consequently removed during checkpoint. Its
restored close callback also retained the original stack and NIC ID,
rather than the destination chosen by the move.

Keep the kind when moving a NIC. Restore its close callback in the stack
that owns the preserved NIC, and remove the stale ownership fields from
the TUN endpoint. Extend the syscall coverage to move a TUN device
before checkpoint and verify its removal when the restored device is
closed.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

source.title: Restore pending NDP jobs at their deadlines
source.body:
Restore pending NDP jobs at their deadlines

IPv6 endpoints preserved by 8bf3dc484 recreated NDP jobs without
scheduling them. Routes, on-link prefixes, and SLAAC addresses learned
from router advertisements could consequently outlive their deadlines
after restore, and temporary address regeneration stopped.

Save each Job instance with its monotonic deadline and completion state.
Rebind its lock and callback on restore and rearm pending instances.
Restore NDP jobs through this shared mechanism.

Make ManualClock save its current time without live timers. The NDP
regressions save and load the full stack, then advance the new clock to
observe expiry and regeneration.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

prs.title: Skip memory usage scans while restoring checkpoint pages
prs.head: 3562ce1685038ecf0455cebfc1de40e2bace13f9

items.body: @tamird what's the motivation for this? are you hitting the race in prod? I recently fixed a usage-scan and checkpoint-creation bug in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16187. It might be simpler to just skip/pause usage scan while restore is ongoing (I thought we already did that) instead of adding so much complexity and letting them progress in parallel.

I haven’t seen this in production. I found it with an allocator test:
it makes an omitted zero page resident between two saved pages, then
calls `UpdateUsage` while `LoadFrom` is still restoring them. On
[master](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/b5043696-15c5-48dd-97e9-72125aa5cf5b),
the scan counted 8,192 bytes when only 4,096 bytes had been restored.

I took your suggestion and dropped the separate accounting copy and
lock annotations. The [revision](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/8cb774707423e9bce5656fff4f242459964523d8)
uses the same scan guard as `SaveTo` until `LoadFrom` has installed the
saved ranges. Background page reads can continue. The test also checks
that the next scan counts the omitted page.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

items.body: Can you do a similar trick as the prior PR to ensure this runs on its own one-shot thread that gets discarded at end of test?

Changed this to use the same initial-thread reservation as 962441d4e and leave the capability test's thread locked until its goroutine exits. Go discards that thread, so the test no longer restores capabilities or unlocks it for reuse.

The privileged AMD64 boot suite passes all 105 cases without skips, and Nogo passes for AMD64 and ARM64.

Updated the cleanup to match 962441d4e more closely: restore effective CAP_NET_RAW and return the thread to the runtime on success; leave it locked for disposal only if restoration fails. source.title: Build BPF with declared LLVM tools and headers
source.body:
Build BPF with declared LLVM tools and headers

BPF genrules used PATH clang and /usr/include, so remote compilation
required worker packages and cross builds used the worker's headers.

Compile BPF programs with LLVM's declared execution-platform tools,
target Linux UAPI headers and libbpf's helper headers. Keep the BPF v1
instruction set explicitly because the selected LLVM defaults to v3 [1].
Align the module versions required by LLVM. The supplier requires Bazel
8.5 or newer for its extension metadata API [2]. Leave Coral registered
for C and C++.

Remove the builder's libbpf-dev requirement. Record libbpf using its
BSD-2-Clause alternative [3]; its upstream notice requires a maintained
audit entry because the canonical classifier does not recognize it.

[1]: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/85ac56026/llvm/lib/Target/BPF/BPFSubtarget.cpp#L75
[2]: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/0b3c45f46
[3]: https://github.com/libbpf/libbpf/blob/f5dcbae73/LICENSE

prs.title: Don't count RACK-lost TCP segments as in flight.
prs.head: 00aaa82b9e9cda8dc25dbe1df6e07a56c68302c5

items.body: I'm also experiencing this. Any updates?

Here is data for this PR from a reproduction of [tailscale/tailscale#21946](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/21946), in which this PR alone ends the stall, and so does #16081 alone. Tailscale 1.104 turned RACK on in the netstack that terminates TCP for `tailscale serve`, Tailscale SSH and tsnet, and after a burst loss that takes the tail, the sender retransmits about two segments per RTO for seconds to tens of seconds. Through two real tailscaled v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), this PR and #16081 together also end it: 0.62–0.72 s per fetch with the tail and the loss probe lost, against 4.0–6.6 s as shipped.

[netstack-rack-repro](https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro) joins a sender and a gVisor client over an emulated 3 ms, 80 Mbit/s path. The sender is gVisor configured as Tailscale configures netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO, MTU 1280), or Linux kernel TCP for comparison. gVisor is the module Tailscale v1.104.2 pins (`a6f909f08a72`, "pin" below) unless noted, with only the PRs' non-test code applied. After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, gets a scripted burst loss; a loss-free fetch takes 0.30 s. Eight trials per cell, each on a new connection:

| sender | tail and probe lost | probe arrives | probe arrives, client without timestamps | hole mid-flight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pin, RACK on (Tailscale 1.104.x) | 3.54–6.03 s (15–27 RTOs) | 3.52–5.82 s (15–26 RTOs) | 0.30 s, but 4 of 8 unfinished at 120 s (0–9 RTOs) | 0.30–0.32 s (0 RTOs) |
| pin, RACK on, no GSO | 3.76–11.2 s (16–52 RTOs) | 3.54–51.3 s (15–245 RTOs) | 0.30 s, but 1 of 8 unfinished at 120 s (0–9 RTOs) | 0.30–0.33 s (0 RTOs) |
| pin, RACK off (`TCPRecovery(0)`) | 0.52–0.55 s (1 RTO) | 0.32–0.56 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.52 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.32 s (0 RTOs) |
| pin + #15432 | 0.64–0.66 s (1 RTO) | 0.32–0.65 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–1.22 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.33 s (0 RTOs) |
| pin + #16081 | 0.54–0.57 s (1 RTO) | 0.53–0.55 s (1 RTO) | 0.30–0.56 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.33 s (0 RTOs) |
| pin + #15432 + #16081 | 0.53–0.57 s (1 RTO) | 0.33–0.58 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.56 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.33 s (0 RTOs) |
| master `4777ee78` | 5.18–10.6 s (23–49 RTOs) | 0.30–11.6 s (0–54 RTOs) | 0.30–0.31 s, but 3 of 8 unfinished at 120 s (0–9 RTOs) | 0.30–0.32 s (0 RTOs) |
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 0.54–0.56 s (1 RTO) | 0.33–0.55 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.30–0.56 s (0–1 RTOs) | 0.31–0.34 s (0 RTOs) |
| Linux 6.18 kernel TCP, CUBIC | 0.60–0.65 s (1 RTO) | 0.30–0.39 s (0 RTOs) | 0.30 s (0 RTOs) | 0.30–0.33 s (0 RTOs) |

The burst: after the first 1000 packets of the response, everything is lost for 150 ms (first column), or until the sender pauses for 3 ms, so that the loss probe and what follows arrive (second and third); in the last column, 16 packets are lost and later ones arrive.

In some trials the pause came in mid-flight instead: later data arrived, as in the last column, and the fetch finished in 0.30–0.33 s without an RTO. That happened in about half the gVisor trials without timestamps (and in all 8 Linux trials, which lost only 10–80 packets), and in at most one trial in eight per gVisor row with timestamps (7 of 8 for Linux). In the two probe columns, those trials account for every RTO-free gVisor result with timestamps, and for every RTO-free result without timestamps except the recoveries from the probe itself in the rows with #15432 (0.34 s). Every RTO, stall and hang in the two probe columns comes from a trial that lost the whole tail.

Without timestamps, the sender takes no RTT sample from the ACKs of retransmitted segments, so during the crawl the RTO doubles at every expiry: in the unfinished trials it reached 102 s after 9 RTOs, with 20 segments retransmitted. The no-GSO row shows that the crawl does not need GSO; its 51.3 s trial followed a spurious retransmission in a warm-up fetch that left ssthresh at 340, so 494 packets were lost.

Two notes:

1. **With #16081.** #16081 stops RACK from starting fast recovery during RTO recovery, and in these scenarios it ends the crawl by itself. This PR still matters with it whenever RACK starts recovery from a delivered loss probe, where only the probe is SACKed above the tail, too little for the scoreboard's `IsLost`, so only `segment.lost` takes the tail out of the pipe. The reproduction shows it when the whole tail is lost and the probe gets through. Without TCP timestamps (Windows clients, by default), RACK can use the probe's SACK: #16081 alone started recovery from the probe in all 4 such trials and still waited for the RTO; with this PR it recovered from the probe in 3 of 5, in 0.34 s (in the other 2, RACK did not start recovery from the probe and the RTO fired). With timestamps, RACK's TSecr test discards that SACK (#16659); with that test fixed, #16081 alone recovered without an RTO in 0 of 8 trials, and with this PR in 7 of 8.

2. **The new tests and #16081.** On master + this PR (rebased) + #16081, every test under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` passes with `go test` (on the `go` branch export, not Bazel) except `TestRACKRecoveryAfterRTOTailLoss` and `TestRACKLossDuringRecovery`. Both reach RACK recovery through the fast recovery that RACK starts right after an RTO, which #16081 removes: after the ACK of segment 1 they expect segments 2–5 at cwnd 5, and with #16081 the sender stays in RTO recovery and sends segments 2 and 3. Starting recovery from a delivered loss probe instead keeps the test on this PR's code and off the RTO path. In an exploratory packet test, after the SACK of a probe for segment 10, this PR retransmits segments 1–7 at once, while master, with or without #16081, sends only segment 1. So such a test still fails without this PR. (Like a client without timestamps, that test's ACKs carry no timestamp option; with timestamps this path needs #16659.) I can write that version of the tests if it helps.

Rebasing onto current master: `resendSegment`'s `writeNext` hunk is already there (7c8d7811a), and `GetPacketWithTimeout`'s GSO check moved to `packetView`.

After RACK marks #2 lost, retransmitting it clears `s1.lost`. This
branch then counts #2 once, and the `HighRxt` branch below counts it a
second time. In this PR’s tail-loss test, the ACK of #1 opens a
five-packet window, but [only #2–#5 are sent](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/e771617b-851e-4019-a76e-f73015f02f74).
[Omitting the second count](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/e3b6733c-2ae1-4ac3-a4a8-93f4a7b9a126)
lets #6 go as well, with GSO both on and off.

Can the flight estimate distinguish a **lost original** from an
**unacknowledged tail probe** whose original might still arrive? The
[probe case](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/4a34011d-e824-431a-a00b-a35326e809ef)
has the opposite error: four transmissions are outstanding at a window
of 11, yet the next write sends eight new packets rather than seven.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: tcp: let RACK use the SACK of a retransmission when timestamps are on
source.body:
`rackControl.update` skips an ACK of a retransmitted segment when the ACK's TSecr is older than the retransmission. That follows RFC 8985, section 6.2, step 2: ignore a retransmitted segment if the ACK's TSecr "indicates the ACK was not acknowledging the last retransmission of the segment". But for an ACK that SACKs a retransmission above a hole, TSecr cannot indicate that. RFC 7323, section 4.3: "An `<ACK>` for an out-of-order segment SHOULD, therefore, contain the timestamp from the most recent segment that advanced RCV.NXT." So such an ACK echoes an earlier segment's timestamp even when the retransmission did arrive, and RACK ignores it.

A common case is a tail loss probe. After a tail loss, the probe is often a retransmission from the tail, and the receiver SACKs it, but RACK ignores that SACK, does not mark the lost tail, and the sender waits for the RTO.

With timestamps on, RFC 8985's pseudocode for this step, which applies the TSecr test to SACKed segments too, rules out its own example. In Figure 1, the SACK of the TLP retransmission of P3 is what lets RACK mark P1 and P2 lost (event 5b), and the SACK of the retransmitted P2 is what lets it mark P1's retransmission lost (event 7a). With a receiver that follows RFC 7323, both ACKs echo P0's timestamp.

This change applies the TSecr test unless SACK blocks cover the whole segment: a cumulative ACK's echoed timestamp does identify the transmission, and a SACK that ends partway through the segment does not show that the rest of it arrived. For a retransmission that is SACKed in full, it keeps only the minimum RTT test. Linux makes the same split: `tcp_clean_rtx_queue` applies its TSecr test (`tcp_skb_spurious_retrans`) to cumulatively acknowledged segments, and `tcp_sacktag_one` passes SACKed ones to `tcp_rack_advance`, which checks only the minimum RTT; `tcp_match_skb_to_sack` tags a packet as SACKed only when a SACK block covers all of it. What this gives up: the SACK of a delayed original that arrives at least the minimum RTT after the retransmission now counts as delivery of the retransmission. gVisor already accepts that without timestamps, and Linux accepts it with them. The change applies to every retransmission that is SACKed in full, not only the probe.

#16660 is complementary: it sends new data as the probe when there is some, even with the congestion window full, so that its SACK is not ambiguous. The probe still has to be a retransmission at the end of a transfer, as in the test below, or when the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds new data back. There this change is what lets RACK act on it, unless the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT (see Measurements).

#16600 changes the same TSecr comparison so that it works across a wrap of the timestamp clock. The two changes are separate but touch adjacent lines in `rack.go`, so whichever merges second needs a small rebase.

## Test

`TestRACKTLPRecoveryWithTimestamps` follows `TestRACKTLPRecovery`, with ACKs that carry timestamps the way a receiver sends them: the SACK of the probe echoes the timestamp of segment 5, the last in-order segment. Without this change, segment 6 is retransmitted only by the RTO, and the test fails; with it, segments 6 and 7 are retransmitted without an RTO. A second case SACKs only the first half of the probe: RACK must not use that SACK, and the RTO retransmits segment 6. It passes without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is skipped for a partial SACK. `TestRACKTLPRecovery` passes either way, because its ACKs carry no timestamps.

`TestRACKCumulativeAckWithOlderTSecr` covers the TSecr test that this change keeps: an ACK that cumulatively acknowledges a retransmitted segment and echoes the original's timestamp gives RACK no sample. It passes with and without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is removed.

There is no packetimpact test for this yet. One in `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go` could check the same case against Linux; I can add it if you'd like.

All tests under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` pass with this change, alone and with #16660. I ran them on this PR's base `f4c82a02` with `bazel test` on Linux arm64 (Bazel 8.8.1, all 25 targets, including the nogo checks), and with `go test` on the `go` branch export on macOS, where `pkg/test/testutil` does not build, so I cut it down to the `Poll` helpers these tests use. The first version of this change also passed on master `4777ee78` and `05154faa`. gVisor's checklocks analyzer (`go vet -vettool`) reports the same findings for the TCP package with this change as without it. I could not run `make lint`; I'm happy to fix anything presubmit finds.

## Measurements

These measurements are from the first version of this change. The revision changes only how RACK treats a SACK that does not cover a whole retransmitted segment, and a paired rerun with both versions found no significant difference between them (`results/2026-10-30/` in the reproduction).

Two gVisor stacks over an emulated path with a 3 ms RTT, plus up to 0.4 ms of seeded jitter that never reorders packets, and 80 Mbit/s toward the client. The sender is set up as Tailscale sets up its netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO). After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, loses everything after its first 1000 packets until the sender pauses for 3 ms; the loss probe and everything after it arrive. Each trial is a new connection. `a6f909f08a72` is the gVisor that Tailscale v1.104.2 pins. Reproduction and raw output: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.31–0.59 s, median 0.55 s | 2 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.32–0.55 s, median 0.34 s | 22 of 24 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 | 8 | 0.33–0.58 s, median 0.54 s | 1 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.32–0.54 s, median 0.33 s | 7 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 | 8 | 0.53–0.55 s, median 0.54 s | 0 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.54–0.58 s, median 0.56 s | 0 of 8 |

In the two trials without an RTO before this change, the burst ended mid-flight and later data was SACKed, so recovery did not need the probe. With this change, 22 of 24 trials recovered without an RTO. In runs of a build that logs each RACK decision (`run-rack-decisions.sh` in the reproduction; master + #15432 + #16081 + this change, 48 trials, two jitter seeds), 37 trials recovered from the probe's SACK, 7 did not need the probe because the burst ended mid-flight, and in the 4 that waited for the RTO, step 2's other test had rejected the probe's sample: its RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.14 ms.

With #16660, the probe here is new data, as Linux sends it (`tcp_send_loss_probe`), and all 24 trials recover without an RTO. Linux is not in this table: with the same drop rule, its burst usually ended mid-flight, so later data arrived and it seldom needed the probe. In 2 of its 32 trials (a 24-trial run and an 8-trial run), it lost the whole tail and recovered from the probe without an RTO.

With a flight this large, recovery from the probe's SACK also needs #15432: without it, the recovery this change starts stalls on the pipe overcount until the RTO, as the last two rows show; see #15432 and tailscale/tailscale#21946.

At the end of a transfer the probe has to be a retransmission, because there is no new data to send, so #16660 cannot help there. In the reproduction's end-of-transfer scenario, a 14,400-byte response (12 packets) loses its last 4 packets, and the probe arrives. The Linux row runs Linux kernel TCP as the sender, over a TUN device through the same path, to the same gVisor client.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master | 24 | 0.22–0.23 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 14 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 5 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change + #16660 | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 16 of 24 |
| Linux 6.18 kernel TCP, CUBIC | 24 | 0.03–0.24 s, median 0.03 s | 20 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081, client without timestamps | 8 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 5 of 8 |

The count varies more from run to run than between builds. With jitter seed 1 throughout, master + #15432 + #16081 + this change recovered without an RTO in 5 of 24 trials in the run above, and an instrumented copy of it in 11 of 24; with a seed of its own for each trial, it recovered in 15 of 24 in the benchmark runs below. In instrumented runs with three jitter seeds, master + this change recovered in 12, 18 and 12 of 24 trials, and master + #15432 + #16081 + this change in 11, 15 and 15 of 24 (42 and 41 of 72). So the differences between the rows with this change above look like run-to-run variation, not differences between the builds. #16660 does not change the probe here, because there is no unsent data. In every instrumented trial that waited for the RTO, RACK had rejected the probe's sample with step 2's other test: the probe's RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.25 ms. On this path that test rejected 61 of the 144 probe samples, and 141 of the 144 probe RTTs were within 0.4 ms of the minimum, the range of the jitter, so it is close to a coin toss. Linux applies the same comparison in `tcp_rack_advance`, but against `tcp_min_rtt`, which also takes the RTT of the handshake (`tcp_synack_rtt_meas`). The handshake's small packets cross the 80 Mbit/s link about 0.12 ms faster than a full segment, while gVisor's RACK minimum comes only from RACK's own samples of data segments; that may be why Linux recovered in 20 of 24. Without client timestamps, where the TSecr test does not apply, the result is similar: 5 of 8 above, and 38 of 72 in instrumented runs, with the same minimum-RTT rejections.

Related: google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081 fix the stall in tailscale/tailscale#21946. With them, when the loss probe gets through mid-transfer, this change leaves 22 of 24 trials without an RTO, against 2 of 24 without it, where the burst ended early (24 of 24 against 3 of 24 in the benchmark runs below). At the end of a transfer, it leaves 41 of 72 instrumented trials without an RTO (15 of 24 in the benchmark runs); in the rest, RACK's minimum RTT test rejects the probe's sample.

With real tailscaled, the effect holds. Through two `tailscaled` v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), with a Linux kernel TCP client and with #15432 and #16081 on the pinned gVisor, 5 of 8 fetches with a delivered loss probe still waited for an RTO (0.35–0.68 s, median 0.62 s); with this change and #16660 as well, none did (0.36–0.47 s, median 0.38 s). That run had both changes together, not each alone.

## Benchmarks

No benchmark in `test/benchmarks` covers loss recovery, so these come from the reproduction's `run-paired-benchmarks.sh`: each sample is one measured fetch on a new connection, 24 per scenario and build. Trial i of each build used jitter seed i, and the builds took turns trial by trial, so drift in the machine's timing affects them alike. `results-to-benchfmt.py` turns the fetches into benchmark lines; `rtos/op` is the fetch's RTO count from gVisor's own counter. `TailLostProbeArrives` is the scenario of the first table; `EndOfTransferTailLost` loses the last 4 packets of a 12-packet response; `TailAndProbeLost` loses the loss probe too, so recovery starts with an RTO either way; `HoleMidFlight` loses 16 packets mid-flight while later ones arrive. Raw output: `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-tsecr-fix.txt`.

```
$ benchstat "#15432+#16081=master-pr15432-16081.txt" "+this change=master-pr15432-16081-tsecr.txt"
goos: linux
pkg: netstack-rack-repro
                      │ #15432+#16081 │             +this change              │
                      │    sec/op     │    sec/op      vs base                │
TailLostProbeArrives      549.0m ± 1%   340.5m ±   1%  -37.98% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    221.00m ± 0%   21.50m ± 928%  -90.27% (p=0.001 n=24)
TailAndProbeLost          552.5m ± 1%   553.0m ±   1%        ~ (p=0.923 n=24)
HoleMidFlight             313.0m ± 1%   315.0m ±   3%        ~ (p=0.183 n=24)
geomean                   380.6m        189.0m         -50.35%

                      │ #15432+#16081 │              +this change               │
                      │    rtos/op    │  rtos/op    vs base                     │
TailLostProbeArrives     1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ±  ?  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
