```
geomean                             ²               ?                       ² ³
¹ all samples are equal
² summaries must be >0 to compute geomean
³ ratios must be >0 to compute geomean
```

At the end of a transfer, a fetch takes either about 0.02 s or, with an RTO, 0.22 s, hence the wide interval. With a jitter seed of its own for each trial, 15 of 24 end-of-transfer trials recovered without an RTO with this change, against 5 of 24 in the run in the table above. In the two scenarios where this change has nothing to act on, benchstat finds no significant difference.

source.title: tcp: send new data as the loss probe when the congestion window is full
source.body:
`probeTimerExpired` sends a previously unsent segment as the loss probe only while `Outstanding < SndCwnd`. After a tail loss the congestion window is usually full, so the probe is a retransmission instead. RACK treats the SACK of a retransmission as ambiguous and can ignore it: because of the TSecr check, or because the probe's RTT sample is below the connection's minimum RTT. Then only the RTO recovers the tail.

RFC 8985, section 7.3, says that the probe SHOULD be a previously unsent segment if one exists and the receive window allows, and that FlightSize can then exceed the congestion window by one packet until the next ACK. Before sending any probe, the sender MUST check that "there is no other previous loss probe still in flight", so that "the sender has at most one additional packet in flight beyond the congestion window limit"; `TLP.end_seq` records both kinds of probe. Section 9.3 calls this the one way RACK-TLP modulates congestion control: "one outstanding loss probe can be sent even if the congestion window is fully used". Linux does the same: `tcp_send_loss_probe` skips the probe while an earlier one is unacknowledged (`tlp_high_seq`) and, when unsent data fits the receive window (`tcp_snd_wnd_test`), calls `tcp_write_xmit` with `push_one == 2` and Nagle off, which forces out one packet past a full congestion window.

This change lets the probe send new data while `Outstanding <= SndCwnd`, so it goes at most one segment past the window, and records a new-data probe as gVisor already records a retransmitted one (`tlpRxtOut`). Without that record, a write while the probe is out could schedule the probe timer again, send a second probe and put a second packet past the window. With it, until a probe of either kind is cumulatively acknowledged (section 7.4) or the RTO fires, no probe timer is scheduled, so no second probe goes out, as section 7.3 requires. An ACK of data not yet sent is not acceptable (RFC 9293, section 3.10.7.4) and does not end the probe. `maybeSendSegment` still checks the receive window, and the probe still counts in `Outstanding`. When there is no new data, or the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds it back, the probe is a retransmission, as before.

Linux also skips the probe while `tlp_high_seq` is set, but it keeps the RTO's earlier deadline, and a write that sends nothing does not restart its probe timer. In gVisor such a write scheduled the probe timer again, and scheduling it disables the retransmission timer, so writes while a probe was out, retransmitted or new, delayed the RTO for as long as they continued. Now that no probe timer is scheduled while a probe is out, the RTO keeps its deadline.

#16659 is complementary: it lets RACK use the SACK of a probe that has to be a retransmission (at the end of a transfer, or when the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds new data back), unless the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT. This change avoids the ambiguity whenever there is new data that the receive window, Nagle and `TCP_CORK` let the probe send.

#16596 also changes the loss probe code: it changes how the ACK of a retransmitted probe ends the TLP episode. This change keeps a probe that sends new data in its own state, but the two changes touch the same lines in `rack.go`, so whichever merges second needs a rebase.

## Test

`TestRACKTLPSendsNewData` fills the initial congestion window and loses all of it with more data queued, then checks that the probe is the next new segment and that nothing is retransmitted. It then writes more data while the probe is unacknowledged and checks that no second probe goes out: the next packet is the RTO's retransmission of the first segment. Without this change, the first probe retransmits the last segment, and the test fails. If the new-data probe is not recorded, the write schedules the probe timer again, a retransmission goes out as a second probe, and the test fails too. `TestRACKTLPLostProbeRTO` repeats the lost probe on a manual clock and checks the RTO's deadline: with no ACK, with writes every 10 ms, with a duplicate ACK, with an ACK of data not yet sent, and with writes after a retransmitted probe, the next data is the RTO's retransmission of the first segment, one RTO after the probe. Without this change, the last case fails as well: the writes delay the RTO. The other TLP tests (`TestRACKTLPRecovery`, `TestRACKTLPFallbackRTO`, `TestNoTLPRecoveryOnDSACK`, `TestNoTLPOnSACK`, `TestRACKOnePacketTailLoss`) pass.

There is no packetimpact test for this yet. One in `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go`, with the window full and data queued, could check against Linux that the probe is new data; I can add it if you'd like. The existing packetimpact TLP tests send each segment before the probe timer fires, so the probe is still a retransmission there.

All tests under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` pass with this change, alone and with #16659. I ran them on this PR's base `f4c82a02` with `bazel test` on Linux arm64 (Bazel 8.8.1, all 25 targets, including the nogo checks), and with `go test` on the `go` branch export on macOS, where `pkg/test/testutil` does not build, so I cut it down to the `Poll` helpers these tests use. The first version of this change also passed on master `4777ee78` and `05154faa`. gVisor's checklocks analyzer (`go vet -vettool`) reports the same findings for the TCP package with this change as without it. I could not run `make lint`; I'm happy to fix anything presubmit finds.

## Measurements

These measurements are from the first version of this change. The revision changes only when the probe timer is scheduled while a probe is out, and how an ACK of data not yet sent is treated, and a paired rerun with both versions found the same RTO counts and fetch times within 1% (`results/2026-10-30/` in the reproduction).

Two gVisor stacks over an emulated path with a 3 ms RTT, plus up to 0.4 ms of seeded jitter that never reorders packets, and 80 Mbit/s toward the client. The sender is set up as Tailscale sets up its netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO). After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, loses everything after its first 1000 packets until the sender pauses for 3 ms; the loss probe and everything after it arrive. Each trial is a new connection, on gVisor master `4777ee78` with #15432 and #16081, which fix the stall that otherwise follows the RTO (tailscale/tailscale#21946). Reproduction and raw output: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.31–0.59 s, median 0.55 s | 2 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.33–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 24 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 | 24 | 0.32–0.55 s, median 0.34 s | 22 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 + this change | 24 | 0.30–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 24 of 24 |

On master + #15432 + #16081, the probe is a retransmission, RACK's TSecr check discards its SACK, and 22 of 24 trials wait for the RTO. In the 2 that don't, the burst ended mid-flight and later data was SACKed, so recovery did not need the probe. #16659 lets RACK use the probe's SACK, except when the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT (2 of 24 here). With this change, the probe is the next new segment, its SACK starts SACK recovery at once, and no trial waits for the RTO. Linux is not in this table: with the same drop rule, its burst usually ended mid-flight, so later data arrived and it seldom needed the probe. In 2 of its 32 trials (a 24-trial run and an 8-trial run), it lost the whole tail and recovered from the probe without an RTO (0.38 and 0.39 s).

With the gVisor that Tailscale v1.104.2 pins (`a6f909f08a72`), eight trials per row:

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 | 8 | 0.33–0.58 s, median 0.54 s | 1 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.30–0.35 s, median 0.34 s | 8 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 + this change | 8 | 0.30–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 8 of 8 |

At the end of a transfer there is no new data for the probe, so this change does not act there.

With real tailscaled, the effect holds. Through two `tailscaled` v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), with a Linux kernel TCP client and with #15432 and #16081 on the pinned gVisor, 5 of 8 fetches with a delivered loss probe still waited for an RTO (0.35–0.68 s, median 0.62 s); with this change and #16659 as well, none did (0.36–0.47 s, median 0.38 s). That run had both changes together, not each alone.

## Benchmarks

No benchmark in `test/benchmarks` covers loss recovery, so these come from the reproduction's `run-paired-benchmarks.sh`: each sample is one measured fetch on a new connection, 24 per scenario and build. Trial i of each build used jitter seed i, and the builds took turns trial by trial, so drift in the machine's timing affects them alike. `results-to-benchfmt.py` turns the fetches into benchmark lines; `rtos/op` is the fetch's RTO count from gVisor's own counter. `TailLostProbeArrives` is the scenario of the first table; `EndOfTransferTailLost` loses the last 4 packets of a 12-packet response; `TailAndProbeLost` loses the loss probe too, so recovery starts with an RTO either way; `HoleMidFlight` loses 16 packets mid-flight while later ones arrive. Raw output: `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-probe-fix.txt`.

```
$ benchstat "#15432+#16081=master-pr15432-16081.txt" "+this change=master-pr15432-16081-tlpnew.txt"
goos: linux
pkg: netstack-rack-repro
                      │ #15432+#16081 │            +this change             │
                      │    sec/op     │   sec/op     vs base                │
TailLostProbeArrives      549.0m ± 1%   335.0m ± 1%  -38.98% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost     221.0m ± 0%   221.0m ± 0%        ~ (p=0.969 n=24)
TailAndProbeLost          552.5m ± 1%   544.0m ± 1%   -1.54% (p=0.008 n=24)
HoleMidFlight             313.0m ± 1%   312.5m ± 2%        ~ (p=0.678 n=24)
geomean                   380.6m        334.9m       -11.99%

                      │ #15432+#16081 │              +this change               │
                      │    rtos/op    │  rtos/op    vs base                     │
TailLostProbeArrives     1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    1.000 ± 0%     1.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
TailAndProbeLost         1.000 ± 0%     1.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
HoleMidFlight            0.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
geomean                             ²               ?                       ² ³
¹ all samples are equal
² summaries must be >0 to compute geomean
³ ratios must be >0 to compute geomean
```

At the end of a transfer there is no new data for the probe, and benchstat finds no difference. In `TailAndProbeLost` the probe is lost as well, and every trial with and without this change recovers through one RTO, with no fast retransmit or SACK recovery; I have not found a mechanism for the 1.5% difference there. With four scenarios compared, a p of 0.008 is weak evidence, and separate, unpaired 24-trial runs found no difference (p=0.223; `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-probe-fix-unpaired.txt`), so I do not read it as an effect of this change.

On top of #16659 (`results/2026-10-28/benchstat-paired-all.txt`), benchstat finds no significant difference in any scenario: in these runs the TSecr fix alone already recovered all 24 `TailLostProbeArrives` trials without an RTO (19 from the probe's SACK; in the other 5 the burst ended mid-flight). In the run in the first table it missed 2 of 24; in instrumented runs of that build, every such miss was a probe whose RTT sample fell below the minimum RTT. With this change the probe is new data, and RACK applies neither of its tests for retransmitted segments to it.

source.title: wgengine/netstack: add TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK to turn off RACK
source.body:
Updates #21946

Since 1.104.0 (#21303), netstack's TCP uses gVisor's RACK-TLP loss detection. In the gVisor that go.mod pins (`a6f909f08a72`), two defects make recovery from a burst loss crawl:

1. `SetPipe` counts segments that RACK marked lost as still in flight. After a tail loss at most the loss probe is SACKed above them, too little for the scoreboard's `IsLost`, so the pipe stays at or above cwnd, and recovery sends almost nothing until an RTO. Fix: google/gvisor#15432 (open).
2. After an RTO, RACK's first loss detection starts fast recovery for the same flight. That cuts ssthresh to 2 and sets cwnd to 5, and with the pipe overcounted (1), each RTO then lets out about two retransmissions. Fix: google/gvisor#16081 (open).

That is the signature in #21946: about two retransmissions per ~200 ms RTO, for seconds to tens of seconds. It stalls TCP that netstack terminates, such as `tailscale serve`, Tailscale SSH and tsnet, while kernel TCP over the same path does not stall.

This PR adds an escape hatch until a gVisor with both fixes is in go.mod:

- `TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK=false` brings back the RFC 6675 SACK loss recovery that netstack used from 1.82 through 1.102.
- `TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK=true` keeps RACK on explicitly.
- Unset keeps gVisor's default, RACK on, because RACK off is several times slower on paths that reorder packets (#20893). If you would rather default to RACK off until the gVisor bump, that is a one-line change; the knob works either way.

tailscaled reads the knob at startup, from its environment: `/etc/default/tailscaled` on Linux, `tailscaled-env.txt` on Windows and macOS (see `envknob.ApplyDiskConfig`).

## Measurements

A two-stack reproduction: netstack configured as `Create` configures it on Linux (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO, MTU 1280, buffer sizes), over an emulated 3 ms, 80 Mbit/s path, to a receiver that offers TCP timestamps, as macOS and Linux do. After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB fetch, after 3 s of idle time, gets a scripted burst loss. The first two columns have eight trials per cell, each on a new connection; the third is one connection with five measured fetches. Reproduction and raw results: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | tail and loss probe lost | tail lost, probe delivered | five fetches on one connection |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1.104.2 as shipped (RACK on) | 3.54–6.03 s, 15–27 RTOs | 3.52–5.82 s, 15–26 RTOs | 3.5, 42.1, 47.3, 48.7, 50.4 s |
| `TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK=false` | 0.52–0.55 s, 1 RTO | 0.32–0.56 s | 0.54–0.56 s |
| v1.104.2's gVisor + google/gvisor#15432 + google/gvisor#16081, RACK on | 0.53–0.57 s, 1 RTO | 0.33–0.58 s | 0.55–0.58 s |
| Linux 6.18 kernel TCP, CUBIC | 0.60–0.65 s, 1 RTO | 0.30–0.39 s | 0.61–0.62 s |

The drop rule takes whatever a sender sends after its 1000th packet, so a sender with a larger window at that moment loses more: in the first column, Linux retransmitted 202–272 packets per fetch, netstack as shipped 35–58. In the second column the burst ends at the first 3 ms gap in what the sender sends. For Linux that gap usually came mid-flight, before the whole tail was sent, so later data arrived and no probe was needed: it lost 6–71 packets in 7 of 8 trials, and in the remaining one (trial 7), which lost the whole tail (263 packets), it recovered from the probe in 0.39 s.

With RACK on as shipped, recovery runs at a median of two retransmissions per RTO. On one connection the stalls grow, because the pinned gVisor's CUBIC also lets the first burst after an idle period grow far beyond the flight before it (fixed upstream by google/gvisor#15604).

A client that does not offer TCP timestamps (Windows does not, by default) turns the crawl into a hang: without timestamps, ACKs of retransmitted segments give no RTT sample, so the RTO keeps doubling. With the probe delivered, 4 of 8 fetches as shipped had not finished after 120 s (RTO backed off to 102 s); with `TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK=false` all took 0.30–0.52 s, and with both gVisor fixes 0.30–0.56 s.

## Testing

- New `TestTCPRACKKnob`: the stack's `tcpip.TCPRecovery` is `TCPRACKLossDetection` when the knob is unset or `true`, and 0 when it is `false`.
- `go test ./wgengine/netstack/` and `go vet ./wgengine/netstack/` pass, on `main` and on v1.104.2.
- End to end with real tailscaled (`e2e/` in the reproduction): two v1.104.2 nodes on a private tailnet, joined by the same emulated path, with a burst loss in each measured 2.8 MB fetch through `tailscale serve`, 8 fetches per row. With the tail and the loss probe lost: as shipped, 4.0–6.6 s; with `TS_NETSTACK_TCP_RACK=false`, 0.61–0.69 s; with google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081, 0.62–0.72 s.

## Follow-up

Once google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081 are merged, bump `gvisor.dev/gvisor` to a `go` branch commit that contains both. A bump without them does not fix the stall: gVisor master `4777ee78` still retransmits about two segments per RTO in the reproduction, 5.2–10.6 s with the tail and the loss probe lost. Its CUBIC fix, google/gvisor#15604, does keep the stalls from compounding on one connection (10.4 s, then 4.8 s per fetch, instead of 42–50 s), and the bump brings that too.

source.title: tcp: preserve timeout recovery until the outstanding flight is acknowledged
source.body:
After an RTO, RACK can enter fast recovery before the pre-timeout flight has
been acknowledged. A new SACK can also replace `RTORecovery` with `Disorder`.
Re-entering fast recovery counts the old flight against the reduced congestion
window again, stalling transmission until the next, doubled RTO.

Reproduce by dropping the initial congestion window and its tail loss probe,
then acknowledging the RTO retransmissions. The regression also delivers the
third retransmission before the second and exercises a real reordering-timer
expiry. Recovery should finish through ACKs, without another RTO.

Preserve `RTORecovery` in duplicate-ACK handling and guard both RACK recovery
entry paths, following [RFC 6582 §3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6582.html#section-3.2), [RFC 8985 §9.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8985.html#section-9.3), and [RFC 6675 §5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6675.html#section-5.1).
The guards act only after an RTO, while that recovery state remains active.
RACK loss marking and SACK bookkeeping continue; the existing ACK boundary
ends timeout recovery.

This change was written with help from OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, and I
reviewed it before sending.

Testing: On master `a9e9db4`, all three RACK cases fail on recovery state
without the fix, while SACK passes. With the fix, all four pass, including
25 runs each. Removing each guard fails its intended case while SACK passes.
The TCP and tcpip Bazel suites also pass: 25 and 198 test targets respectively
([GitHub Actions](https://github.com/AyoubAchour/net-switch/actions/runs/39496207361),
Bazel 8.8.1, Ubuntu x64).

source.title: wgengine/netstack: add TS_NETSTACK_ENABLE_RACK opt-out
source.body:
Since 1.104.0 (#21303), netstack's TCP uses gVisor's RACK-TLP loss
detection again. In the gVisor that go.mod pins, RACK's loss marks do
not reduce the SACK recovery pipe, and after an RTO, RACK starts fast
recovery for the same flight, with ssthresh 2 and cwnd 5. After a
burst loss, the sender can then retransmit about two segments per RTO
for seconds to tens of seconds, and for minutes when the client does
not offer TCP timestamps (Windows' default), because the RTO then
keeps backing off. That stalls TCP that netstack terminates, such as
tailscale serve, Tailscale SSH and tsnet, while kernel TCP over the
same path does not stall.

Add TS_NETSTACK_ENABLE_RACK as an explicit opt-out without changing
the default. Unset keeps gVisor's default, RACK on; true keeps it on
explicitly. Setting it to false brings back the RFC 6675 SACK loss
recovery that netstack used from 1.82 through 1.102, until go.mod has
a gVisor with the fixes (google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081).
Keep RACK enabled by default because disabling it is several times
slower on paths that reorder packets (#20893).

Test the default, explicitly enabled, and explicitly disabled cases.

Updates #21946
Fixes #22045

The purpose is to give contributors a baseline when syscall expectations

prs.head: 9c1aeb0686a60878ecb92d6fe7694324dfabebbe

items.body:
I compared the existing pointer, map, and slice state benchmarks on both
sides of this change. None of the six encoding/decoding cases showed a
statistically significant timing difference in this run; their median
allocation counts and bytes per operation were unchanged.

I also benchmarked `tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` with a nonzero
`Timestamp`, so this measures the old UnixNano hook against the new binary
codec through a real caller:

| Operation | Before | After | Change | Allocs before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Save | 9.710 µs | 12.207 µs | +25.72% | 80 → 94 |
| Load | 12.674 µs | 13.997 µs | +10.44% | 138 → 151 |

Allocated bytes increased from 5,624 to 6,528 per save and from 6,024 to
6,320 per load. The encoded message grew from 494 to 521 bytes. The time
comparison was significant for save (p<0.001) and load (p=0.015), with ten
samples per version.

Both binaries were compiled first, then measured in ten alternating
before/after pairs on one Linux AMD EPYC worker, pinned to the same CPU
with GOMAXPROCS=1 and Go 1.27.1. Each benchmark used a 500 ms duration;
two warmups were excluded. These are state-serialization microbenchmarks,
not whole-sandbox checkpoint timings, and the timestamp comparison does
not isolate reflection from the changed representation.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/003fd04d-7d4e-4f55-9a77-584d353c93ab)
retains all raw samples and benchstat output. All 22 benchmark actions and
benchstat passed. The parent failed afterward because cleanup named two
source files deleted by the candidate; the source tree was already clean.
The measurements were preserved and not rerun.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

> I compared the existing pointer, map, and slice state benchmarks on both sides of this change. None of the six encoding/decoding cases showed a statistically significant timing difference in this run; their median allocation counts and bytes per operation were unchanged.
>

> 
> Operation	Before	After	Change	Allocs before → after
> Save	9.710 µs	12.207 µs	+25.72%	80 → 94
> Load	12.674 µs	13.997 µs	+10.44%	138 → 151
> Allocated bytes increased from 5,624 to 6,528 per save and from 6,024 to 6,320 per load. The encoded message grew from 494 to 521 bytes. The time comparison was significant for save (p<0.001) and load (p=0.015), with ten samples per version.
> 
> Both binaries were compiled first, then measured in ten alternating before/after pairs on one Linux AMD EPYC worker, pinned to the same CPU with GOMAXPROCS=1 and Go 1.27.1. Each benchmark used a 500 ms duration; two warmups were excluded. These are state-serialization microbenchmarks, not whole-sandbox checkpoint timings, and the timestamp comparison does not isolate reflection from the changed representation.
> 
> The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/003fd04d-7d4e-4f55-9a77-584d353c93ab) retains all raw samples and benchstat output. All 22 benchmark actions and benchstat passed. The parent failed afterward because cleanup named two source files deleted by the candidate; the source tree was already clean. The measurements were preserved and not rerun.
> 
> Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

OK. So a real cost, but what's not answered yet is how much this is amortized on a real-world application checkpoint.

However, given that we already have something that works, that this would be a regression, and that building on this mechanism (which IIUC you are planning to do), perhaps it's worth looking at whether this can be solved without this overhead? Perhaps via code generation like the rest of the stateify package, perhaps with a generic function with a type switch (which IIRC will inline correctly on each type-specific invocation to effectively remove the `switch` so long as the types are distinguishable, we use this trick in https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/5dd59c99442c6692227bdff0e1f8f973d96ade07/pkg/bpf/input_bytes.go#L51 for example).
Yeah, I'm pushing to optimize this a bit.
If it finds other stateify runtime optimizations, all the better btw. Every millisecond counts in that path.

Updated in [bfeafd451](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/bfeafd451).
Type names, fields and codec dispatch are now cached at registration;
Save/Load no longer constructs an adapter for each binary-coded value.

The follow-up `benchstat` comparison uses the same timestamp-bearing
`tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` value for all three implementations:

```text
Measure               Original hooks   Initial codec   Revised
Save (us/call)                  8.066           9.351     6.881
Load (us/call)                 10.164          10.991     8.813
Save (allocs/call)                 80              94        68
Load (allocs/call)                138             151       125
Encoded bytes                    494             521       521
```

Relative to the original conversion hooks, Save is 14.70% faster and
Load is 13.29% faster (both p<0.001, n=12). Compared with the initial
codec implementation, they are 26.41% and 19.81% faster. The 27-byte
encoding increase remains.

The ordinary map-decoding control measured 324.9 ns/op versus 331.5 for
the original implementation (no significant difference, p=.682). It was
2.49% slower than the initial codec implementation (317.0 ns/op,
p=.008). An [earlier comparison](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/d67982e1-db7e-40c6-a307-52e95aa38215)
measured a 5.88% slowdown against that implementation; its cause remains
unestablished.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/91d7662c-227f-4afd-bdc2-e465c4f117e2)
used one Linux AMD64 worker, precompiled binaries, fixed CPU affinity,
and twelve balanced three-version blocks. The measured sources were
[original hooks](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/6500a6c00),
[initial codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/b27217132), and
[revised codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a8081ccb5); the
amendment preserves that implementation after rebasing. These are
focused
serialization measurements, not complete-checkpoint or application
throughput results.

Assisted-by: Codex

Updated the codec dispatch to use type switches while preserving
Register(Type). Explicit state methods take precedence, Type-only empty
structs retain their existing behavior, and binary codecs handle the
remaining registered foreign structs. Names and fields still come from
the existing type databases.

The comparison used the original hooks, the previous cached-flag codec,
and this switch on one worker, with 12 balanced blocks of the same
pointer/map/slice and ReceivableControlMessages benchmarks. Compilation
completed before measurement, with no fresh compilation during samples.
All versions use the same benchmark bodies; original to switch includes
the full codec change.

```text
                         Original    Cached flag    Type switch
Timestamp save (us/op)      9.5225       8.4035         8.2445
Timestamp load (us/op)     12.2540      10.6320        10.5390
Save allocations/op           80           68             68
Load allocations/op          138          125            125
Encoded bytes                 494          521            521
```

the cached-flag version across all eight benchmarks. Timestamp save and
load each used 96 fewer bytes per operation, with unchanged allocation
counts. Compared with the original hooks, timestamp save was 13.42%
faster and load was 14.00% faster in this sample (p < .001); none of the
six ordinary benchmarks showed a significant timing difference.

or proof of equivalent performance. The larger binary time format also
preserves zero values and numeric zone offsets. This version and these
measurements do not include BinaryAppender.

source.title: Allow libc thread creation in cgo filters
source.body:
Allow libc thread creation in cgo filters

The cgo seccomp policies allowed clone3, but their legacy clone rule
only accepted the Go runtime's thread arguments. The musl pthread_create
used by the static plugin runtime calls legacy clone with parent-settid
and child-cleartid flags and nonzero TID pointers, so that call was
denied.

Permit musl's exact thread flags in the Sentry and gofer cgo policies.
Keep the Go rule and require cgo for the additional libc rule. Exercise
the generated filters with both thread forms and reject process,
namespace and exit-signal variants in non-instrumented builds.

source.title: Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit
source.body:
Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit

Updating oom_score_adj for an exited, unreaped process could fail for a
nonroot caller: Linux makes the process's proc files root-owned after
exit [1], so opening the file failed with EACCES. The no-op-on-exit
handling added in 88f736992 covered ENOENT and ESRCH but missed this case.

Share the existing pidfd liveness check with the OOM-score helper and
ignore EACCES only after confirming that the process has exited. Preserve
the original error when the process is alive or its state is unknown.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/fs/proc/base.c#L1848-L1869

source.title: Restore original cgroup membership in tests
source.body:
Restore original cgroup membership in tests

Cgroup2Test moved the test process back to the mounted cgroup root after
migration instead of the group it started in. This discarded its original
membership. In a delegated cgroup namespace, the move could also fail with
EBUSY when the namespace root had enabled controllers, leaving test groups
occupied.

Save the original v2 membership before changing groups or controllers and
restore it during scope cleanup and fixture teardown. Report restoration
errors instead of ignoring them.

source.title: Validate netfilter query sizes and permissions
source.body:
Validate netfilter query sizes and permissions

67fcf4020 fixed the missing-table error that had stopped Syzkaller [1],
but request validation still differed from Linux. GET_INFO accepted
oversized buffers and checked their length before permissions, while
GET_ENTRIES looked up the table before checking the declared entry size.

Require exact request sizes before table lookup and check GET_INFO
permissions first, matching Linux's IPv4 and IPv6 paths [2][3]. Extend the
existing IPv4 missing-table regressions and cover the same size and
permission precedence for IPv6.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/49879#01a114dd-05ce-42c1-8321-2df04d84e781
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/69f80fef3/net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/69f80fef3/net/ipv6/netfilter/ip6_tables.c

source.title: Preserve XML test suites during collation
source.body:
Preserve XML test suites during collation

The per-case report collation introduced by d54df9b21 extracted test
cases by searching for XML delimiters. A report containing several
self-closing cases retained only its first case; self-closing cases
after the last explicit closing tag were also lost. Such reports can
come from the discovery fallback that runs the entire test binary.

Parse and combine complete test suites, preserving their attributes,
case contents and properties. Sum the report counts and durations and
retain the earliest timestamp. Parse all inputs before replacing the
output so malformed reports cannot silently produce partial results.

Keep the private collator separately testable with actual input and
output files, including mixed failure, skip and self-closing cases.
Include the runner tests in the existing unit CI selection.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Bind SYN cookies to the client sequence number
source.body:
Bind SYN cookies to the client sequence number

A duplicate ACK could recreate an accepted socket after the original
connection closed. SYN cookies added the client's sequence number
outside the hash, so the advances caused by both FINs canceled during
validation. The server then accepted a socket whose peer had already
finished closing.

Hash the client's initial sequence number instead. Preserve the cookie's
MSS and expiration encoding, and exercise duplicate closing ACKs both
queued behind the first ACK and delivered after the endpoint closes.

Assisted-by: Codex

items.body: i am not familiar enough with changes at PR, probably @nybidari can take a look

## Code Review

This pull request updates the TCP CUBIC congestion control implementation to comply with RFC 9438. Key changes include tracking the window at the start of an epoch with cwndEpoch, updating the Reno-friendly window estimate calculation based on received ACKs, and introducing HandleWindowRestart to manage idle periods. Additionally, comprehensive unit tests have been added to validate these updates. The reviewer suggested optimizing the cubicCwnd calculation by replacing math.Pow(t, 3.0) with direct multiplication t * t * t to improve performance on hot paths.

LGTM. This fixes a real stall: HyStart lowered `Ssthresh` before the slow-start check, so congestion avoidance started with `WMax = 0`. It also makes CUBIC epochs start at the actual window, which matches Linux `bictcp_update()` and RFC 9438 §4.2/§4.3. I traced the recovery, RTO and restart paths and found no correctness problems. `//pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` passes locally at the head commit, and the PR does not overlap with anything changed on master since its base.

Non-blocking nits:
1. Please cite the Linux analogues in comments: `bictcp_update()` (epoch init) on `enterCongestionAvoidance`, and `tcp_cwnd_restart()` / `CA_EVENT_CWND_RESTART` on the new `HandleWindowRestart` interface method.
2. Idle restart differs from Linux, which raises ssthresh in `tcp_cwnd_restart()` and shifts `epoch_start` by the idle time in `cubictcp_cwnd_event(CA_EVENT_TX_START)`. A one-line comment on why a new epoch is used here would help.
3. Comment cleanup: drop the reference to the old implementation in `TestCubicFastConvergenceStartsAtCurrentWindow`, shorten the `cwndEpoch` doc, and update "since last congestion event" in `cubicCwnd`/`getCwnd`.
4. The commit message doesn't mention that Reno now clears `SndCAAckCount` on idle restart. Please add a sentence, since it changes Reno behavior too.
5. Optional: before/after `test/benchmarks/tcp` numbers, and/or an e2e test for the `sendData()` restart call site.

**PR description / commit message:**
Please mention that Reno also gains `HandleWindowRestart`, which clears `SndCAAckCount`. Without it, stale credit could add several segments right after the idle-restart reduction to `InitialCwnd`. Also consider dropping the `<!-- codex-thread: … -->` marker from the PR body.

**Security:** No security impact found. The change is limited to netstack's TCP congestion-control arithmetic: no new host interactions, allocations or locks. Peer-driven ACKs grow the new ACK-driven `W_est` by at most about one segment per ACKed segment, and none of the new arithmetic can panic or reach NaN/Inf from untrusted input. The new `cwndEpoch` field is unexported and is zero-safe when restoring older checkpoint images.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Thanks for addressing all the feedback. The Linux/RFC references are accurate, the cwnd_prior initialization now lives only in the first slow-start exit, with a test assertion and no change in behavior, and the commit message covers the Reno change. LGTM.

[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Using math.Pow(t, 3.0) is significantly slower than direct multiplication t * t * t because math.Pow handles arbitrary real exponents and has substantial function call and computational overhead. Since cubicCwnd is evaluated on every ACK in congestion avoidance, optimizing this to t * t * t provides a noticeable performance improvement.

```suggestion
return c.C*t*t*t + max(c.WMax, c.cwndEpoch)
```
citation needed. did you benchmark it?

I got curious so I did, gemini-code-assist is correct.

```
                   │   pow.txt    │               mul.txt               │
                   │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
     X-20            13.670n ± 5%   1.912n ± 2%  -86.01% (p=0.000 n=20)
     CubicCwndX-20   12.625n ± 2%   1.934n ± 2%  -84.68% (p=0.000 n=20)

```

Replaced `math.Pow(t, 3)` with `t*t*t`, keeping multiplication by `C`
after the cube. Thanks for benchmarking it. The existing tests pass on
AMD64 and ARM64.

Assisted-by: Codex

Nit: shorten to one line, e.g. `// cwndEpoch is cwnd at the start of the current epoch (cwnd_epoch in RFC 9438).` The reason for `max(WMax, cwndEpoch)` is clearer as a short comment on `cubicCwnd` itself.

Shortened the field comment. The explanation of why the curve can start above WMax is now on cubicCwnd.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Please reference the Linux analogue here: this mirrors the `epoch_start == 0` initialization in `bictcp_update()` (net/ipv4/tcp_cubic.c), which also uses `K = 0, origin = cwnd` when `last_max_cwnd <= cwnd`.

Added the reference to Linux bictcp_update: the epoch starts at the current cwnd with K = 0 when cwnd is already at or above the remembered maximum.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: `WLastMax == 0` as a sentinel only matters for the first HyStart exit (RFC 9438 §4.10: `cwnd_prior = cwnd`). Consider moving it into the `numCongestionEvents == 0` branch in `updateSlowStart` next to `c.WMax = …` so the special case lives in one place.

Moved the initial cwnd_prior assignment into updateSlowStart's no-congestion-event branch and added an assertion to the existing HyStart exit test. A prior window recorded on timeout still survives the restart.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: "from last congestion event" is now inaccurate. Epochs also start at HyStart exit and idle restart, and `t` is relative to K. Maybe "computes W_cubic(t) for t seconds relative to K (RFC 9438 §4.2)".

Updated the comment to define t relative to K, and removed the redundant claim that every epoch follows congestion.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Linux handles idle differently: `tcp_cwnd_restart()` raises ssthresh (so the sender usually slow-starts back), and `cubictcp_cwnd_event(CA_EVENT_TX_START)` shifts `epoch_start` by the idle time (cf. RFC 9438 §5.8). Starting a fresh epoch at the reduced window seems reasonable given gVisor doesn't touch ssthresh here, but please add a short comment saying why, and reference those Linux functions.

source.title: Initialize CUBIC congestion-avoidance epochs
source.body:
Initialize CUBIC congestion-avoidance epochs

HyStart ended slow start without initializing CUBIC's growth curves.
After repeated loss, fast convergence could also start the curve below
the window retained by recovery. Initialize each epoch from the actual
window, while retaining the remembered maximum for fast convergence [1].
When an idle sender restarts with a smaller window, CUBIC restarts its
epoch if still in congestion avoidance. Reno clears SndCAAckCount so
ACKs received before the idle period do not grow the new window.

Replace the elapsed-time Reno-friendly estimate with RFC 9438's
ACK-driven estimate [2]. Preserve fractional growth and restore Reno's
full increase rate once the estimate regains the pre-loss window. Keep
that window across timeout recovery, and consume ACK credit only once
when transitioning between the Reno-friendly and cubic regions.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9438.html#section-4.2
[2]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9438.html#section-4.3

[rebased head]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/776b86bce2baa17457cb9375e8a15f8b437d5737

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

## Code Review

This pull request initializes the EndSequence field in the rackControl struct and introduces a new test, TestRACKInitialDeliverySequence, to ensure correct behavior with initial sequence numbers. The reviewer identified an additional issue where RTTSeq should also be initialized to the initial sequence number (iss) to prevent incorrect sequence comparisons when the ISN is in the upper half of the sequence space, and provided a code suggestion to address this.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Similar to `EndSequence` and `FACK`, `RTTSeq` is a sequence number field (`seqnum.Value`) in `rackControl` used for sequence comparisons (specifically in `updateRACKReorderWindow` to filter DSACKs once per round trip). If `RTTSeq` is left uninitialized (defaulting to `0`), and the connection's ISN is in the upper half of the sequence number space (i.e., `iss > 2^31`), the comparison `snd.SndUna.LessThan(rc.RTTSeq)` (which evaluates `(iss + 1).LessThan(0)`) will incorrectly evaluate to `true` on the very first ACK. This causes any DSACK received on the first ACK to be prematurely ignored. Initializing `rc.RTTSeq` to `iss` prevents this sequence comparison bug.

```suggestion
rc.EndSequence = iss
	rc.RTTSeq = iss
```

Thanks, confirmed. RTTSeq now starts at the connection ISN too. The
regression covers the first DSACK expansion, suppression within the same
round, and expansion after the round boundary for low, high and wrapping
ISNs. The original high/wrap cases fail; the corrected TCP/RACK suites on
both CPUs, focused race coverage and owning analyzers pass.

source.title: Initialize RACK sequence markers from the ISN
source.body:
Initialize RACK sequence markers from the ISN

Manual-clock TCP tests can transmit at monotonic time zero, tying RACK's
unset timestamp. Comparing packet sequences with a zero delivery marker
could then report loss before any delivery.

The initial DSACK round boundary also used zero. For high initial
sequence numbers, this suppressed reordering-window growth regardless of
the clock origin.

Initialize both markers relative to the connection's ISN. Cover initial
delivery ordering and DSACK expansion once per round with low,
high-half, and wrapping sequence numbers.

source.title: tcp: let RACK use the SACK of a retransmission when timestamps are on
source.body:
`rackControl.update` skips an ACK of a retransmitted segment when the ACK's TSecr is older than the retransmission. That follows RFC 8985, section 6.2, step 2: ignore a retransmitted segment if the ACK's TSecr "indicates the ACK was not acknowledging the last retransmission of the segment". But for an ACK that SACKs a retransmission above a hole, TSecr cannot indicate that. RFC 7323, section 4.3: "An `<ACK>` for an out-of-order segment SHOULD, therefore, contain the timestamp from the most recent segment that advanced RCV.NXT." So such an ACK echoes an earlier segment's timestamp even when the retransmission did arrive, and RACK ignores it.

A common case is a tail loss probe. After a tail loss, the probe is often a retransmission from the tail, and the receiver SACKs it, but RACK ignores that SACK, does not mark the lost tail, and the sender waits for the RTO.

With timestamps on, RFC 8985's pseudocode for this step, which applies the TSecr test to SACKed segments too, rules out its own example. In Figure 1, the SACK of the TLP retransmission of P3 is what lets RACK mark P1 and P2 lost (event 5b), and the SACK of the retransmitted P2 is what lets it mark P1's retransmission lost (event 7a). With a receiver that follows RFC 7323, both ACKs echo P0's timestamp.

This change applies the TSecr test unless SACK blocks cover the whole segment: a cumulative ACK's echoed timestamp does identify the transmission, and a SACK that ends partway through the segment does not show that the rest of it arrived. For a retransmission that is SACKed in full, it keeps only the minimum RTT test. Linux makes the same split: `tcp_clean_rtx_queue` applies its TSecr test (`tcp_skb_spurious_retrans`) to cumulatively acknowledged segments, and `tcp_sacktag_one` passes SACKed ones to `tcp_rack_advance`, which checks only the minimum RTT; `tcp_match_skb_to_sack` tags a packet as SACKed only when a SACK block covers all of it. What this gives up: the SACK of a delayed original that arrives at least the minimum RTT after the retransmission now counts as delivery of the retransmission. gVisor already accepts that without timestamps, and Linux accepts it with them. The change applies to every retransmission that is SACKed in full, not only the probe.

#16660 is complementary: it sends new data as the probe when there is some, even with the congestion window full, so that its SACK is not ambiguous. The probe still has to be a retransmission at the end of a transfer, as in the test below, or when the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds new data back. There this change is what lets RACK act on it, unless the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT (see Measurements).

#16600 changes the same TSecr comparison so that it works across a wrap of the timestamp clock. The two changes are separate but touch adjacent lines in `rack.go`, so whichever merges second needs a small rebase.

## Test

`TestRACKTLPRecoveryWithTimestamps` follows `TestRACKTLPRecovery`, with ACKs that carry timestamps the way a receiver sends them: the SACK of the probe echoes the timestamp of segment 5, the last in-order segment. Without this change, segment 6 is retransmitted only by the RTO, and the test fails; with it, segments 6 and 7 are retransmitted without an RTO. A second case SACKs only the first half of the probe: RACK must not use that SACK, and the RTO retransmits segment 6. It passes without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is skipped for a partial SACK. `TestRACKTLPRecovery` passes either way, because its ACKs carry no timestamps.

`TestRACKCumulativeAckWithOlderTSecr` covers the TSecr test that this change keeps: an ACK that cumulatively acknowledges a retransmitted segment and echoes the original's timestamp gives RACK no sample. It passes with and without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is removed.

There is no packetimpact test for this yet. One in `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go` could check the same case against Linux; I can add it if you'd like.

All tests under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` pass with this change, alone and with #16660. I ran them on this PR's base `f4c82a02` with `bazel test` on Linux arm64 (Bazel 8.8.1, all 25 targets, including the nogo checks), and with `go test` on the `go` branch export on macOS, where `pkg/test/testutil` does not build, so I cut it down to the `Poll` helpers these tests use. The first version of this change also passed on master `4777ee78` and `05154faa`. gVisor's checklocks analyzer (`go vet -vettool`) reports the same findings for the TCP package with this change as without it. I could not run `make lint`; I'm happy to fix anything presubmit finds.

## Measurements

These measurements are from the first version of this change. The revision changes only how RACK treats a SACK that does not cover a whole retransmitted segment, and a paired rerun with both versions found no significant difference between them (`results/2026-10-30/` in the reproduction).

Two gVisor stacks over an emulated path with a 3 ms RTT, plus up to 0.4 ms of seeded jitter that never reorders packets, and 80 Mbit/s toward the client. The sender is set up as Tailscale sets up its netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO). After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, loses everything after its first 1000 packets until the sender pauses for 3 ms; the loss probe and everything after it arrive. Each trial is a new connection. `a6f909f08a72` is the gVisor that Tailscale v1.104.2 pins. Reproduction and raw output: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.31–0.59 s, median 0.55 s | 2 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.32–0.55 s, median 0.34 s | 22 of 24 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 | 8 | 0.33–0.58 s, median 0.54 s | 1 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.32–0.54 s, median 0.33 s | 7 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 | 8 | 0.53–0.55 s, median 0.54 s | 0 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.54–0.58 s, median 0.56 s | 0 of 8 |

In the two trials without an RTO before this change, the burst ended mid-flight and later data was SACKed, so recovery did not need the probe. With this change, 22 of 24 trials recovered without an RTO. In runs of a build that logs each RACK decision (`run-rack-decisions.sh` in the reproduction; master + #15432 + #16081 + this change, 48 trials, two jitter seeds), 37 trials recovered from the probe's SACK, 7 did not need the probe because the burst ended mid-flight, and in the 4 that waited for the RTO, step 2's other test had rejected the probe's sample: its RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.14 ms.

With #16660, the probe here is new data, as Linux sends it (`tcp_send_loss_probe`), and all 24 trials recover without an RTO. Linux is not in this table: with the same drop rule, its burst usually ended mid-flight, so later data arrived and it seldom needed the probe. In 2 of its 32 trials (a 24-trial run and an 8-trial run), it lost the whole tail and recovered from the probe without an RTO.

With a flight this large, recovery from the probe's SACK also needs #15432: without it, the recovery this change starts stalls on the pipe overcount until the RTO, as the last two rows show; see #15432 and tailscale/tailscale#21946.

At the end of a transfer the probe has to be a retransmission, because there is no new data to send, so #16660 cannot help there. In the reproduction's end-of-transfer scenario, a 14,400-byte response (12 packets) loses its last 4 packets, and the probe arrives. The Linux row runs Linux kernel TCP as the sender, over a TUN device through the same path, to the same gVisor client.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master | 24 | 0.22–0.23 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 14 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 5 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change + #16660 | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 16 of 24 |
| Linux 6.18 kernel TCP, CUBIC | 24 | 0.03–0.24 s, median 0.03 s | 20 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081, client without timestamps | 8 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 5 of 8 |

The count varies more from run to run than between builds. With jitter seed 1 throughout, master + #15432 + #16081 + this change recovered without an RTO in 5 of 24 trials in the run above, and an instrumented copy of it in 11 of 24; with a seed of its own for each trial, it recovered in 15 of 24 in the benchmark runs below. In instrumented runs with three jitter seeds, master + this change recovered in 12, 18 and 12 of 24 trials, and master + #15432 + #16081 + this change in 11, 15 and 15 of 24 (42 and 41 of 72). So the differences between the rows with this change above look like run-to-run variation, not differences between the builds. #16660 does not change the probe here, because there is no unsent data. In every instrumented trial that waited for the RTO, RACK had rejected the probe's sample with step 2's other test: the probe's RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.25 ms. On this path that test rejected 61 of the 144 probe samples, and 141 of the 144 probe RTTs were within 0.4 ms of the minimum, the range of the jitter, so it is close to a coin toss. Linux applies the same comparison in `tcp_rack_advance`, but against `tcp_min_rtt`, which also takes the RTT of the handshake (`tcp_synack_rtt_meas`). The handshake's small packets cross the 80 Mbit/s link about 0.12 ms faster than a full segment, while gVisor's RACK minimum comes only from RACK's own samples of data segments; that may be why Linux recovered in 20 of 24. Without client timestamps, where the TSecr test does not apply, the result is similar: 5 of 8 above, and 38 of 72 in instrumented runs, with the same minimum-RTT rejections.

Related: google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081 fix the stall in tailscale/tailscale#21946. With them, when the loss probe gets through mid-transfer, this change leaves 22 of 24 trials without an RTO, against 2 of 24 without it, where the burst ended early (24 of 24 against 3 of 24 in the benchmark runs below). At the end of a transfer, it leaves 41 of 72 instrumented trials without an RTO (15 of 24 in the benchmark runs); in the rest, RACK's minimum RTT test rejects the probe's sample.

With real tailscaled, the effect holds. Through two `tailscaled` v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), with a Linux kernel TCP client and with #15432 and #16081 on the pinned gVisor, 5 of 8 fetches with a delivered loss probe still waited for an RTO (0.35–0.68 s, median 0.62 s); with this change and #16660 as well, none did (0.36–0.47 s, median 0.38 s). That run had both changes together, not each alone.

## Benchmarks

No benchmark in `test/benchmarks` covers loss recovery, so these come from the reproduction's `run-paired-benchmarks.sh`: each sample is one measured fetch on a new connection, 24 per scenario and build. Trial i of each build used jitter seed i, and the builds took turns trial by trial, so drift in the machine's timing affects them alike. `results-to-benchfmt.py` turns the fetches into benchmark lines; `rtos/op` is the fetch's RTO count from gVisor's own counter. `TailLostProbeArrives` is the scenario of the first table; `EndOfTransferTailLost` loses the last 4 packets of a 12-packet response; `TailAndProbeLost` loses the loss probe too, so recovery starts with an RTO either way; `HoleMidFlight` loses 16 packets mid-flight while later ones arrive. Raw output: `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-tsecr-fix.txt`.

```
$ benchstat "#15432+#16081=master-pr15432-16081.txt" "+this change=master-pr15432-16081-tsecr.txt"
goos: linux
pkg: netstack-rack-repro
                      │ #15432+#16081 │             +this change              │
                      │    sec/op     │    sec/op      vs base                │
TailLostProbeArrives      549.0m ± 1%   340.5m ±   1%  -37.98% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    221.00m ± 0%   21.50m ± 928%  -90.27% (p=0.001 n=24)
TailAndProbeLost          552.5m ± 1%   553.0m ±   1%        ~ (p=0.923 n=24)
HoleMidFlight             313.0m ± 1%   315.0m ±   3%        ~ (p=0.183 n=24)
geomean                   380.6m        189.0m         -50.35%

                      │ #15432+#16081 │              +this change               │
                      │    rtos/op    │  rtos/op    vs base                     │
TailLostProbeArrives     1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ±  ?  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
TailAndProbeLost         1.000 ± 0%     1.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
HoleMidFlight            0.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
geomean                             ²               ?                       ² ³
¹ all samples are equal

```

At the end of a transfer, a fetch takes either about 0.02 s or, with an RTO, 0.22 s, hence the wide interval. With a jitter seed of its own for each trial, 15 of 24 end-of-transfer trials recovered without an RTO with this change, against 5 of 24 in the run in the table above. In the two scenarios where this change has nothing to act on, benchstat finds no significant difference.

prs.head: 9e1d8226db095d6711bbb80be043856450f1f818

items.body:
Instead of adding this method, can we defer releasing the view to handle the leak in error cases. Something like:

```
view := pkt.ToView()
ok := false
defer func() {
	if !ok {
		view.Release()
	}
}()
....
checker.IPv4(c.t, view, checker.SrcAddr(StackAddr), checker.DstAddr(TestAddr))
ok = true
return view
```

I replaced the new AsView API with the existing ToView and cleanup.Make.
Each reader defers Clean immediately after obtaining the view, then calls
Release when returning ownership to the caller. This covers Fatal/Goexit
without a conditional cleanup flag. CheckNoPacketTimeout still releases
an unexpected packet before aborting.

The cleanup, TCP, dual-stack and context analyzer checks pass. A temporary
probe also reproduced the old leaks and confirmed cleanup through all
four real abort paths. The probe is not part of the change.

source.title: Wait for TCP receive timestamp readiness
source.body:
Wait for TCP receive timestamp readiness

Linux can return from SO_TIMESTAMP before receive timestamping becomes
active. TcpSCMPriority sent its checked data immediately and could
receive only TCP_INQ, failing the control-message ordering assertions.
Linux's timestamp selftest also waits for activation [1].

Exchange one-byte probes on the existing native TCP connection until a
receive timestamp arrives, retaining the enabled socket for the ordering
check. Bound readiness by one monotonic deadline and report the count of
untimestamped probes. The original ancillary-message assertions remain
the behavior under test.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/ce6f6cffa

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Match Nogo sources to compiler order
source.body:
Match Nogo sources to compiler order

Nogo appended embedded sources after a rule's own files, while rules_go
prepends them. Go object paths identify named methods by their position
in the type's method list, preserving compiler source order [1]. The
mismatched order could therefore attach an imported fact to a different
method. In one observed failure, Float64.Add received StateLoad's escape
facts and produced false diagnostics [2].

Use the public GoInfo source list for targets that expose it. For binary
and test targets that expose only archives, prepend each embed's sources
in the compiler's order while retaining the target's own files. Preserve
the existing proto and C-wrapper analysis scope and dependency facts.

[1]: https://github.com/golang/tools/blob/ea2f152dc/go/types/objectpath/objectpath.go#L718-L724
[2]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/0f8f9fff-f449-4154-88ae-5d8054fba75f

source.title: Avoid late checkpoint waits in tests
source.body:
Avoid late checkpoint waits in tests

TestCheckpointRestoreAnnotation started its workload before issuing
WaitCheckpoint. That API waits for the next generation after the RPC
arrives, so a fast checkpoint could finish first and leave the test
waiting for another checkpoint that the workload never requested.

Wait for the existing proc-fd response instead. The workload opens that
file before triggering its checkpoint, so the response remains tied to
the intended generation. Remove the same registration assumption from
two other test paths: their synchronous Checkpoint call already reports
completion and errors, and starting a waiter goroutine did not establish
that the server had registered it.

Keep the next-generation API used by runsc wait --checkpoint. Exercise
that contract directly with an already completed generation and the next
generation's error, using synctest to wait for registration.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Consolidate GPU driver preparation
source.body:
Consolidate GPU driver preparation

Installation and checksum commands used separate download and hashing
paths. Share one transfer that copies every byte, including final data
returned with EOF, and rejects failed transfers. Recognize absent
NVIDIA .run installers by HTTP status and continue validating the other
architecture after an expected missing installer.

Resolve the host checksum when selecting the requested driver. Before
removing an existing driver, require a successful host inspection and
PCI preflight, then download, verify and close the replacement
executable. Propagate the operation context through host commands and
distinguish a missing nvidia-smi from a failed installed-driver query.

Use the same host eligibility selection for installation and listing,
and replace complete output files so a shorter list cannot leave stale
data.

source.title: Consolidate GPU driver preparation
source.body:
Consolidate GPU driver preparation

Separate installation and checksum paths handled final reads and
transfer errors differently, and checksum validation stopped after the
first absent architecture. Unify the transfer so it copies all returned
data, reports failures and checks both architectures.

Resolve the publicly installable host driver before installation. Before
removing an existing driver, require successful host inspection and PCI
preflight, then download, verify and close the replacement executable.
Propagate the operation context through host commands and distinguish a
missing nvidia-smi from a failed installed-driver query.

Keep public installer availability beside each architecture's registered
hash. Eight ARM64 entries have known hashes but their configured public
URLs return 404 [1]. The corresponding driver ABIs remain supported.
Require HTTP 404 for declared absence so new publication and other HTTP
or transport failures remain visible. Reject invalid metadata before
making requests.

Use the same public host selection for installation and listing. Run the
read-only listing as the caller that owns its temporary output file;
Linux protected_regular rejects root opening that file with O_CREAT.
Replace complete output files so shorter lists cannot leave stale data.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/50538

source.title: Declare image contexts and CUDA helper builds
source.body:
Declare image contexts and CUDA helper builds

CUDA test images compiled their sample runners with a separate Go 1.25
Docker stage. The runners were outside Bazel's Go build and analysis
graph, and repository SDK upgrades did not update their compiler.

Build both runners with the repository SDK and package their static
binaries with the image sources. Stage that architecture-selected
context before Make hashes or builds either CUDA image, so helper and
SDK changes invalidate the image cache. The archive also supplies
declared inputs for remote image builds without invoking Bazel from
inside a build action.

Analyzing these programs also exposes a recursive mutex acquisition in
one runner: ExitCode called Done while holding the mutex that Done
takes. Release the lock before waiting, as the other runner already
does, and update both programs to satisfy the newly enabled analyzer
checks.

The ASCII image converter continues to use its separate Go Docker stage.

items.body: r? @nybidari

Really impressive and long-overdue cleanup, @tamird! Replacing `tcpip.Address`, `tcpip.Subnet`, and transport address/port pairs with standard library `net/netip` types removes a huge amount of custom prefix logic and allocation churn across the stack.

Given the scale of this change (166 files, ~9k lines diff), would you be open to breaking this up into a few smaller, stacked PRs? That would make review, bisection, and merging much smoother:

1. **`pkg/state` serialization support:** Registering `netip.Addr`, `netip.Prefix`, and `netip.AddrPort` via `registerBinary` and the tests in `pkg/state/tests/netip_test.go` can land as a standalone, zero-risk PR first.
2. **Pre-refactoring test cleanups:** The IPv6 control-message fixture bugfix (19-byte literal) and converting non-contiguous masks to CIDR in `stack_test.go` can also land independently ahead of time.
3. **Core Netstack Migration:** The remaining type alias switch and caller updates in `pkg/tcpip` and sentry.

> Given the scale of this change (166 files, ~9k lines diff), would you be open to breaking this up into a few smaller, stacked PRs? That would make review, bisection, and merging much smoother:

Certainly, happy to break it up.

> 1. **`pkg/state` serialization support:** Registering `netip.Addr`, `netip.Prefix`, and `netip.AddrPort` via `registerBinary` and the tests in `pkg/state/tests/netip_test.go` can land as a standalone, zero-risk PR first.

That's true, but kind of pointless because that code would also be inert until (3) lands. So I'd rather not do this artificial split.

> 2. **Pre-refactoring test cleanups:** The IPv6 control-message fixture bugfix (19-byte literal) and converting non-contiguous masks to CIDR in `stack_test.go` can also land independently ahead of time.

Makes sense, I'll do this.

> 3. **Core Netstack Migration:** The remaining type alias switch and caller updates in `pkg/tcpip` and sentry.

I think this will reduce the diff by less than 100 loc, fwiw.

I'll address the other comments of course. I'm on EU time right now, so these updates will come tomorrow.

Prefactoring landed:
- https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15770
- https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15771

This is ready for another look please!

Addressed invalid-address handling in both locations.

Assisted-by: Codex

LGTM! Thanks for addressing the feedback, adding the regression tests for `filterAddress` and `isSpecified`, and landing the prefactorings ahead of time.

The transition to standard `net/netip` types across the stack is a great milestone and significantly cleans up address handling and allocation overhead across netstack.

Indexing `addrBytes[i]` or `maskBytes[i]` inside the loop can panic out-of-bounds if `filterAddr` has a different address family or length than `addr`/`mask`, or if an invalid `netip.Addr{}` is provided (where `AsSlice()` returns nil).

Consider guarding lengths up front:
```go
if len(addrBytes) == 0 || len(addrBytes) != len(maskBytes) || len(addrBytes) != len(filterBytes) {
	return false != invert
}
```

Added the length checks before indexing, with an explicit case for an omitted IPHeaderFilter so existing wildcard rules still match. The regression covers invalid addresses, mismatched families and wildcard filters.
Changed this to `addr.IsValid() && !addr.IsUnspecified()`, so the zero value is correctly treated as unspecified.

source.title: Report state dependency cycles without recursion
source.body:
Report state dependency cycles without recursion

Return the dependency-cycle error even when the first incomplete object
only waits on a cycle, or a branch leads into a different cycle. The
recursive reporter could panic on user callbacks or recurse indefinitely
instead of describing the blocked restore.

After completion propagation, every incomplete object still has an
incomplete blocker. Follow one such blocker per object until a node
repeats, and report that cycle. Allocate traversal state only when restore
cannot complete.

Strengthen the existing deadlock checks to require the cycle diagnostic;
accepting any error had hidden the nil-callback panic.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

Exercise example network modes with a listener

The document-processing example's isolation test accepted both a
successful connection and a failed command. Its host-network test only
wrote a file, so neither test detected an incorrect network mode.

Replace both with connections to a listener in the test process. Host
networking must reach that listener; isolated networking must not.
Require the probe's distinct exit code so sandbox setup errors and
timeouts cannot pass as isolation. This also removes the dependency on
an external DNS server and netcat.

prs.head: 36555ddbd52fc854d391ced0f1833ce12ed2944b

items.body:
Restoring cheap registration makes sense: startup should not pay for field
metadata that is only needed by save/restore. The inline comments cover a
repeatability bug in the new test and the split ownership of registration.

Could the title and description describe this as deferring ordinary type
metadata work until save/restore in non-race builds? Validation still runs
there, and binary registrations still validate eagerly, so "Verify
registered types in race builds only" does not describe the full behavior.
Please also include the command and before/after startup measurements
behind the 0.3 ms improvement so the result is reproducible.

This is a source review; I have not run the repeated-test case.

Assisted-by: Codex

The registration test now measures only the calls made by `Register`,
and `registerName` is the sole writer to the name-to-type map. That
addresses both inline comments. Code LGTM.

Could you add the command and before/after measurements behind the
0.3 ms figure to the description? That would give us a startup baseline
we can rerun.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

This assertion fails when the test is repeated in one process with
`-test.count=2`. The Save/Load calls below increment
`lazyTypeFieldsCalls`, and nothing resets it, so the second run attributes
the previous run's metadata lookups to `Register`.

Please compare the counter immediately before and after registration, or
otherwise isolate the observation. More generally, could this regression
focus on registration not calling `StateFields`? The direct assertions
about both global maps couple it to the storage implementation, while the
generic round-trip overlaps existing state tests.

This introduces a second place that publishes entries into
`globalTypeDatabase`: non-race ordinary registration writes here, while
race-enabled and binary registration go through `register`. The policy
also has to be reconstructed from `raceEnabled` checks in `Register`,
`register`, and `lookupTypeInfo`.

Could we give name-to-type registration one owner and separate it from
metadata collection/validation? That would make the eager versus deferred
work explicit without duplicating the map update. The cheap path should
still avoid `StateFields` and reverse-map construction; binary types still
need their explicit metadata because they do not implement `Type`.

The race-only integrity checks are useful. The concern is spreading their
policy across the registration and lookup paths, not removing them.

source.title: tcp: reject ambiguous loss-probe RTT samples
source.body:
tcp: reject ambiguous loss-probe RTT samples

Tail loss probes bypassed resendSegment's RTT measurement invalidation. A
probe retransmitting the measured sequence reset its measurement time,
so a later ambiguous ACK changed SRTT and RTO using time since the probe.

Move the existing invalidation to sendSegment's retransmission branch so
all data retransmission paths apply Karn's rule (RFC 6298, section 3).
Timestamp-based ACK measurements remain independently eligible. Add a
packet regression covering the ambiguous ACK, echoes of either timestamp,
and resumed measurement when new data is acknowledged.

Assisted-by: Codex

So, an interesting quirk is that `archive/zip` is in this place in the import list because it internally gets rewritten to a different, hardened drop-in replacement for that package, which has a different import path that requires it to be in the second half of the imports list.

Another way forward here might be to create a "proxy" package for `archive/zip` at `//pkg/zip`, similar to the `//runsc/flag` package we have today. Could be its own base PR.

Check Go import groups with goimports

The Go formatting check accepted standard-library imports mixed into
nonstandard import groups. Use the pinned goimports in format-only mode
to catch these mistakes without adding or removing imports. Build and
run the formatter through Bazel, replacing the separate gofmt
installation and Go version lookup.

Run make lint and lint-fix through the existing Bazel builder, as lint-

Accept architecture-independent KCOV records

The KCOV test assumes every reported PC lies in the top 2 GiB of the
address space. gVisor encodes package, function and block identifiers
instead of instruction addresses, and Linux's address layout also varies
by architecture and configuration.

Check that coverage records are nonzero and fit within the mapped buffer.
Remove the unused constant that still describes the old 32-bit encoding.
The existing test fails before this change and passes afterward in both
instrumented AMD64 gVisor configurations.

source.title: Honor bound devices for IPv6 multicast selection
source.body:
Honor bound devices for IPv6 multicast selection

IPV6_MULTICAST_IF checked the interface recorded by a scoped address
bind, but ignored SO_BINDTODEVICE. A socket bound to a global address
could therefore select a conflicting multicast interface even after
being explicitly bound to another device.

Check the socket option binding as well as the scoped address binding.
Allow zero to clear the multicast selection without changing either
binding, matching Linux. Extend the existing syscall regression to bind
the device explicitly and check selection state after errors and reset.

source.title: Wait for native TCP timestamp activation
source.body:
Wait for native TCP timestamp activation

TcpSCMPriority expected a timestamp on the first packet after enabling
SO_TIMESTAMP. With CONFIG_JUMP_LABEL, Linux schedules netstamp_work to
activate packet timestamping asynchronously [1], so that packet could
arrive with only TCP_INQ.

Send and consume fresh payloads until native timestamping is ready,
using the existing timeout as a monotonic readiness bound. Retry only a
valid sole TCP_INQ record. Keep timestamp-before-INQ ordering, record
lengths, queue values and absence of extra records strict on every
response; malformed or reordered metadata fails immediately. Preserve
gVisor's existing optional timestamp behavior.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/fd73f4a66/net/core/dev.c#L2395-L2424

prs.title: Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs
prs.head: b143d86cb32a1eaa516324f52423b395a0123126

items.body:
Thanks for this PR! 

Linux uses Minshall's variant of Nagle where a partial segment:
- is sent if all the outstanding segments (unacked) are full sized segments.
- waits if there is atleast one small sized segment which is unacknowledged. 

My understanding is the change here waits for an ACK for both cases while sending a partial segment. That check isn't new, but now applies it to the tail of a split write. Previously the remaining partial packet copied the previous packet's flags which was sent and skipped Nagle. My concern is for the loopback cases with no offload or GSO and we enable nagle by default in runsc. Even with GSO, it still waits when only full-sized segments are in flight, where Linux would send it. 

Can you please add a test for an idle connection without GSO and verify whether the partial segment goes out without waiting for an ACK?

If it waits, I think the fix would be something like tracking the end of the last sent partial segment and holding only while it's unacknowledged (similar to linux).

> Can you please add a test for an idle connection without GSO

Regarding [Nayana's request](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15926#issuecomment-6295602307):

The earlier change incorrectly treated all unacknowledged data as a
reason to hold a partial segment. Linux's Minshall variant waits only
when an earlier partial segment is still unacknowledged.

The amendment records that segment's end sequence number, including a
partial GSO tail. An idle MSS-plus-tail write now sends the tail without
waiting for the full segment's ACK. Later small writes wait until the
partial segment is fully acknowledged; full-sized sends and
retransmissions do not replace that marker. TCP_CORK keeps its separate
hold.

The new regression covers idle and full-only outstanding prefixes, with
and without GSO, then partial and exact-end ACKs. All four cases
reproduce the old failure and pass with the fix. Both complete TCP
suites and the owning analyzers pass, as does canonical BUILD lint.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex, acting on behalf of Tamir Duberstein.

Internal presubmits were failing, all good now.
nit: this can just be `if seg.payloadSize()%s.MaxPayloadSize != 0 {` retransmissions never get here.

Removed the extra guard. The `SndNxt` bound already excludes
retransmissions. This also fixes fresh data released by the CORK timer:
that path assigns flags before sending, so it did not satisfy `newData`
and its partial tail was not recorded.

I added CORK expiry to the existing regression in both GSO modes. Both
cases fail before the change and pass afterward; the existing Nagle/CORK
controls, owning analyzers and buildifier also pass.

source.title: Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs
source.body:
Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs

With segmentation offload enabled, TCP's send budget can cover several
segments. Nagle compared queued data with that entire budget and could
hold full-sized writes until a probe timer fired.

Use the MSS to decide whether Nagle or TCP_CORK has enough data to send.
Send the full-segment prefix while retaining a partial tail for later
coalescing. Leave that tail unassigned until it can be sent, so a window
update cannot bypass the same decision. Preserve the existing exceptions
for short windows and writes that cannot be combined. Nagle permits full
segments while earlier data remains unacknowledged [1].

Exercise full writes and held tails with and without offload, using a
stopped clock so retransmission timers cannot hide a stalled write.
Complete requested checksum offload in the channel fixture so packet
checks can validate aggregate GSO output.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html#section-3.7.4

source.title: Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit
source.body:
Updating oom_score_adj for an exited, unreaped process could fail for a
nonroot caller: Linux makes the process's proc files root-owned after
exit [1], so opening the file failed with EACCES. The no-op-on-exit
handling added in 88f736992 covered ENOENT and ESRCH but missed this case.

Share the existing pidfd liveness check with the OOM-score helper and
ignore EACCES only after confirming that the process has exited. Preserve
the original error when the process is alive or its state is unknown.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/fs/proc/base.c#L1848-L1869
