Use rules_qemu for cross-architecture generators

Use the released rules_qemu module [1] and its public user toolchain for
cross-architecture seccomp generation. Register the four existing host
and target pairs and run the generator directly through the selected
emulator. Native generators and the fastbuild stub run directly.

Remove the Debian archive extraction and host-specific emulator aliases.
Audit the user toolchain's complete emulator archive family through
Bazel's repository mappings. Bind each archive to QEMU's upstream notice
[2], since the packaging repository's MIT license does not cover QEMU.

[1]: https://github.com/hermeticbuild/rules_qemu/tree/de0cdb392
[2]: https://github.com/qemu/qemu/blob/98b060da3/COPYING

prs.title: Restore metric tests to routine CI
prs.head: a52b53673b4b5d9585685592d9c188197bb7f520

items.body:
[🤖] 1 issue found:

- **[minor · concurrency]** Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race (`Makefile:269`, inline)

[🤖] **[minor · concurrency] Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race**

This change makes all three `make unit-tests` CI jobs run `//pkg/metric:metric_test`, but `TestMetricProfiling` fails intermittently when the CPU is busy, as it is during `make unit-tests`. `writeProfilingMetrics` (`pkg/metric/profiling_metric.go:645-647`) signals `doneProfilingMetrics` before it clears `profilingMetricsStarted`, so `StopProfilingMetrics` can return while the flag is still set. The next subtest's `StartProfilingMetrics` then fails with "profiling metrics have already been started". The race predates this PR and does not depend on the architecture; the exclusion removed here kept it out of CI.

**Suggested fix:** Fix the race before removing the exclusion, or keep `-//pkg/metric:metric_test` until it is fixed. In `writeProfilingMetrics`, capture the channel when the goroutine starts and clear the flag before signaling:

```go
func writeProfilingMetrics[...](...) {
	done := doneProfilingMetrics
	...
	sink.Close()
	profilingMetricsStarted.Store(false)
	done <- stats
	close(done)
}
```

Capturing `done` is required: with a plain reorder, the next `StartProfilingMetrics` reassigns the global while the old writer still uses it. The race detector then reports a race between lines 287 and 647, and runs panic with "send on closed channel" (100/100 runs failed). Verified: with the fix, 0 failures in 1,100 loaded runs and 220 race-detector runs.

<details><summary>Details (evidence, reproduction and test code)</summary>

**Evidence:** `StopProfilingMetrics` returns right after it receives from `doneProfilingMetrics` (line 748). `StartProfilingMetrics` needs `profilingMetricsStarted.CompareAndSwap(false, true)` (line 264). If the writer goroutine is descheduled between the send and `Store(false)`, a Start that follows Stop fails.

Results of `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=N` on a 32-core amd64 host ("paired" means PR head and head+fix ran at the same time):
- 32 parallel runs (bazel default): head 4/200 failed.
- Paired, 32 parallel runs each: head 32/400 and 14/400; fix 0/400 and 0/400.
- `--config=race`: head 9/40 and 20/80; fix 0/40 and 0/80 (the 80-run pair ran concurrently). No DATA RACE reports.

Every failure is `metric_test.go:1228: StartProfilingMetrics error: got 'profiling metrics have already been started'`, spread over six subtests. Runs pass when executed one at a time on an idle machine.

`TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop` (attached) restarts profiling 200 times right after `StopProfilingMetrics`. Paired under load, it failed 110/300 runs at head and 0/300 runs (60,000 restarts) with the fix.

The original #10045 failure is fixed: an ARM64 build of the test under qemu-aarch64 passes at head and fails with "did not panic" when the IsNaN check is removed.

**Reproduced with a test** (`pkg/metric/metric_test.go`): `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=300 --test_output=summary   (run concurrently with: <same command>; slot fix = worktree + scratch/max/fix.patch). Earlier runs used --runs_per_test=200/400 (existing TestMetricProfiling only) and --config=race --runs_per_test=40/80.` → Fails intermittently on the PR head under parallel load, always with 'profiling metrics have already been started'. Passes every run with the fix applied under the same concurrent load.

**Test code:**

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
index cb33abdd9..9f0a3586a 100644
--- a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
+++ b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
@@ -1430,3 +1430,34 @@ func TestMetricProfiling(t *testing.T) {
 		})
 	}
 }
+
+// TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop checks that StartProfilingMetrics
+// succeeds as soon as StopProfilingMetrics returns.
+func TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop(t *testing.T) {
+	defer resetTest()
+	if _, err := NewUint64Metric("/foo", Uint64Metadata{
+		Cumulative:  true,
+		Sync:        true,
+		Description: fooDescription,
+	}); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("NewUint64Metric: %v", err)
+	}
+	if err := Initialize(); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Initialize: %v", err)
+	}
+	dir := t.TempDir()
+	for i := 0; i < 200; i++ {
+		f, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, "profiling-metrics")
+		if err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("CreateTemp: %v", err)
+		}
+		if err := StartProfilingMetrics(ProfilingMetricsOptions[*os.File]{
+			Sink:    f,
+			Metrics: "/foo",
+			Rate:    time.Millisecond,
+		}); err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("iteration %d: StartProfilingMetrics: %v", i, err)
+		}
+		StopProfilingMetrics()
+	}
+}
```

</details>

Stop now clears the started flag after receiving the writer’s final statistics. The send is the writer’s last access to the channel, so an immediate restart can safely replace it. Fixed in a52b53673b4b5d9585685592d9c188197bb7f520.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: Restore metric tests to routine CI
source.body:
Restore metric tests to routine CI

Commit a30d5fc67 rejected NaN bucketer parameters explicitly, fixing
ARM64's panic regression in #10045. Remove the remaining unit-test
exclusion and ARM tag so routine CI exercises these tests again.

The profiling writer signaled completion before clearing the started
flag. StopProfilingMetrics could therefore return while a subsequent
StartProfilingMetrics would still reject the restart. Clear the flag in
Stop after receiving the final statistics, and remove the channel close:
only the CAS-winning Stop receives, and the writer must not access the
shared channel after the next session can replace it.

`socket_inet_loopback_nogotsan_test` fails on environments where `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range` is not writable inside an unprivileged user + network namespace:

`Cannot prepare test network: PosixError(errno=13 Permission denied) open(/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range, 0x201, 0)`

Two suggestions here:
1. Like `MaybeLimitEphemeralPorts()` in `test/util/socket_util.cc`, can we check `access("/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range", W_OK) == 0` (or ignore `EACCES`) instead of failing fatally? When the sysctl isn't writable on the host, the test already falls back to `SKIP_IF(nports > 1000)` in `socket_inet_loopback_nogotsan.cc`.
2. Nit: `else if (strcmp(argv[1], "--limit-ephemeral-ports") == 0)` is chained onto `else if (!SetupContainer().ok())`, which only runs because `SetupContainer().ok()` returns `true`. It would be clearer to check `--limit-ephemeral-ports` in a separate `if` after `SetupContainer()` succeeds.

The setup helper now tolerates EACCES from the actual sysctl open or write,
so a host that denies the change can reach the existing large-range skip.
Other setup errors still fail. I also separated flag handling from the
SetupContainer result check.

`limit_ephemeral_ports = True` currently sets `container = True` and passes `--limit-ephemeral-ports` to all platform variants, including default netstack runs (`network == "none"`).
For non-hostnet sandboxed runs, the sandbox uses its own virtual `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range` (updated by `MaybeLimitEphemeralPorts()` inside the test) rather than the host namespace's sysctl. Should `--limit-ephemeral-ports` only be applied when `network == "host"` (and/or `platform == "native"`)?

The option now takes effect only for native and host-network variants.
That condition controls both forcing a private container and passing the
setup flag; netstack variants retain their in-test range adjustment.
Nit: `test/syscalls/linux/socket_netlink_util.h` and `test/util/capability_util.h` in `setup_container.cc` are unused. Could you remove them?

Removed both headers and the unused socket_netlink_util dependency. The
capability_util dependency remains because it supplies the still-used
linux_capability_util header.

source.title: Report the host's ephemeral port range in hostinet
source.body:
Report the host's ephemeral port range in hostinet

Host-networked applications read a fixed ephemeral port range from
procfs, even when their sockets use a different range in the host network
namespace. Read the host value during initialization and refresh it from
the destination host on restore.

Run the existing port-exhaustion tests in a private network namespace
with a small range. Hostinet cannot change that sysctl from inside the
sandbox; without this setup, the tests skip rather than exhaust the
host's much larger range. Extend the existing restore test to check the
destination range.

source.title: Restore tracereplay tests to routine CI
source.body:
Restore tracereplay tests to routine CI

TestBasic used its absolute temporary directory in the Unix-domain socket
address. Bazel's TEST_TMPDIR can make that address exceed sockaddr_un's
limit, failing bind before any trace replay as reported in #10045.

Resolve the input file before entering a test-owned temporary directory,
then use a relative socket pathname. Keep the directory's absolute path
long to cover this failure and let testing clean up the fixture.

Remove the tracereplay unit-test exclusion.

NVIDIA driver ABI parser, which inspects headers for gVisor's supported
architectures. LLVM's default enables every backend, unnecessarily
building code generators for architectures this parser does not use.

That warrants broader discussion because it will cause ordinary feature work to occasionally flip a test from failing to passing.

It's not clear to me why runtime updates are the obvious right time to update these fixtures though (other than to add new tests that are failing)

Retried all five excluded cases on the current gVisor qualification
branch in both directfs and goferfs modes. PHP reports each as

PHP now [detects non-terminal standard streams itself](https://github.com/php/php-src/commit/831597748),

The skip decision now belongs to PHP, and these cases can run when a
terminal is available.

source.title: Support comment matches in nftables compatibility
source.body:
Support comment matches in nftables compatibility

iptables-nft rules using -m comment fail because the nft-compat
frontend neither advertises the match nor accepts its expression.
The legacy iptables implementation already supports it, but does not
handle nftables requests.

Support revision 0 and retain its opaque 256-byte payload through the
existing no-op match representation. Linux's comment match always
succeeds; it does not validate or interpret the comment bytes [1].
Reject unsupported revisions and malformed payload sizes with the
corresponding nft-compat errors. Share the comment layout size with
legacy iptables in the Linux ABI definitions. Extend the existing
syscall cases for revision lookup, valid families, unterminated data,
size errors and exact match payloads in rule dumps.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/netfilter/xt_comment.c

Validation on the integration source with the same executable patch:
16 selected native Linux/gVisor cases pass without skips [2]. The full
package, Nogo and client qualification passes 877 cases with 88 existing
skips [3].

[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/39144545744
[3]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/f2403420-3b0e-45bd-bfc2-a114ba4435ad

source.title: Save and restore KCOV state
source.body:
Save and restore KCOV state

Checkpointing a process with an open KCOV descriptor failed because
kernel.Kcov had no state serializer. The existing KCOV syscall suite
exposes this as soon as save/restore is enabled: saving fails after
opening the descriptor, and restoring the incomplete image reports EOF.

Generate the serializer for the coverage mode, buffer and task links.
Restore its allocator from the load context, as SpecialMappable does, so
the saved mapping remains usable after restore. Leave the mutex out of
the image; checkpointing stops the task that can access the buffer.

Add a direct Save/Load regression that verifies the initialized coverage
mode and size and restores the allocator from the load context. This
exercises serialization without a coverage-enabled runtime.

Validation on [integration source 5d199298a][source] passed eight owners
and 133 cases, with no skips or gaps. All six KCOV cases ran in four
ordinary/save variants; both save variants completed 41 restores. The
[remote result][result] also covers kernel/sys unit suites and
analyzers.

That integration includes the separate size/mmap correction in #15932.
This standalone change preserves master's existing size/mmap behavior;
its serialization patch differs from the qualified patch only in import
alias spelling. The standalone head was not separately re-executed. The
direct regression and owning analyzers passed on AMD64 and ARM64 with
the standalone KCOV implementation; removing the allocator-restoration
assignment made the regression fail at its intended assertion.

[source]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/5d199298a88d6f959a930dc2abb6cdaba3cca4e9
[result]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/cb40dbb8-86e4-47b8-81c7-4a66684fc4be

source.title: Wait for fork setup before freezing children
source.body:
Wait for fork setup before freezing children

The freezer tests could freeze a child before libc returned from
`fork()` and restored its temporary blocked signal mask. A subsequent
`SIGTERM` then stayed blocked, making the test report that the frozen
child failed to terminate. The `SIGQUIT` phase could also freeze before
the child installed its default disposition.

Wait for a readiness token after child setup and before freezing in both
fatal-signal tests. Keep the existing signal assertions, thaw behavior,
and deadlines.

prs.title: tcp: cap the RACK probe timeout at the RTO when no RTO timer is armed
prs.head: 8147e9ad3c95c67a0a9dd560f37aff9d7842f861

items.body:
Thanks for your pull request! It looks like this may be your first contribution to a Google open source project. Before we can look at your pull request, you'll need to sign a Contributor License Agreement (CLA).

View this [failed invocation](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15972/checks?check_run_id=117919379963) of the CLA check for more information.

For the most up to date status, view the checks section at the bottom of the pull request.

Thanks, both fair. Pushed e9c2848: the test now runs on `faketime.NewManualClock()` and waits on a TCP probe until the first ACK has advanced `SndUna` before the second write. That race also mattered for correctness: with the ACK unprocessed the RTO timer is still armed, and the existing code already caps the PTO there, so the test could pass without the fix. It then advances virtual time by exactly the RTO read from the probe and expects the probe retransmission. No wall-clock bound is left. Without the rack.go change it fails every time; with it, it passed 20 out of 20 runs.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Thanks, done in 8147e9a.

`schedulePTO` now takes `advancingRTO`. After a transmission, with no RTO timer armed, the PTO is bounded by one RTO from the oldest outstanding segment's `xmitTime`. After an ACK that advances SND.UNA it stays one RTO from now, as in `tcp_schedule_loss_probe(sk, advancing_rto)`.

That needed one more change: `postXmit` also rescheduled the PTO when nothing was sent, as when `sendData` runs right after an ACK, so the ACK's bound was replaced by the oldest-segment one. Linux schedules a loss probe in `tcp_write_xmit()` only after sending, so `postXmit` now keeps an already scheduled PTO when nothing was sent.

Some observations, for you to check:

1. The bound is not applied on every path: on the ACK path `schedulePTO` runs before the acknowledged segments leave `writeList`, so `writeList.Front()` is still the segment just acknowledged, and Linux counts from the ACK there.
2. If the oldest segment's RTO has already passed, the PTO is left uncapped, as in Linux (`if (rto_delta_us > 0)`). The case is narrow: after a probe fires, `postXmit` re-arms the resend timer, so this branch is mostly reached when a send races the probe timer. The alternative is to fire the probe right away; happy to switch if you prefer that.
3. With the RTO timer armed nothing changes: the PTO is still capped at its target and the timer disabled.
4. After a probe, the RTO timer is re-armed one RTO from now, following RFC 8985 section 7.3, while Linux's `tcp_rearm_rto()` counts from the oldest outstanding segment. I left that as it is.

Tests, all on the manual clock, with the setup shared in `newIdleRACKConn`:

- `TestRACKTLPNotLaterThanOldestRTO`: a second segment, then a third one SRTT before the second's RTO; the probe must come at that RTO. It fails on e9c2848.
- `TestRACKTLPOneRTOAfterAck`: half of a segment is acknowledged an SRTT after it was sent; no probe may come before one RTO from the ACK, then the probe must. It fails if the oldest-segment bound is applied on the ACK path, or without the `postXmit` change.

Both passed 30 out of 30 runs. `tcp_rack_test` and the other test targets under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp` pass too (run with `go test`, not Bazel).

Is anything else needed for this to be merged, or is it good to go from your side?

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

In `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/test/e2e/tcp_rack_test.go:498-514` (`TestRACKTLPNotLaterThanRTO`), consider either using `faketime.NewManualClock()` (via `context.NewWithOpts(t, context.Options{..., Clock: clock})` or a unit test in `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/rack_test.go`) or synchronizing on a TCP probe after `c.SendAck(seq, maxPayload)` before calling `write(data[maxPayload:])`:
1. Because `c.SendAck` enqueues the ACK asynchronously to the endpoint's processor goroutine, `write(data[maxPayload:])` on the next line can acquire `e.LockUser()` before the first ACK is processed (so the second segment isn't guaranteed to be sent on an idle connection).
2. Checking wall-clock `time.Since(sent) < 200*time.Millisecond` against a 50ms timer could flake on heavily loaded CI runners.

*(Assisted by Gemini)*

`pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/rack.go:196-201` (non-blocking): on the send path with data already outstanding, Linux bounds the PTO by the RTO measured from the oldest unacked segment's send time (`tcp_rto_delta_us()` in `tcp_schedule_loss_probe()`, net/ipv4/tcp_output.c), not from now. Since `postXmit` re-arms the PTO on every new transmission, a sender that keeps transmitting can still push the probe out by up to one RTO per send. Bounding against something like `s.writeList.Front().xmitTime.Add(s.RTO)` on that path would match Linux. This is already a strict improvement over before, so fine to leave as a TODO / follow-up.

*(Assisted by Gemini)*

User resolution narrowed signed numeric requests and group-file IDs
without checking their range. Invalid selected passwd records also fell

passwd record structure and group record length before reading IDs.

matching, and the existing treatment of unrelated malformed records.

underlying syntax and range errors.

source.title: Wait for veth operational state in the netlink test
source.body:
Wait for veth operational state in the netlink test

Bringing both veth ends up changes carrier immediately, but Linux
updates IFLA_OPERSTATE asynchronously through linkwatch [1]. The test
can therefore observe IF_OPER_LOWERLAYERDOWN after both flag changes
have succeeded, instead of the eventual IF_OPER_UP.

Poll RTM_GETLINK with a bounded monotonic timeout before asserting the
final state. Keep malformed replies and an interface that never becomes
operational as failures.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e5f0a698b/Documentation/networking/operstates.rst#L132-L147

prs.head: b039155d0869ebda7eb3973a6f8b79fab4f6d001

items.body:
LGTM. The change is small, opt-in for procfs only, and matches Linux (`fs/proc/generic.c:proc_lookup_de()` returning `-ENOENT`; `fs/namei.c:filename_create()`/`lookup_open()` returning lookup errors ahead of EEXIST, EROFS and `may_create()`). The new `ProcTest.Create` syscall test is thorough. Releasing `dirMu` is safe because every `dirMu` holder also holds `fs.mu`, which the caller holds for writing. The branch merges cleanly with master. Nits, none blocking:

1. **PR description scope.** It should also say that `link()`/`rename()` to a missing procfs destination now return ENOENT, that rename now sees uncached existing procfs destinations, and that non-creating lookups of overlong procfs names return ENOENT instead of ENAMETOOLONG. All of these match Linux.
2. **RenameAt consistency.** `RenameAt` still returns `ENAMETOOLONG` for an overlong `newName` on procfs; consider guarding it with `!fs.NoNegativeDentries` like the other sites.
3. **Comments.** Shorten the lock-balancing comment in `checkCreateLocked` and the `NoNegativeDentries` field comment, and cite `proc_lookup_de()` in the field comment.
4. **Unrelated churn.** Revert the `ok` → `exists` rename and the blank-line move in `SymlinkAt`.
5. **Tests (optional).** Add a `link()` case to `ProcTest.Create`. Consider moving the read-only precedence check to a syscall test (read-only `proc` mount in a temp dir) so it is validated natively.

**Security:** No security impact found. The change only makes procfs create-type syscalls (mkdir/mknod/symlink/link/rename/`O_CREAT`) fail earlier, at lookup. It adds no host interaction, and `MayExec` on the parent is still checked first, so no new existence oracle appears. Skipping `NAME_MAX` is bounded by `PATH_MAX`, and the procfs lookups that see the name (map lookups and `parseIDName`) do bounded work. Releasing `dirMu` temporarily is safe because every `dirMu` holder also holds `fs.mu`, which the caller holds for writing.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Replies from Codex on Tamir’s behalf for b039155d08. All four [syscall cases](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/4e216e66-ac92-4b08-9cf1-8e88d351d138) passed on native Linux, systrap DirectFS, and systrap shared.

Thanks. All feedback is addressed: rename/link on procfs now look up the destination first, matching do_linkat()/do_renameat2(), and the new syscall tests cover link, rename and read-only precedence natively. LGTM.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude
Shortened the comment to the lock transition and its invariant: the caller holds fs.mu for writing while revalidation takes parent.dirMu, so parent.children cannot change across the unlock.
Nit: unrelated rename (`ok` → `exists`); please revert to keep the diff focused.
Restored `ok`; this lookup is unchanged.

For consistency with `stepExistingLocked`/`OpenAt`, should this check also be skipped when `fs.NoNegativeDentries`? On Linux, `rename("/proc/version", "/proc/<NAME_MAX+1 chars>")` returns ENOENT from the procfs lookup (`do_renameat2()` → `lookup_one_qstr_excl()`), not ENAMETOOLONG. `checkCreateLocked` would then return the lookup error.

Procfs now looks up both rename entries before the directory write checks and leaves the length check to the filesystem. The syscall case covers short and NAME_MAX+1 missing destinations with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE disabled. It also checks RENAME_NOREPLACE on an existing entry and rename to the same inode; ordinary kernfs filesystems keep their previous checks.
Nit: unrelated whitespace move; please revert.
Restored the original spacing in `SymlinkAt`.
The field comment now names Linux’s `proc_lookup_de`, specifies how lookup treats overlong names, and explains why synthetic mountpoint creation is exempt.

`LinkAt` also goes through `checkCreateLocked` and changes behavior here (EPERM → ENOENT). Consider adding `EXPECT_THAT(link("/proc/version", missing.c_str()), SyscallFailsWithErrno(ENOENT));` (Linux: `do_linkat()` → `filename_create()` fails before `may_linkat()`/EXDEV).

Added hard-link coverage for missing short and overlong proc names. I also found that the cross-mount and directory-source checks ran before destination lookup. The new test uses each kind of source against a missing and an existing destination; procfs now returns ENOENT and EEXIST respectively, as in `do_linkat`.

Optional: this precedence (ENOENT/EEXIST over EROFS) has a direct Linux equivalent, so a syscall test would validate it natively, e.g. mount a fresh `proc` with `MS_RDONLY` on a temp dir (requires `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`) and repeat the mkdir/symlink/mknod/open checks.

Moved the read-only precedence matrix into a syscall test. It remounts a bind of `/proc/self` read-only: the native runner’s user namespace does not own the PID namespace and cannot mount a new procfs. It checks ENOENT and EEXIST from mkdir, symlink, mknod, and open, plus EROFS from rename. The unit test now covers only gVisor’s synthetic mountpoint exception.

Optional (hardening): on procfs, `dst` being non-nil here depends on `checkCreateLocked` returning EEXIST only after `revalidateChildLocked` has inserted the child into `dstDir.children`. If that ever changes, `rename(2)` on `/proc` would hit the `dst == nil` panic below and crash the sandbox. It's correct today. Consider a short comment noting the invariant, or returning the looked-up dentry from `checkCreateLocked` instead of re-reading the map.

Documented the invariant at the map read: successful revalidation inserts the child and returns EEXIST while the filesystem write lock protects the map. The existing assertion remains to catch an invariant violation.

source.title: Preserve procfs lookup errors during creation
source.body:
Preserve procfs lookup errors during creation

Creating a missing procfs entry could return `EPERM` or `EACCES`, and renaming to an overlong procfs name could return `ENAMETOOLONG`. [Linux procfs](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/fs/proc/generic.c#L225-L245) instead returns `ENOENT` from lookup. For creation, this error also takes precedence over a read-only mount’s `EROFS`.

Preserve that lookup result for procfs `mkdir`, `symlink`, `mknod`, `open(O_CREAT)`, `link`, and `rename`. [Hard links](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/fs/namei.c#L4508-L4528) now look up the destination before rejecting a cross-mount or directory source. [Rename](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/fs/namei.c#L4623-L4643) checks both entries first: `RENAME_NOREPLACE` rejects an existing destination, and renaming an entry to itself succeeds before parent write checks. Other kernfs filesystems retain their existing checks. gVisor can still create synthetic procfs mountpoints.

Four syscall cases exercise these paths, including short and overlong names and creation on a read-only bind mount. [All four passed on native Linux, systrap with DirectFS, and systrap with shared filesystem access](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/4e216e66-ac92-4b08-9cf1-8e88d351d138).

prs.title: Report per-interface multicast support
prs.head: b584529cbf05e11ed7ba8f59b2706c554bf78250

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, well-scoped change that matches Linux: `ether_setup()` sets `IFF_MULTICAST` for veth/bridge/TAP, `tun_net_initialize()` sets it for TUN, and `loopback_setup()` does not set it for `lo`. SIOCGIFFLAGS and RTM_GETLINK both go through `nicStateFlagsToLinux`, so they stay consistent. The PR merges cleanly with current master, and master has no equivalent fix.

Minor points, none blocking:

1. `LinkInfoKind`: the native run can fail on hosts where ipip/sit/ip6_tunnel/gre are loaded. Fallback tunnel devices (`sit0`, `tunl0`, `ip6tnl0`, …) are created in every new netns without `IFF_MULTICAST`. Please assert only on the links the test creates, plus `lo`.
2. Optional: cite the Linux source of the defaults at the `Multicast: true` call sites (`ether_setup()` / `tun_net_initialize()`).
3. PR description: the first sentence ("Interfaces with usable IPv6 addresses…") is narrower than the actual bug, which was that no netstack interface reported `IFF_MULTICAST`. The commit message wording is more accurate.

**Security:** No security impact: the new bit only sets `IFF_MULTICAST` in the existing SIOCGIFFLAGS/RTM_GETLINK replies, and nothing in netstack uses it to make a decision. It is set from trusted runsc-side config or fixed Linux defaults, and the sandbox cannot change it. The change adds no host syscalls, seccomp changes or new untrusted-input parsing. The only new information the sandbox sees is one host flag on interfaces it already imports, which is consistent with Linux.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude
Replies from Codex on Tamir’s behalf for b584529cbf.

Thanks. LinkInfoKind now checks only the links it creates, plus lo, so fallback tunnel devices no longer break native runs, and the Linux references at the veth, bridge, and TUN/TAP sites are accurate. LGTM.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

On native Linux, a fresh netns can also contain fallback tunnel devices when their modules are loaded and `net.core.fb_tunnels_only_for_init_net=0`: `sit0`, `tunl0`, `ip6tnl0`, `gre0`, `ip_vti0`, … These have `IFF_NOARP` and lack `IFF_MULTICAST`, so this check fails there. Consider checking only the links this test creates, e.g. skip names other than `lo`/`veth1`/`veth2`/`br0`, or check those four explicitly after the loop.

LinkInfoKind now looks up `veth1`, `veth2`, `br0`, and `lo` by name and requires all four. It checks their flags through both netlink and SIOCGIFFLAGS without assuming anything about extra tunnel interfaces. The case [passed on native Linux and both systrap filesystem modes](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/995e78a5-ff82-471e-bbbf-b54977fd17e9).
Nit: worth a short Linux reference here and in `newBridge`, e.g. `// Linux veth_setup() → ether_setup() sets IFF_MULTICAST.`
Added the Linux references at both creation sites: `veth_setup` and `br_dev_setup` each call `ether_setup`, which sets `IFF_MULTICAST`.
Nit: `// Linux tun_net_initialize() sets IFF_MULTICAST for both TUN and TAP (via ether_setup()).`
The TUN/TAP comment now names `tun_net_initialize`: TUN sets `IFF_MULTICAST` directly, and TAP inherits it from `ether_setup`.

source.title: Report per-interface multicast support
source.body:
Report per-interface multicast support

Interfaces with usable IPv6 addresses were reported without
IFF_MULTICAST through SIOCGIFFLAGS and netlink. Java consequently
treated them as unable to multicast and skipped its IPv6 socket tests.

Preserve each imported host interface's multicast flag through network
setup and NIC state. Apply Linux defaults to sandbox-created veth,
bridge, TUN and TAP devices, and preserve the flag across network
namespace moves. Import the actual loopback flag too: Linux permits
changing it, and device type alone does not determine multicast support.
The new option controls the reported flag, not packet reception.

Validation on the qualification branch passed the owning unit and
analyzer checks, focused ioctl/netlink and TUN/TAP tests, and both Java
PromiscuousIPv6 bodies in directfs, shared-filesystem and native-
reference modes. Each Java body exercised both IPv6 multicast scopes,
including expected receives and nonreceives. The same ABI regression
failed before the fix. Checkpoint roundtrips and flag mutation were not
tested.

source.title: Wait for FUSE before copying benchmark inputs
source.body:
Wait for FUSE before copying benchmark inputs

Filesystem benchmarks started the FUSE helper through Docker exec, which
can return before the helper mounts the filesystem. Copying benchmark
inputs at that point could race with the mount: files created in the
original tmpfs would disappear from view when FUSE covered it.

Have the helper signal readiness after WaitMount succeeds, and wait for
that signal before copying the inputs. Observe the helper's exit so a
failed mount also stops the wait. Mount setup remains outside the timed
benchmark region.

source.title: netstack: fix forwarded IPv6 checksums
source.body:
netstack: fix forwarded IPv6 checksums

Forwarding IPv6 packets with extension headers could replace valid TCP
and UDP checksums with invalid ones. Software checksum recalculation
used the IPv6 base header's next-header field, which identifies the
first extension rather than the upper-layer protocol.

Build the pseudoheader with the protocol of the matched TCP or UDP
header. Extend the existing masquerade test with hop-by-hop and
destination options, explicitly validate UDP checksums, and cover the
same protocol selection at the packet buffer boundary.

source.title: Reject overflowing metric timestamp offsets
source.body:
Metricsviz accepts unsigned 64-bit nanosecond offsets, then converts them
to time.Duration. Offsets above MaxInt64 become negative and place samples
before the collection start instead of rejecting the invalid log.

Limit offsets to the nonnegative time.Duration range and retain the
parser's range error. Check the valid endpoints and overflowing values
through the existing metrics log parser.

The standalone parser suite passes, but its analyzer build encounters an
existing Docker protobuf dependency error [1]. Both analyzer owners pass
for AMD64 and ARM64 with the separate #16098 build-graph correction [2].
This PR contains only the timestamp change.

[1]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/3a2b9b90-3dfb-4956-b574-41beca7ab0e4
[2]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/c4c42ec5-0c53-4b81-8742-6cefbbffdd46

source.title: Wait for accepted connections in TCP restore tests
source.body:
Wait for accepted connections in TCP restore tests

A probe can be accepted before its readiness notification is consumed.
The next probe then wakes on the old notification and fails with
ErrWouldBlock before its handshake finishes. This caused the multiple-
connection restore case to fail during a TCP test run.

Share a bounded accept loop between the probe fixtures. Register a fresh
waiter for each connection and recheck Accept after notifications, keeping
the existing five-second limit.

source.title: Align nested test cgroup namespace and mount
source.body:
Align nested test cgroup namespace and mount

The rootful nested-runtime tests mounted host cgroupfs while Docker
selected a private cgroup namespace. On a cgroup v2 host with
nsdelegate, this mismatch caused clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) to fail with
ENOENT before the gofer executed.

Use the host cgroup namespace for variants that bind host cgroupfs, so
/proc/self/cgroup and the mounted hierarchy describe the same namespace.
Variants without that mount retain Docker's default namespace selection.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

A dual-stack wildcard bind reserves the port for IPv4 and IPv6. Connecting to a mapped peer sets `effectiveNetProtos` to IPv4 and releases the IPv4 reservation. Cleanup then misses the remaining IPv6 reservation. Could it release the family the endpoint still owns?

[This syscall test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/1d322cb0b/test/syscalls/linux/socket_inet_loopback.cc#L263-L323) closes the connection with a reset and rebinds the same port. source.title: tcp: release the port of a wildcard-bound endpoint when it is closed
source.body:
tcp: release the port of a wildcard-bound endpoint when it is closed

Fixes #16102

### Compatibility

`COMPATIBILITY:NEW-APP-CONFIG` — fixes source-port exhaustion in the repeated wildcard-bound connections used by the BusyBox `nc` healthchecks reported in #16102

### Problem and fix

A wildcard bind reserves its port using the wildcard address, but connecting replaces the endpoint local address with the connected address

A dual-stack wildcard bind also reserves both IPv6 and IPv4, while connecting to an IPv4-mapped peer changes `effectiveNetProtos` to IPv4 and releases the IPv4 reservation

Cleanup must therefore use the reservation address and the network protocols still owned by the endpoint, rather than the connected address and effective protocols

- Record `boundAddr` and `boundNetProtos` for explicit binds, implicit connect reservations and accepted tuples
- Release the IPv4 reservation with its complete metadata and retain the IPv6 reservation for close
- Use the recorded reservation in both close and cleanup paths, with `checklocks` annotations on the new fields

Rebased onto `0bbcbf9de7626fcecba97f37723dce80b435d73d`

### Regression coverage

Adapted the syscall test suggested by @tamird into `SocketInetLoopback.WildcardBoundPortReleasedOnClose`, covering IPv4 wildcard and dual-stack wildcard connections to an IPv4 peer

The test uses an abortive close to avoid TIME_WAIT and verifies that both IPv4 and IPv6-only wildcard binds can reuse the port

The review reproducer passes on Linux and fails on the previous PR implementation with `EADDRINUSE` for the IPv6-only bind

The updated test passes on both Linux and gVisor, replacing the duplicate Go behavior test

### Local validation

Linux ARM64 in a Colima-backed Ubuntu container, Bazel 8.8.1

- Focused regression on native Linux and gVisor systrap — passed
- Full `socket_inet_loopback` suite on native Linux and gVisor systrap — passed, 8 shards each
- TCP and ports package tests — all 28 targets passed, including nogo and checklocks analysis for ARM64 and AMD64
- Ports, TCP and dual-stack tests with race detection and lockdep enabled together — all 3 targets passed
- `make lint` — passed
- `make lint-cc` — passed with the compilation database scoped to the affected syscall target and its 16 source files
- `git diff --check` — passed

```sh

bazel test $common --test_output=errors --test_sharding_strategy=disabled \
  --test_filter=SocketInetLoopback.WildcardBoundPortReleasedOnClose \
  //test/syscalls:socket_inet_loopback_test_native

make syscall-tests DOCKER_BUILD=false BAZEL_OPTIONS="$common" \
  TARGETS=//test/syscalls:socket_inet_loopback_test_runsc_systrap_shared \
  OPTIONS="--test_sharding_strategy=disabled --test_filter=SocketInetLoopback.WildcardBoundPortReleasedOnClose"

bazel test $common --test_output=errors \
  //pkg/tcpip/ports/... //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...

make syscall-tests DOCKER_BUILD=false BAZEL_OPTIONS="$common" \
  TARGETS=//test/syscalls:socket_inet_loopback_test_native

make syscall-tests DOCKER_BUILD=false BAZEL_OPTIONS="$common" \
  TARGETS=//test/syscalls:socket_inet_loopback_test_runsc_systrap_shared

bazel test $common --config=race --config=lockdep --test_output=errors \
  //pkg/tcpip/ports:ports_test //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp:tcp_test \
  //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/test/e2e:dual_stack_test

make lint DOCKER_BUILD=false BAZEL_OPTIONS="$common"
python3 tools/gen_compile_commands.py //test/syscalls/linux:socket_inet_loopback_test
make lint-cc DOCKER_BUILD=false
git diff --check
```

### Performance

Added `BenchmarkWildcardBindClose` and compared the master base against this change with the same benchmark and build flags

Alternating before/after execution order, 32 samples per version, Linux ARM64 with 6 vCPUs

| Metric | Before | After | Comparison |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time | 1253 ns/op | 1275 ns/op | +1.76%, p=0.016 |
| Allocation bytes | 4960 B/op | 4960 B/op | unchanged |
| Allocations | 26 allocs/op | 26 allocs/op | unchanged |

The benchmark measures a small bind/close overhead, with no additional allocations

Each sample runs the built test binary with `-test.run='^$' -test.bench='^BenchmarkWildcardBindClose$' -test.benchmem -test.count=1`, followed by `benchstat` comparison

These are local results, not a claim that GitHub CI has passed

prs.title: Add `pkg/state` benchmark for kernel serialization.
prs.head: 8f26710e0cbd6ffc4f357b2d44cee4e8a3d4b767

items.body:
This exercises real kernel types and generated state methods, which is useful coverage for serializer optimization. The inline findings concern resource lifetime, the graph being encoded, CPU measurement, and checkpoint producer identity. These are source-review findings; the benchmark was not executed during this review.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

LGTM. The stub address space fixes the per-decode resource leak, and the CPU samples now exclude benchmark timer bookkeeping.

I accept the intentionally partial restore as the encode fixture. It exercises the production codec on a fresh graph each iteration; I have no evidence that completing kernel restoration would materially improve these measurements. The documented benchmark setup also addresses my producer-version concern.

Two nonblocking notes inline. Please also refresh the sample output in the description: it still shows the old combined benchmark and custom allocation/wall-time metrics, rather than the new Decode/Encode subbenchmarks.

Reviewed the source and restore paths; I did not run the benchmark.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

[🤖] 1 issue found:

- **[minor · bug]** Forced GC before each timed call means Decode never pays for GC and Encode always does, depending on an unrelated 5 MiB buffer (`test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go:369`, inline)

LGTM. The revision addresses the GC-accounting finding: only the state file is loaded, and both timed codec operations exclude percentage-triggered GC. The shared memory files now have cleanup as well.

This is a useful isolated codec benchmark. Allocation counts complement its timings; they do not measure the GC cost of those allocations. One nonblocking clarification inline about the memory-limit setting.

Reviewed the updated source and runtime/restore contracts; I did not rerun the benchmark or reproduce the measurements in the preceding review.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

**Release the platform resources created by each decoded kernel.**

This cleanup only closes the synthetic stdio pipes. Each live [`MemoryManager.afterLoad`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/sentry/mm/save_restore.go#L45-L57) also creates an address space through the supplied Systrap platform. Those address spaces never reach [`Release`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/sentry/platform/systrap/subprocess.go#L520-L531), so they cannot return to the reuse pool. The subprocess's [request goroutine](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/sentry/platform/systrap/subprocess.go#L401-L410) retains it; the forced GC does not reclaim these resources.

Consequently, increasing `b.N` accumulates host resources instead of repeating the operation with bounded resource use. Please give each decoded kernel a valid teardown outside the measured interval. A bare `k.Release()` is not yet an established fix: its [full-initialization precondition](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/sentry/kernel/kernel.go#L2504-L2509) is not satisfied by this raw load path.
Done (using a stub platform)

**Complete the restore semantics before measuring the encode workload.**

`loadKernel` returns after raw `state.Load`, but restore hooks leave a different graph pending further initialization. For example, TCP's [`afterLoad`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/endpoint_state.go#L137-L143) resets the nginx listening endpoints to `StateInitial`. This `state.Save` then serializes that value through [`saveState`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/endpoint_state.go#L101-L104), rather than their original `StateListen`. The saved pending-restore list also remains populated. Production [`Stack.Restore`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/pkg/tcpip/stack/stack.go#L2255-L2267) consumes that list and restores the endpoints.

That changes the graph and its zero/nonzero values, which directly affects the encoder optimizations this benchmark is meant to compare. Please prepare a graph with completed restore semantics outside the encode timing, or obtain the encode fixture separately, and check its relevant state outside timing. Counting output bytes alone cannot detect this difference.
Not worth it. Difficult to fix and doesn't change the effective graph object much, benchmark is correct enough for its purposes.

**Keep timer bookkeeping outside the CPU interval.**

The CPU snapshots surround `b.StartTimer()` and `b.StopTimer()`, while the wall snapshots surround only `fn`. In Go 1.27.3, [both timer methods call `runtime.ReadMemStats`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.3/src/testing/benchmark.go#L138-L160), which [stops the world and flushes allocation caches](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.3/src/runtime/mstats.go#L356-L382). The CPU metric therefore charges two extra heap-statistics operations to each codec invocation. Their cost can also change with the codec's heap behavior.

Please move the CPU snapshots immediately around `fn`, inside the active benchmark timer, so timer/statistics bookkeeping is excluded from that interval. I have not measured the size of this bias.
Done

**Validate or explicitly pin the checkpoint producer used for comparisons.**

The same-tree requirement below is only reported after a decoding failure. A stale installed runtime can remain wire-compatible and silently supply an older kernel graph: the normal [`run-benchmark` target](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/Makefile#L740) loads benchmark images but does not rebuild/install the configured runtime.

The discarded metadata already includes [`runsc_version`](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/runsc/boot/restore.go#L876), which the [production restore path checks](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/e266f71eb/runsc/boot/controller.go#L477-L480). Please validate and record the intended producer/consumer relationship before timing, together with the checkpoint identity. An explicitly pinned older checkpoint could also be useful for codec comparisons, but should be deliberate. A version string alone will not establish exact source identity if development binaries share the same unstamped version.
The version is always meaningless on dev builds. Not a concern in the benchmark run setups we have.

Nonblocking cleanup: register `b.Cleanup(mf.Destroy)` for each successfully created MemoryFile. `NewMemoryFile` starts a releaser goroutine that retains the file until `Destroy`, so these setup-owned descriptors and goroutines otherwise survive until process exit. Registering cleanup here also covers a file replaced in the ResourceID map. This is parent-setup cleanup, not the per-iteration growth fixed by the stub platform.

Nonblocking documentation: please retain a short comment that this deliberately re-encodes a partially restored kernel. For example, TCP restore hooks leave endpoints in their initial state pending `Stack.Restore`. That is acceptable for this codec fixture; documenting it here will keep future users from treating the encoded output as a validated checkpoint roundtrip.

[🤖] **[minor · bug] Forced GC before each timed call means Decode never pays for GC and Encode always does, depending on an unrelated 5 MiB buffer**

`cpuTime` runs `runtime.GC()` right before every timed call. This resets the heap goal to about twice the live heap, so a collection happens inside the timed window only when the call allocates more than the remaining headroom. Whether `ns/op` and `cpu-ns` include GC work is therefore a step function of allocation volume versus whatever else happens to be live. It is not a consistent property of the codec.

In this benchmark the two subbenchmarks end up on opposite sides of that threshold:
- **Decode:** the closure reads `files[...]` after its loop (lines 121-127) only to report sizes. That keeps the 5 MiB `pages.img` buffer, which decoding never reads, alive during every timed decode. Live heap is about 8.2 MB and the goal about 16.8 MB. Decoding allocates about 5.5 MB per op, so no collection ever starts inside the window. The GC work caused by decoding is always paid by the next forced `runtime.GC()`, outside the timer and outside `cpu-ns`.
- **Encode:** live heap is about 4.3 MB and the goal about 9.0 MB, while encoding allocates about 8.3 MB per op. So every timed call includes one collection. On a 32-CPU machine that collection is about 40% of Encode's reported `cpu-ns` (38.5 ms vs about 22 ms without it, at about 25 ms wall).

The consequences for using this benchmark to compare `pkg/state` optimizations:
- Decode and Encode times are measured under different GC accounting, so they cannot be compared with each other.
- Decode time ignores the GC cost of its allocations.
- Changes that move allocation volume or unrelated retained memory across the headroom produce large jumps unrelated to the actual work. For example, releasing the pages buffer alone makes identical decode work cost about 35% more `cpu-ns`.

The `cpuTime` comment says fn is charged for the collections its own allocations cause. That holds for Encode but not for Decode.

**Evidence:** Mechanism:
- `cpuTime` (lines 372-384) calls `runtime.GC()` immediately before `fn`, so each call starts on a freshly collected heap with goal ≈ 2× live heap (GOGC=100).
- The Decode closure captures `files` (lines 121-127). Only `stateFile` is needed for decoding (line 112).
- The Encode closure does not reference `files`, so the pages data is collected before Encode runs.
- The Decode benchmark reports 5549507 B/op; Encode reports 8302236 B/op; `pages-file-B` is 5259264.

Measurement:
- I added per-call counters to `cpuTime`: `/gc/cycles/automatic:gc-cycles`, `/gc/heap/live:bytes` and `/gc/heap/goal:bytes` from `runtime/metrics`. The cycle count is read before `fn` and again after a `runtime.GC()` placed after `fn` (outside the timer), which completes any cycle that started during `fn`.
- I ran the benchmark with `--test.benchtime=40x` on a quiet 32-CPU VM.
- As written: Decode had 0 automatic cycles in 41/41 timed calls (live 8.20 MB, goal 16.83 MB, cpu 20.6 ms, wall 19.4 ms). Encode had 1 cycle in 41/41 calls (live 4.29 MB, goal 9.00 MB, cpu 38.5 ms, wall 24.8 ms).
- Same code, but the non-state-file entries of `files` set to nil before `b.Run`: Decode had 1 cycle in 41/41 calls (live 2.94 MB, goal 6.30 MB), cpu 27.8 ms.
- Automatic GC disabled only inside the timed call (`debug.SetGCPercent(-1)` around `fn`): 0 cycles in every call. Decode cpu was 17.6 ms with and without the retained buffer. Encode cpu was 22.2 ms, about equal to wall.
- An earlier run on a loaded machine showed the same cycle counts.

**Reproduced with a test** (`test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go`): `bazel build //test/benchmarks/checkpointfile:checkpointfile_test && B=bazel-bin/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile_test_/checkpointfile_test; for mode in keep drop; do if [ $mode = drop ]; then export DROP_FILES=1; else unset DROP_FILES; fi; $B --runtime=runsc --test.bench=. --test.run="^$" --test.benchtime=40x 2>&1 | grep -oE "GCDIAG.*"; done` → I added per-call counters to `cpuTime`: automatic GC cycles from `runtime/metrics`, read before the timed call and after a `runtime.GC()` that follows it, plus live heap and heap goal. Then I ran `bazel-bin/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile_test_/checkpointfile_test --runtime=runsc --test.bench=. --test.benchtime=40x` as root.
- As written: Decode had 0 automatic collections in 41/41 timed calls (live ≈8.2 MB, goal ≈16.8 MB, cpu ≈20.6 ms). Encode had 1 collection in 41/41 calls (live ≈4.3 MB, goal ≈9.0 MB, cpu ≈38.5 ms, wall ≈24.8 ms).
- With the unrelated pages and metadata buffers released before `b.Run`, the same Decode work had 1 collection per call and cpu ≈27.8 ms.
- With automatic GC disabled inside the timed call: 0 collections everywhere, Decode cpu ≈17.6 ms with or without the buffer, Encode cpu ≈22.2 ms.

<details><summary>Test code</summary>

```diff
diff -ru a/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go b/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go
--- a/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go	2026-10-22 21:27:51.692906789 +0000
+++ b/test/benchmarks/checkpointfile/checkpointfile.go	2026-10-22 21:28:17.953939766 +0000
@@ -30,6 +30,7 @@
 	"os"
 	"path/filepath"
 	"runtime"
+	"runtime/metrics"
 	"strings"
 	"testing"
 	"time"
@@ -101,7 +102,19 @@
 	}
 	plat := stubPlatform{sys}
 
+	if os.Getenv("DROP_FILES") == "1" {
+		// Keep only the state file alive, as a variant of the same benchmark
+		// that holds no unrelated data on the heap.
+		for name := range files {
+			if name != checkpointfiles.StateFileName {
+				files[name] = nil
+			}
+		}
+		runtime.GC()
+	}
+
 	b.Run("Decode", func(b *testing.B) {
+		curPhase = "decode"
 		b.ReportAllocs()
 		var cpu time.Duration
 		for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
@@ -127,6 +140,7 @@
 		b.ReportMetric(float64(total), "checkpoint-total-B")
 	})
 	b.Run("Encode", func(b *testing.B) {
+		curPhase = "encode"
 		b.ReportAllocs()
 		var cpu time.Duration
 		var encodedBytes int64
@@ -373,16 +387,30 @@
 	b.Helper()
 	b.StopTimer()
 	runtime.GC()
+	s := []metrics.Sample{{Name: "/gc/cycles/automatic:gc-cycles"}, {Name: "/gc/heap/goal:bytes"}, {Name: "/gc/heap/live:bytes"}}
+	metrics.Read(s)
+	auto0, goal, live := s[0].Value.Uint64(), s[1].Value.Uint64(), s[2].Value.Uint64()
 	b.StartTimer()
 	cpu0 := processCPU(b)
+	t0 := time.Now()
 	err := fn()
+	wall := time.Since(t0)
 	cpu1 := processCPU(b)
+	b.StopTimer()
+	// Completes any automatic cycle that started while fn ran.
+	runtime.GC()
+	metrics.Read(s)
+	auto1 := s[0].Value.Uint64()
+	b.StartTimer()
 	if err != nil {
 		b.Fatal(err)
 	}
+	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "GCDIAG phase=%s wall_us=%d cpu_us=%d autoGCs=%d live=%d goal=%d\n", curPhase, wall.Microseconds(), (cpu1 - cpu0).Microseconds(), auto1-auto0, live, goal)
 	return cpu1 - cpu0
 }
 
+var curPhase string
+
 // processCPU returns the user and system CPU time of the process.
 func processCPU(b *testing.B) time.Duration {
 	var ru unix.Rusage
```

</details>

**Suggested fix:** There are two parts. With both applied, every timed call gets the same GC accounting, and Decode no longer depends on the pages buffer.

1. Keep only what the timed code needs alive. Compute the size metrics before `b.Run` and drop `files`:
```go
stateFile := files[checkpointfiles.StateFileName]
sizes := make(map[string]int, len(files))
total := 0
for name, f := range files {
	sizes[name] = len(f)
	total += len(f)
}
files = nil // report sizes[...] and total instead of len(files[...])
```

2. Make GC accounting the same for every call, for example by turning off automatic GC only for the timed call:
```go
func cpuTime(b *testing.B, fn func() error) time.Duration {
	b.Helper()
	b.StopTimer()
	runtime.GC()
	gcPercent := debug.SetGCPercent(-1) // no collection inside the timed call
	b.StartTimer()
	cpu0 := processCPU(b)
	err := fn()
	cpu1 := processCPU(b)
	b.StopTimer()
	debug.SetGCPercent(gcPercent)
	b.StartTimer()
	if err != nil {
		b.Fatal(err)
	}
	return cpu1 - cpu0
}
```
Then update the comment: `ns/op` and `cpu-ns` exclude GC, and B/op and allocs/op show allocation pressure. If GC cost should stay in the time metrics, the alternative is to end every call with one forced collection inside the measured interval, so each call pays for its own garbage.

I verified the `SetGCPercent(-1)` variant: 0 in-window collections for every call, and Decode cpu-ns ≈17.6 ms with or without the retained buffer.
Done

Nonblocking: `SetGCPercent(-1)` still permits collection when Go's memory limit is reached ([runtime documentation](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2aae1000e/src/runtime/debug/garbage.go#L82-L95)). Could the benchmark instructions specify `GOMEMLIMIT=off` (the default), or qualify the comment's no-GC guarantee as requiring a nonbinding memory limit? That would make the measurement conditions explicit without changing a caller's memory policy.

source.title: Use rules_go static linking for portable tools
source.body:
Use rules_go static linking for portable tools

The shim and command-line tools run outside the build environment, the
webhook image contains only its executable, and the test helper runs in
containers. Benchmark binaries are also built in a container and run on
the host. These targets already requested static linking, but their
C++ fully_static_link feature did not set rules_go's static mode.

Use the Go rules' static attribute for these six consumers so their
race and cgo configurations also request a self-contained executable.
The ioctl sniffer's embedded preload library remains a shared library.

source.title: Allow root-module Linux header defaults
source.body:
Projects such as gVisor need newer Linux UAPI declarations while keeping
an older libc target. Today, choosing those headers requires adding a
kernel constraint to each target platform or carrying a local patch.

Allow the root module to configure an indexed default header release
through kernel_headers.configure(default_version = "6.6"). An explicit
kernel constraint takes precedence. Omitting the tag preserves the
libc-derived defaults, so existing consumers keep their current headers.

Requested in google/gvisor#16236:
https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16236#issuecomment-6382396542

source.title: Select Linux UAPI headers independently
source.body:
Select Linux UAPI headers independently

Use Linux 6.18 UAPI headers for targets without an explicit kernel
version constraint. The glibc 2.28 default otherwise selects Linux 4.19
headers, which lack declarations such as `NFT_MSG_DESTROYTABLE` used by
gVisor's netfilter syscall tests.

The header choice applies to both glibc and musl without changing the
target libc or execution platform. Explicit kernel constraints still
take precedence. Projects that do not set a default keep the existing
libc-based selection.

[The upstream implementation][1] landed after hermetic-llvm 0.8.26.
gVisor pins 0.8.24, so this change carries the interface as a patch to
that release. Updating to a BCR version with the interface removes the
need for the local patch.

[1]: https://github.com/hermeticbuild/hermetic-llvm/commit/3dd710dd9cb57adc0a8baf4220f5bc1e38ebd9bc

source.title: Stop port-forward readiness polling on timeout
source.body:
Stop port-forward readiness polling on timeout

The readiness goroutine kept running after the 30-second timeout, and its writes to the last command result raced with timeout diagnostics.

source.title: Clean up canceled HTTP readiness probes
source.body:
Clean up canceled HTTP readiness probes

WaitUntilContainerServing passed its caller context to deferred probe
cleanup. When the caller canceled a readiness wait, Docker kill and
remove inherited that cancellation and left the probe container behind.

Detach cleanup from caller cancellation while preserving context values.
The readiness operation still stops when canceled, and its temporary
container can be removed before the helper returns.

source.title: Fix RACK packet-test assumptions
source.body:
Fix RACK packet-test assumptions

The reordering test sent four packets, induced loss, then waited for
four more without acknowledging any of them. Netstack's Reno reduced
the window to two packets, so the test stalled before checking RACK.
Linux leaves enough room to mask this assumption. Even with Reno
selected on both sides, Linux halves the congestion window rather than
the flight size [1] and permits the second flight.

Send eight packets in the first flight so halving it leaves room for
the second flight. Keep four packets in the second flight: its three
SACKed packets exercise reordering beyond the duplicate-ACK threshold.
Wait for a retransmission before reporting duplicate bytes, then
advance the fixture to the cumulative ACK position.

Use TCP_INFO's send MSS for payloads and SACK ranges. The fixed
536-byte writes exceeded netstack's 500-byte send MSS, making the
fixture's sequence numbers disagree with the packets on the wire.
Check full payloads and register cleanup before assertions.

Delay retransmission ACKs longer than the warmup ACKs, leaving margin
above RACK's minimum RTT [2]. Correct the corresponding source comment
and require the netstack suite to pass.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/8bb7eca97/net/ipv4/tcp_cong.c#L453-L459
[2]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8985.html#section-6.2

source.title: Validate FIB attributes by netlink ID
source.body:
Validate FIB attributes by netlink ID

The FIB policy used positional entries starting at zero, but its netlink
attributes start at one. Flags therefore bypassed the mask check, and the
destination register was checked only after narrowing it to eight bits.
A register value of 257 was accepted as register 1.

Index the policy by attribute ID and validate network-order register and
flag values with the existing maximum and mask validators, matching
Linux [1]. Extend the netlink initialization cases to cover register
truncation, unknown flags and the supported register boundary.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/ab185e0c4/net/netfilter/nft_fib.c#L21-L26

source.title: proc: Reject invalid task directory names
source.body:
proc: Reject invalid task directory names

Prevent oversized numeric names from wrapping to a live task ID during
procfs lookup. For example, /proc/<PID + 2^32> currently opens the same
task as /proc/<PID>. Parse task IDs within their signed 32-bit range
before converting them, and reject leading-zero aliases in both the
procfs root and /proc/<PID>/task, matching Linux [1].

Add syscall coverage for oversized and leading-zero names in both
directories. The unchecked conversion was found while reviewing
CodeQL's integer-conversion findings.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/fs/proc/util.c#L3-L23

source.title: Disable glibc rseq in the systrap test process
source.body:
Disable glibc rseq in the systrap test process

Systrap forks a stub and unmaps the address space it inherits from the
parent. When glibc has registered a restartable sequences area, the
kernel can still access that area after the stub unmaps it. In race
builds the test hangs waiting for the stub to finish a munmap, before
it can exercise a single context switch.

Start the test with the same glibc tunable that runsc sets for a sentry
linked with cgo. The tunable must be present when glibc starts.

source.title: Reject noncanonical file descriptor names in procfs
source.body:
Reject noncanonical file descriptor names in procfs

Linux exposes descriptor 3 as /proc/self/fd/3. Looking up fd/03 or
fd/+3 returns ENOENT, and fdinfo follows the same rule [1]. gVisor
accepted both spellings because its descriptor lookups used a signed
integer parser.

both the canonical name and the aliases against an open descriptor.

prs.title: Preserve SACK on connections accepted with SYN cookies
prs.head: 0b06fce451fe2bff770f870740690f3e1772b859

items.body:
LGTM. The encoding is a correct, minimal version of Linux's `cookie_init_timestamp()` / `cookie_timestamp_decode()`. Rounding the TSval down keeps timestamps monotonic, and the cookie's authentication bits are unchanged. The PR merges cleanly onto current master. Non-blocking suggestions:

1. **Test gap:** add a cookie case with TS on, the peer *not* offering SACK, and stack SACK enabled. That is the "clear the bit" path, and nothing covers it now. The removed `sackPermitted:false` cookie case used to cover something similar. A cookie case with SACK offered but no TS would pin the fallback.
2. Reference Linux `cookie_init_timestamp()` / `cookie_timestamp_decode()` (`net/ipv4/syncookies.c`) in a comment next to the encode/decode, and make the `cookieTimestampSACK` comment say what the bit means.
3. `protocol.sackPermitted()`: add a doc comment and `// +checklocksexclude:p.mu`, as on the neighbouring accessors.
4. PR description / commit message: mention the `sackPermitted()` cleanup in `connect.go`/`endpoint.go`/`protocol.go`. Also note that cookies apply when `TCPAlwaysUseSynCookies` is set, not only "when the SYN queue fills".
5. Optional: extend `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_syncookie_test.go` to check that the cookie SYN-ACK echoes SACK-permitted, for Linux parity. Possible follow-up: encode window scale the same way, as Linux does.

**Security:** I see no security impact. The change only affects netstack and adds no host interaction. The SYN-cookie authentication bits are unchanged, and the only new peer-controlled input is the TSecr low bit. That bit can only enable SACK, which any peer could already negotiate, and `maybeEnableSACKPermitted()` still gates it on the stack setting. SACK state stays bounded by the existing scoreboard limit and the accept-queue limit.

---

Updated in 0b06fce451. The new cases check both the SACK option on the SYN-ACK and the accepted socket’s behavior when a packet arrives out of order.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Thanks — all comments addressed; the new cookie_no_peer_sack / cookie_no_timestamp cases pin the clear-bit and no-TS paths nicely. LGTM. (Extending the packetimpact syncookie test to check SACK-permitted remains a nice-to-have follow-up.)

nit: say what the bit means rather than who echoes it, and point at Linux. E.g.:
`// cookieTimestampSACK is the bit of the SYN-ACK TSval that records SACK negotiation for SYN cookie connections; the peer returns it in TSecr. See Linux's TS_OPT_SACK in net/ipv4/syncookies.c.`
The constant now describes the negotiated SACK bit in the SYN-ACK timestamp and points to Linux’s `TS_OPT_SACK`.

Consider adding "Analogous to Linux's cookie_init_timestamp()." Linux uses the low 6 TSval bits (WS, SACK, ECN) and rounds down the same way. That would also make a follow-up that recovers window scale here easy to spot.
Added the `cookie_init_timestamp()` reference and explained the reason for rounding down: the first data packet’s timestamp must not go backward.

nit: reference Linux's cookie_timestamp_decode() here. FWIW Linux rejects the cookie if this bit is set while SACK is now disabled. gVisor's `maybeEnableSACKPermitted()` just ignores the bit, which is fine, but a short note on the difference would help.
The decode site now points to `cookie_timestamp_decode()`. If SACK was turned off before the final ACK, gVisor accepts the connection without SACK; Linux rejects that cookie.
Please add a doc comment and `// +checklocksexclude:p.mu` to match `Option`/`SetOption`/`SendBufferSize`.
Added the method comment and `+checklocksexclude:p.mu`. The ordinary handshake and the cookie path both read the setting under that lock.

Every case now has the peer offer SACK. Under cookies, nothing covers TS on, peer *not* offering SACK, and stack SACK enabled, which is the path where the bit must be cleared. If the bit were always set, this test would still pass (the sack=false subtests are hidden by the stack check). `TestSackDisabledAccept` sends no TS, so it never reaches the new code. Could you add a peer-SACK dimension, plus a cookie case with no TS, to pin the fallback?

Added both cases: timestamps without a SACK offer, and a SACK offer without timestamps. The test checks the actual SYN-ACK option and whether the accepted socket reports a gap. The [packet test also passed on Linux and netstack](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/3b4196fa-7d21-4522-b081-f37d967e43e6).

Optional: worth a short comment that TSecr isn't covered by the cookie hash, so this bit is peer-controlled. That's fine here: it can only request SACK, which the peer could negotiate anyway, and `maybeEnableSACKPermitted()` still checks the stack setting. If window scale is ever recovered this way (as Linux does), that value will need bounds-checking, since a peer controls it.
Documented that the cookie does not authenticate the echo. A peer can request SACK through that bit just as it can in the SYN, and neither path can override a disabled stack setting.

source.title: Preserve SACK on connections accepted with SYN cookies
source.body:
Preserve SACK on connections accepted with SYN cookies

When the SYN queue fills, or TCPAlwaysUseSynCookies is enabled, the
listener sends a cookie without remembering the peer's SACK offer. The
accepted socket then cannot report data that arrives beyond a hole.

Encode SACK negotiation in one bit of the SYN-ACK timestamp. Recover
it from the peer's echo after validating the cookie. This preserves the
sequence-number cookie's authentication bits. Linux also recovers TCP
options from the echoed timestamp [1].

Use the same locked protocol lookup for ordinary handshakes and cookies
so both respect the stack's SACK setting.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4bb9081d75c82ec4957c50034cb0ea449/net/ipv4/syncookies.c#L23-L83

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, well-measured memory reduction (about 624 B per inode for every `vfs.FileLocks` user), and it follows the same approach Linux uses for `inode->i_flctx` in `locks_get_lock_context()`. All accesses to the pointer happen under `Locks.mu`, the nil-tree paths are handled correctly, and the PR merges cleanly with current master. These nits are all optional:

1. Keep the `// locks is ...` field doc style and add the nil-until-first-lock note to it, instead of replacing the description.
2. Add a short comment at the allocation in `LockRegion` that references Linux's `locks_get_lock_context()` (allocates lazily, never on `F_UNLCK`).
3. Keep a `Preconditions: r.Start <= r.End.` line on the relocated `unlock`, since it still panics otherwise.
4. Consider extending `TestUnusedFileLocks` to also cover `LockRegion` on a zero-value `Locks` (lock → conflicting `TestRegion` → unlock).
5. Consider annotating the `locks` field with `// +checklocks:mu` so checklocks enforces the protection that the comment describes.

**Security:** I reviewed this against the SECURITY.md taxonomy and found no security impact. The change stays inside the Sentry and adds no host interactions or new validation paths. Every access to the lazily allocated tree happens under `Locks.mu`. Unlock and query on a nil tree get a terminal iterator, so they can't panic. Worst-case memory per inode is the same as before, so a sandboxed app gains no new DoS or memory-amplification lever.

source.title: Allocate advisory file lock trees on first use
source.body:
Allocate advisory file lock trees on first use

Each tmpfs inode reserves 640 bytes for POSIX and BSD advisory lock
trees, whether or not a process locks the file. Store a pointer to each
tree and allocate it under the existing mutex on the first lock
request. Querying or releasing a lock on an untouched file allocates
nothing.

On AMD64 this reduces a regular tmpfs file from 1,392 to 768 bytes and
a directory from 1,048 to 424 bytes. Each tree that is actually used
costs one 320-byte allocation. A checkpoint of a warmed Bazel server
contained 9,130 tmpfs inodes and just one separately allocated lock
tree across the entire restored system [1][2].

prs.title: Clear the parent-death signal under the task mutex
prs.head: ff770a72187cd725f6679dc0246062ce1b72fe8b

items.body:
LGTM. This fixes a real data race: `parentDeathSignal` was documented as guarded by `t.mu`, and parent exit reads it under `t.mu`, but `commitIDChange` and the two exec paths wrote it without the lock. Routing those writes through `SetParentDeathSignal` and enforcing `+checklocks:mu` is the right fix. There are no lock-ordering concerns: the writers hold no other kernel locks, and the reader's order is `TaskSet.mu` → `Task.mu`. Semantics still match Linux's `commit_creds()` / `begin_new_exec()`, and the existing `uidgid.cc`/`prctl.cc` tests cover the behavior. The change applies cleanly to current master, which still has the unlocked writes.

**Security:** No security impact: the change only takes `Task.mu` around existing `parentDeathSignal = 0` stores, removing a data race on an in-sandbox privilege-boundary field without changing Linux-visible semantics. It adds no host interaction, new untrusted-input handling, or lock-order risk, since the new `Task.mu` acquisitions are leaf locks taken with no other kernel locks held. The `+checklocks:mu` annotation also guards against future unlocked accesses.

source.title: Clear the parent-death signal under the task mutex
source.body:
Clear the parent-death signal under the task mutex

An exiting parent reads its child's parent-death signal under the task
mutex. Credential changes and privileged exec clear the signal without
taking that mutex and can race with the read.

Use SetParentDeathSignal when installing new credentials or completing

source.title: tcp: ACK window overruns while FIN is unread
source.body:
After acknowledging a FIN, gVisor could silently discard data that
crossed the receive window's right edge. Linux sends an ACK when the
receive queue is still nonempty [1]. This matters when the application
has not consumed EOF, or has read only part of the data sent with FIN.

Check the payload end against the advertised window before processing
the closing state. Remember an unread standalone FIN until an ordinary
read consumes EOF. When the FIN carries data, draining the last byte
empties the receive queue; no separate EOF read is necessary.

The packet tests exercise both cases on Linux and netstack. They also
check that peeking at EOF leaves the FIN pending and that the same
overrun gets no reply after the application drains the queue.

All 56 netstack cases passed, as did 54 of 56 on Linux 7.0 [2]. Both
new cases and all closing-state cases passed on both stacks. The two
Linux failures are in the unchanged established-state test: it expects
silence after an invalid ACK at offsets 1 and 2, but Linux replied.
On the same Linux kernel, those two cases also failed on the parent
without this change [3]. The separate fix in #16378 covers them.

items.body: [🤖] PR merged as 89a4c4973f51a7db4cc2250080d2b6fa77aae9c0

LGTM. This is a small fix that keeps `rcvWnd` consistent with what goes on the wire, and it matches Linux's `tcp_select_window()`, which stores the scale-aligned `new_win` in `tp->rcv_wnd`. The test extension reproduces the premature reopen after a scaled-zero advertisement. The PR rebases cleanly on current master. Optional nits:

1. `receiver.acceptable()` is now partly redundant. Its comment ("r.rcvWnd could be much larger than the window size we advertised") is no longer true, and its clamp/round-down is a no-op. Consider simplifying it to `RcvNxt.Add(r.rcvWnd)`, here or in a follow-up.
2. Consider pointing the new `rcv.go` comment at the Linux equivalent (`tcp_select_window()`) rather than listing the consumers.
3. FYI: Linux rounds the retained window up (`ALIGN(cur_win, 1 << rcv_wscale)`) so it never shrinks. gVisor rounds down. Now that the rounded value is stored, the keep-current-window branch can move the right edge left by up to `2^wscale−1` per ACK when `toGrow` is false. The grow branch corrects it for MSS-sized traffic, so I don't think it needs changing, but a sentence in the commit message would help future readers.

**Security:** No security impact. The change only makes `r.rcvWnd` match the scale-aligned window that is actually advertised, which can only make it smaller. It adds no host interactions, allocations, locks, or panics, and the shift cannot overflow because `scaledWnd ≤ 0xFFFF` and the locally chosen scale is at most 14. Peer- and app-driven inputs reach the same bounded window and buffer logic as before.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

@EtiennePerot, could you re-review [the receive-window update](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/compare/68bb9a238540e16c5784dc0153e9d15a7d94a3a7...f5e35772f5ff7143e634613dc55a0e2356556cec)? Lucas found that rounding could withdraw space already advertised. The receiver now preserves those bytes, and the wire test checks the right edge as well as the zero-window probe you reviewed.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Thanks, this addresses everything. acceptable() now uses the stored window, and the retained window rounds up like Linux's ALIGN(cur_win, 1 << rcv_wscale) in tcp_select_window(), so already-advertised space is never retracted. The extended test covers both the right edge and the scaled-zero probe. LGTM.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Nit: suggest `// Like Linux's tcp_select_window(), remember the window as the peer decodes it.` instead of listing consumers.

Follow-up: with `r.rcvWnd` now always `<= MaxUint16 << RcvWndScale` and scale-aligned, the clamp/round-down in `acceptable()` is a no-op. Its comment ("r.rcvWnd could be much larger than the window size we advertised") is also stale. Consider simplifying it to `header.Acceptable(segSeq, segLen, r.RcvNxt, r.RcvNxt.Add(r.rcvWnd))`.
`acceptable` now uses `rcvWnd` directly. The SYN advertises an unscaled window, and subsequent ACKs store the window as the peer decodes it.

FYI: Linux rounds the retained window up in the no-shrink path (`ALIGN(cur_win, 1 << rcv_wscale)` in `tcp_select_window()`), but this rounds down. Now that the rounded value is stored, the `else { newWnd = curWnd }` branch can move the right edge left by up to `2^wscale-1` per ACK when `toGrow` is false (MSS-sized traffic gets corrected by the grow branch). Fine by me given this test's scaled-zero premise; maybe mention it in the commit message.

This did reproduce: after 50,000 bytes, the previous head advertised 555,328 remaining where it still owed the peer 555,344. [The wire test](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/d6e64bdd-82d4-483a-8c68-ee426eaacdd4) now checks that every ACK covers the unconsumed bytes. [The amended receiver](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/f5e35772f5ff7143e634613dc55a0e2356556cec) rounds up when rounding down would retract that space. The same test also checks that the window eventually reaches zero and stays closed after a partial read.
Nit: the second sentence could be shortened to "A probe must still see a zero window."
Shortened the comment to say that the probe must still see a zero window.

source.title: tcp: remember the advertised receive window
source.body:
tcp: remember the advertised receive window

After advertising a zero window, a probe following a partial application
read received a 50,016-byte window even though the available space
remained below the reopening threshold. Window scaling had discarded low
bits from the packet header but left them in rcvWnd, so the probe
skipped zero-window reopening checks.

Store the decoded advertised window after scaling and capping it. Extend
the existing scaled-window test with a partial read and a probe that
must still receive a zero-window ACK, before the remaining read reopens
it.
