source.title: tcp: preserve the receive window advertised to the peer
source.body:
tcp: preserve the receive window advertised to the peer

Window scaling discards low bits from the receive window. Remembering
the larger, unscaled value can make a zero-window probe reopen the
window before the application has drained enough data. Conversely,
rounding down the remaining window after a partial segment can
withdraw space already offered to data in flight.

Store the window as the peer decodes it. When rounding down would move
the right edge left, round up one window unit, as Linux does in
tcp_select_window() [1]. Use that same window when deciding whether
to accept an incoming segment.

Exercise both edges on the wire: ACK a byte inside the last window
unit without retracting the rest, then exhaust the window and check
that a partial read does not reopen it.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/fe584bc4c81b02bab4766513d57a33f5f4af02b3/net/ipv4/tcp_output.c#L295-L309

Load xtables matches before testing INET rules

A standalone INET comment rule fails with ENOENT on Linux when the
xt_comment module is not loaded. The kernel can request the IPv4 or
IPv6 module alias, but there is no alias for the combined INET family.

Query a supported IPv4 revision before installing an INET match rule.
Use a supported revision for setup even when the rule under test must
reject an unsupported one.

prs.title: tcp: report duplicate data below the cumulative ACK
prs.head: c451fa7d68e7b7809142c5daba0cd46a9cffe4fc

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, well-scoped addition of receiver-side D-SACK (RFC 2883). It follows Linux's `tcp_send_dupack()` / `tcp_data_queue()` → `tcp_dsack_set()` behaviour for duplicates below RCV.NXT, and the plumbing refactor keeps behaviour the same for existing callers. The e2e test covers the important cases (full duplicate with queued SACK ordering, partial duplicate filling a gap, no persistence, SACK disabled). It merges cleanly with current master, and the tcp e2e and unit tests pass locally.

Optional follow-ups / nits:
1. Linux also generates D-SACK for FIN-bearing segments (its `end_seq` counts FIN) and in non-ESTABLISHED synchronized states (FIN-WAIT-1/2, CLOSE-WAIT). The common "spurious retransmit of the final data+FIN" case therefore still gets no D-SACK. Please either widen the condition or add a comment explaining the limits, and mention them in the description.
2. Duplicates above RCV.NXT (`tcp_data_queue_ofo()` → `tcp_dsack_set()`/`tcp_dsack_extend()`) are a natural follow-up.
3. A `test/packetimpact` test would show parity with native Linux on the wire.
4. Add a doc comment to `Endpoint.sackBlocks`, settle on one RFC citation style, and shorten the comments slightly (see inline).

**PR description / commit message:**
Consider adding one sentence on scope: D-SACK is generated only in ESTABLISHED, not for FIN-bearing segments, and only for data below RCV.NXT (duplicates of out-of-order data are not yet reported).

**Security:** No security concerns. The new D-SACK generation runs entirely inside netstack under the existing endpoint lock. It only echoes the peer's own sequence range, capped at RCV.NXT, and it adds no host interaction, saved state, or reachable panic. It sends no more ACKs than the existing out-of-window/duplicate-data path already did, and it matches Linux `tcp_send_dupack()` / `tcp_data_queue()` behaviour.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Thanks — the FIN / non-ESTABLISHED D-SACK cases now match Linux tcp_send_dupack(), the queued-FIN case sends a single D-SACK FIN ACK, and the new test steps cover both. LGTM; D-SACK for out-of-order duplicates and a packetimpact parity test can come as follow-ups.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Linux D-SACKs here in any synchronized state and also for FIN-bearing segments (`tcp_send_dupack()` uses `end_seq`, which counts FIN), so a spurious retransmit of the final data+FIN gets no D-SACK from us. Fine as a follow-up, but please either relax the `state == StateEstablished` / FIN conditions or add a short comment explaining the limits. Optional shorter comment: `// Report only the already-acknowledged prefix (RFC 2883 section 4; Linux tcp_send_dupack()).`

Removed the established-state and data-only restrictions. The duplicate range now includes a FIN's sequence number. The receiver test replays both a data-plus-FIN segment and a bare FIN after the read half closes.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: shorter: `// Send after draining so the ACK covers any gap the new suffix filled (RFC 2883 section 4.2; Linux tcp_data_queue()).` Also, `!r.closed` drops the D-SACK when draining consumed a queued FIN (that FIN ACK goes out without it). That's rare and harmless, but worth a word in the comment if it's intentional.

The duplicate block now travels with the FIN ACK itself, including when the new suffix fills a gap and drains a queued FIN. The test checks that single cumulative ACK and its duplicate interval.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Please add a doc comment, e.g. `// sackBlocks returns the SACK blocks to include in an outgoing segment with the given flags.` Optional: rename it (e.g. `currentSACKBlocks`) so it doesn't share a name with the `sackBlocks` parameters of `sendRaw`/`sendEmptyRaw`/`makeOptions`.

Renamed the helper currentSACKBlocks and documented which outgoing segments receive the ordinary blocks.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: `sendEmptyRaw` is variadic but `sendRaw`/`sendEmptyAck` take a slice, so callers have to spread with `...`. A plain `[]header.SACKBlock` argument (`nil` at the handshake call sites) would be more consistent.

sendEmptyRaw now takes a slice, like sendRaw and sendEmptyAck. Handshake callers pass nil.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: one sentence is enough, e.g. `// sendDSACK sends an ACK whose first SACK block is duplicate, without adding it to the SACK history (RFC 2883 section 4).` Please also use one RFC citation style across the PR (currently `§4`, `, §4.2`, `, section 4`).

Shortened the description of sendDSACK and made the RFC 2883 references consistent.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: tcp: report duplicate data below the cumulative ACK
source.body:
tcp: report duplicate data below the cumulative ACK

A sender that retransmits data already acknowledged by the receiver
gets the same ACK it would get for a gap. With SACK negotiated, put
the duplicate sequence range in the first SACK block of the response
so the sender can recognize a spurious retransmission [1].

Report only the previously acknowledged prefix when a segment crosses
RCV.NXT. Advance the cumulative ACK through any queued data that the
new suffix makes contiguous. If that consumes a queued FIN, return the
duplicate block in its ACK. A retransmitted final segment also reports
the FIN's sequence number, as Linux tcp_send_dupack() does [2]. Keep
the duplicate block out of the receiver's ordinary SACK history.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2883#section-4
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c1fb1e9176028d02ef86f3cf76aa2476/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L4481-L4501

prs.title: Keep ssthresh on repeated TCP retransmission timeouts
prs.head: 8c03c2e9ce3d2e3a1db11d7a02ff519abd22c640

items.body:
Thanks, this is a real RFC 5681 §3.1 bug, and moving the cwnd=1 reset into the sender is a nice cleanup. Main concerns:

1. **Partial ACK diverges from Linux.** `tcp_ack()` clears `icsk_retransmits` on any SND.UNA advance, so `tcp_enter_loss()` reduces ssthresh again on the next RTO. The `partial_ack` case asserts the opposite. I'd replace the per-segment `rtoRetransmitted` flag with sender state that mirrors `icsk_retransmits` (set on a timer retransmit, cleared when SND.UNA advances). That also removes the new segment field and the split/clone reasoning.
2. **Local send errors.** Linux counts a failed timer retransmit (`tcp_update_rto_stats()` runs before `tcp_retransmit_skb()`). Matching that removes the `maybeSendSegment` signature change and the `rack.go`/`sack_recovery.go` churn. With cwnd = 1, only `Front()` can be sent, so `sendData` doesn't need to return a segment.
3. **Zero-window probes.** `s.zeroWindowProbing || …` forces a reduction even on a repeat. Linux's `tcp_probe_timer()` changes neither ssthresh nor cwnd. Please hold (or skip) here, or explain why reducing is intended. The current comment explains marking, not reducing.
4. **Tests.** The e2e test does tell old from new behavior. Please add a packetimpact test comparing `tcpi_snd_ssthresh` against Linux after repeated RTOs, with and without a partial ACK. Also add a third expiry and a SACK-enabled variant.
5. **Nits.** Keep a short RFC 5681 "LW = 1 segment" note at `s.SndCwnd = 1`, cite `tcp_enter_loss()`, and fix "split imposed by the send window" in the description (the split comes from the 1-MSS cwnd budget). Possible follow-up: an RTO during fast recovery still reduces ssthresh twice, unlike Linux.

**PR description / commit message:**
"after any split imposed by the send window": the split here comes from the 1-MSS cwnd budget (it also caps GSO), not the peer's window. Please also mention that the cwnd=1 reset moved from `HandleRTOExpired` into the sender, and state the Linux behavior being matched (`tcp_enter_loss()`), including how partial ACKs are handled.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Linux `tcp_enter_loss()` keeps ssthresh only while in Loss with `icsk_retransmits != 0`, and `tcp_ack()` clears that on *any* SND.UNA advance, including a partial ACK of the retransmitted segment. Could this be a sender field (e.g. `rtoRepeat bool`) set after the timer retransmit and cleared in `handleRcvdSegment` when SND.UNA advances? That matches Linux, drops `segment.rtoRetransmitted`, and avoids reasoning about splits. Please also cite `tcp_enter_loss()` here.

Moved the state to the sender. A cumulative ACK that advances SndUna clears it, including an ACK for part of the oldest segment. A SACK-only ACK does not. The loss path now cites Linux tcp_enter_loss().

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Why force a reduction for zero-window probes? Linux handles these in `tcp_probe_timer()`/`tcp_send_probe0()`, which change neither ssthresh nor cwnd. Here every probe expiry pushes Reno's ssthresh to 2 (`Outstanding` is 0). Holding (`false`) seems closer to Linux. If reducing is intended, the comment should say why. Right now it only explains why probes don't mark data.

Agreed. A zero receive window with no bytes in flight now sends a persist probe before changing cwnd or ssthresh. The existing zero-window test checks both values at the actual probe. A window that shrinks while data is outstanding still enters the retransmission path; Linux distinguishes these cases in tcp_probe_timer() and tcp_retransmit_timer().

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Keep a short reason from the deleted CC code: `// RFC 5681 section 3.1: LW is one segment regardless of IW.` (Linux: `tcp_snd_cwnd_set(tp, tcp_packets_in_flight(tp) + 1)` in `tcp_enter_loss()`.)

Restored the RFC 5681 section 3.1 explanation next to the one-segment loss window.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

With cwnd = 1 and `writeNext == writeList.Front()`, only `Front()` can be sent here. Linux also counts the attempt when `tcp_retransmit_skb()` fails locally (`icsk_retransmits` is bumped in `tcp_update_rto_stats()` before the retransmit). If we follow Linux, this can be `if s.writeNext != s.writeList.Front() { … }` (or set the sender flag unconditionally), and `sendData`/`maybeSendSegment` keep their old signatures.

The sender now records the attempt before calling sendData, so a local transmit failure does not turn the next timeout into another first timeout.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

The error return only exists to exclude locally failed retransmits from the repeat marker, which Linux doesn't do (see the comment on 694). Consider reverting this along with the `rack.go`/`sack_recovery.go` call sites.

Reverted those send signatures and their RACK and SACK call-site changes. The retry decision no longer depends on a segment transmission return value.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Nit: document the parameter instead: "HandleRTOExpired is invoked when the retransmit timer expires. reduceThreshold is false on a repeated timeout, when ssthresh must be held (RFC 5681 section 3.1)."

Documented reduceThreshold on HandleRTOExpired, including the RFC 5681 section 3.1 condition for retaining ssthresh.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

If the repeat state moves to the sender (see snd.go:644), this field and the `clone()` copy can go. Otherwise: it fits in existing padding (no size change) and is cleared by `newSegment()`, so that's fine.

Removed the field and its clone copy from segment. Splitting or trimming a segment no longer carries congestion-control state.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
LGTM. This matches Linux: on a repeat, `bictcp_recalc_ssthresh()` isn't called, but `cubictcp_state(TCP_CA_Loss)` → `bictcp_reset()` still resets the epoch. Maybe add a one-line reference to that.

Added the Linux references and kept the two effects separate: CUBIC restarts the epoch on every loss timeout, but a repeat does not recalculate ssthresh.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

On Linux, this partial ACK clears `icsk_retransmits`, so the second RTO calls `ssthresh()` again and you'd get `max(cwnd/2, 2)`, not 5/7. Unless there's a reason to differ, this case should expect a reduction. A packetimpact test reading `tcpi_snd_ssthresh` on the DUT would settle it against native Linux.

Confirmed with [the same packetimpact test on Linux and gVisor](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/41a38860-e1bf-4a91-8278-ea68ef60b656). Linux 5.15 Reno held ssthresh at 5 when no bytes were ACKed; after an ACK for 268 of the oldest segment’s 536 bytes, the next timeout reduced it to 2. gVisor now holds at 4 with no ACK and reduces it to 2 after 250 of 500 bytes. In both cases the retransmission began at the first unacknowledged byte. The [packet fixture](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/1b7e2b178966a50105b7cfbb15f29d1b1c13a647/test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go#L93) reads TCP_INFO after matching that sequence. The deterministic regression now expects the reduction.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Consider a third `expire` in `same_segment` to show the hold persists past the second RTO, and a SACK-enabled variant (the RTO path resets the scoreboard, and `sendData` skips SACKed segments).

Added a third expiry and a SACK-only case for Reno and CUBIC. With no cumulative progress, the third timeout still holds the first threshold. The SACK case reports the second segment while leaving the first unacknowledged.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

source.title: tcp: preserve timeout recovery until the outstanding flight is acknowledged
source.body:
After an RTO, RACK can enter fast recovery before the pre-timeout flight has
been acknowledged. A new SACK can also replace `RTORecovery` with `Disorder`.
Re-entering fast recovery counts the old flight against the reduced congestion
window again, stalling transmission until the next, doubled RTO.

Reproduce by dropping the initial congestion window and its tail loss probe,
then acknowledging the RTO retransmissions. The regression also delivers the
third retransmission before the second and exercises a real reordering-timer
expiry. Recovery should finish through ACKs, without another RTO.

Preserve `RTORecovery` in duplicate-ACK handling and guard both RACK recovery
entry paths, following [RFC 6582 §3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6582.html#section-3.2), [RFC 8985 §9.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8985.html#section-9.3), and [RFC 6675 §5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6675.html#section-5.1).
The guards act only after an RTO, while that recovery state remains active.
RACK loss marking and SACK bookkeeping continue; the existing ACK boundary
ends timeout recovery.

This change was written with help from OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, and I
reviewed it before sending.

Testing: On master `a9e9db4`, all three RACK cases fail on recovery state
without the fix, while SACK passes. With the fix, all four pass, including
25 runs each. Removing each guard fails its intended case while SACK passes.
The TCP and tcpip Bazel suites also pass: 25 and 198 test targets respectively
([GitHub Actions](https://github.com/AyoubAchour/net-switch/actions/runs/39496207361),
Bazel 8.8.1, Ubuntu x64).

prs.title: Reject writes to immutable proc task directories
prs.head: 542182833d848ed8eee0289ef59275cad83079d1

items.body:
Thanks. Modeling `S_IMMUTABLE` on `/proc/PID` and `/proc/PID/task/TID` in `taskOwnedInode.CheckPermissions` is the right approach, and the rename and `access(2)` results now match `inode_permission()`/`may_delete()`.

1. **Regression (blocking):** kernfs `OpenAt` calls `CheckPermissions(ats)` before its "directory opened for writing" EISDIR check. With this PR, a root `open("/proc/self", O_WRONLY|O_RDWR)` returns EPERM instead of EISDIR. Linux's `may_open()` returns `-EISDIR` for a directory with `MAY_WRITE` before calling `inode_permission()`, and `do_open()` does the same for `O_CREAT` on an existing directory. Please move the EISDIR checks ahead of `CheckPermissions` in kernfs `OpenAt` (the plain, `rp.Done()`, and existing-child paths). Add `open(dir, O_WRONLY)` and `open(dir, O_RDWR)` → EISDIR cases to `ImmutableTaskDirectories`, with and without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. This also fixes the existing non-root EACCES-vs-EISDIR divergence.
2. Please give the inline `interface{ CheckSyntheticMountpointWrite(...) }` assertion a name, and update the `checkCreateLocked` doc comment to say `forSyntheticMountpoint` also bypasses immutability. Optionally, consider dropping the carve-out: no current caller creates synthetic mountpoints under `/proc/<pid>`, and Linux would reject such a mkdir anyway.
3. Nits: use `linuxerr.Equals` in the new Go test, like the neighboring tests, and drop the `errors` import. The `CheckPermissions` comment could name `proc_pid_instantiate()`/`proc_task_instantiate()` as the source of `S_IMMUTABLE`.

The branch is up to date with master; there are no conflicts in the touched files.

**Security:** No security impact. The change only adds an EPERM deny path for `MayWrite` on `/proc/PID` and `/proc/PID/task/TID`, which matches Linux `S_IMMUTABLE`. The synthetic-mountpoint carve-out runs exactly the owner/mode check that existed before and is reachable only from runtime mount setup, not from sandboxed syscalls. No new host interactions, panics, allocations, or locks are introduced.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Thanks for moving the directory `EISDIR` checks into `Dentry.mayOpen` ahead of `CheckPermissions` and adding the `OpenImmutableTaskDirectories` syscall tests. Everything looks good.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-By: Claude

This now returns EPERM before kernfs `OpenAt` reaches its EISDIR check, so a root `open("/proc/self", O_WRONLY)` changes from EISDIR (matching Linux) to EPERM. Linux's `may_open()` returns `-EISDIR` for `S_IFDIR` + `MAY_WRITE` before `inode_permission()`. Please move the dir+write (and `O_CREAT` on an existing dir) EISDIR checks in kernfs `OpenAt` ahead of `CheckPermissions`. Nit: the comment could name the source of the flag, e.g. "Linux's proc_pid_instantiate() and proc_task_instantiate() set S_IMMUTABLE, which inode_permission() checks before mode bits."

Moved the existing-directory checks ahead of CheckPermissions. Writable opens, O_TRUNC, and O_CREAT without O_EXCL on an existing directory now return EISDIR before procfs checks immutability. The procfs comment now names proc_pid_instantiate(), proc_task_instantiate(), and inode_permission().

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16473/commits/9e15e32f54af24eaf3b465b364148b93fe581e45).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Please make this a named (unexported) interface instead of an inline one, so the hook is discoverable. Also update the `checkCreateLocked` doc comment above: `forSyntheticMountpoint` now also bypasses inode immutability. (Optional: is the carve-out needed? Nothing creates synthetic mountpoints under `/proc/<pid>` today, and plain EPERM would be simpler.)

Named the interface syntheticMountpointWriter and updated checkCreateLocked’s comment. I kept the exception for MakeSyntheticMountpoint: the runtime can create an in-memory mountpoint under a live PID or TID without changing the proc inode. The test drops only effective CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE for the denied attempt, requires EACCES, then verifies that the original credentials succeed.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16473/commits/9e15e32f54af24eaf3b465b364148b93fe581e45).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Nit: use `linuxerr.Equals(linuxerr.EACCES, err)` like `TestSyntheticMountpointCreation` above, and drop the `errors` import.

I tried linuxerr.Equals here. MakeSyntheticMountpoint wraps the original EACCES twice with %w, and linuxerr.Equals compares its argument directly; the test failed with “permission denied” on both the PID and TID paths. The neighboring test calls MkdirAt directly and receives the unwrapped errno. I kept errors.Is(err, linuxerr.EACCES) here so we check the actual MakeSyntheticMountpoint operation and still require that exact cause.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16473/commits/9e15e32f54af24eaf3b465b364148b93fe581e45).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Please also add `open(dir, O_WRONLY)` and `open(dir, O_RDWR)` → `EISDIR` here, both with and without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. Linux's `may_open()` returns EISDIR before the immutable check, and gVisor currently returns EPERM with this change.

Added ProcTask.OpenImmutableTaskDirectories for /proc/self and /proc/thread-self, with and without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE when available. It checks O_WRONLY, O_RDWR, O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC, and O_CREAT|O_RDONLY for EISDIR. Linux passed; both gVisor modes failed on the previous code and passed with the reordered check.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16473/commits/9e15e32f54af24eaf3b465b364148b93fe581e45).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, correct fix: forcing `--gofer-network-namespace=new` keeps runsc's pinned null-netns bind mount out of the per-sandbox `--root`, so `close()` and caller-owned temp dirs can be removed again. `shared_root` is a reasonable opt-in for callers that want to keep sharing the netns. The branch merges cleanly with master. Non-blocking suggestions:

1. Please add a mock-based unit test in `sandboxexec/sandbox/python/tests/sandbox_test.py` covering three cases: the default argv includes `--gofer-network-namespace=new`, `shared_root` yields `--shared-root <dir>` without forcing `new`, and `shared_root=""` raises `ValueError`.
2. Consider `os.path.abspath(shared_root)`, for consistency with how bind-mount sources are normalized.
3. PR description: mention that callers reusing one `runtime_dir` across sandboxes no longer share the null netns implicitly and should pass `shared_root`. Also note why this differs from the Go SDK, which calls `specutils.UnmountNullNetNS` in `Close()`.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Thanks for addressing the feedback — adding the unit tests, normalizing `shared_root` with `os.path.abspath`, and clarifying the stacked-mount cleanup docs and PR description. LGTM.

[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Could you add a mock-based test in tests/sandbox_test.py for this branch? It should check that the default argv contains `--gofer-network-namespace=new`, that `shared_root=d` yields `--shared-root d` without `new`, and that `shared_root=""` raises ValueError. The existing tests only `assertIn` other flags, so a regression here would go unnoticed (CI likely runs rootless, where `null` already falls back to `new`).

Added constructor tests for all three cases: the default starts the gofer in a new namespace, an explicit shared root replaces that flag, and an empty value raises ValueError without invoking runsc.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16492/commits/ca87e0a2feca78a38602066c0c70a8c8b78c3133).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Nit: `os.path.abspath(shared_root)` would match how bind-mount sources are normalized in `_normalize_mounts`.

An explicit shared_root is now made absolute relative to the caller's working directory, as with the bind mount source. The test supplies a relative path and checks the exact path passed to runsc.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16492/commits/ca87e0a2feca78a38602066c0c70a8c8b78c3133).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Concurrent cold starts can stack several bind mounts on `null-netns` (see `pinNullNetNS`), so a single `umount` may not be enough. Consider "must unmount all mounts on its null-netns file (e.g. `umount` until it fails) before removing it."

Confirmed in pinNullNetNS: concurrent first users can stack bind mounts on the same file. The API now tells callers to wait for all users and unmount every layer before removing the shared directory.

[Amended commit](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16492/commits/ca87e0a2feca78a38602066c0c70a8c8b78c3133).

prs.title: Compare UDP checksums as transmitted on the wire
prs.head: beb37f745205fd9a9c9ef0a248787377d22e8d2a

items.body:
LGTM. This fixes a real flake. The old UDP expectations ignored RFC 768's computed-zero → `0xffff` encoding, and they sometimes seeded a `0` (checksum-disabled) field that the update methods correctly left alone. I reproduced it with a standalone simulation of the source-port path: ≈2/65536 failures per random trial under the old assertion (a few percent per test run), and 0 under the new one. The new expectations match Linux (`udp_send_skb()`, and `__udp_manip_pkt()` mapping a zero result to `CSUM_MANGLED_0`).

Optional nits:
1. The two deterministic triples only exercise the zero transition for the source-port update. Adding `check(0xfffe, 1, 2)` and `check(0xfffe, 2, 1)` would cover `SetDestinationPortWithChecksumUpdate` as well.
2. Consider saying in the PR description/commit message that this fixes a flaky test, to help with CI triage.

---

Nit: these triples only hit the computed-zero transition in the "Source port" subtest; the destination-port update lands on ordinary values. Consider also adding `check(0xfffe, 1, 2)` and `check(0xfffe, 2, 1)` so `SetDestinationPortWithChecksumUpdate` is covered too.

prs.title: Keep timed-out SACK recovery from restarting
prs.head: b7d9ced514fd9ea5d4159b36b42ae16a22dbe634

contexts.name: scan-pr
contexts.workflow: Google GitHub Admin: Actions Workflow Security Scan

source.title: tcp: preserve timeout recovery until the outstanding flight is acknowledged
source.body:
After an RTO, RACK can enter fast recovery before the pre-timeout flight has
been acknowledged. A new SACK can also replace `RTORecovery` with `Disorder`.
Re-entering fast recovery counts the old flight against the reduced congestion
window again, stalling transmission until the next, doubled RTO.

Reproduce by dropping the initial congestion window and its tail loss probe,
then acknowledging the RTO retransmissions. The regression also delivers the
third retransmission before the second and exercises a real reordering-timer
expiry. Recovery should finish through ACKs, without another RTO.

Preserve `RTORecovery` in duplicate-ACK handling and guard both RACK recovery
entry paths, following [RFC 6582 §3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6582.html#section-3.2), [RFC 8985 §9.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8985.html#section-9.3), and [RFC 6675 §5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6675.html#section-5.1).
The guards act only after an RTO, while that recovery state remains active.
RACK loss marking and SACK bookkeeping continue; the existing ACK boundary
ends timeout recovery.

This change was written with help from OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, and I
reviewed it before sending.

Testing: On master `a9e9db4`, all three RACK cases fail on recovery state
without the fix, while SACK passes. With the fix, all four pass, including
25 runs each. Removing each guard fails its intended case while SACK passes.
The TCP and tcpip Bazel suites also pass: 25 and 198 test targets respectively
([GitHub Actions](https://github.com/AyoubAchour/net-switch/actions/runs/39496207361),
Bazel 8.8.1, Ubuntu x64).

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, test-only change that does what it says:

1. The `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` drop is the right fix for `TestCreateController`. `generic_permission()` would otherwise let a privileged worker create the subdirectory under the 0555 parent. The only cleanups that run afterwards are owner-permitted `chmod` and `RemoveAll`, so they keep working.
2. The extracted `capabilitytest.DropEffective` keeps the old thread-safety properties and makes the failure path simpler: the modified thread is always discarded instead of being restored on a best-effort basis.
3. I checked the remaining `runsc/cgroup` tests, and none of them need a host cgroup mount or D-Bus, so removing `local` looks safe.
4. Optional nit: mention in the package doc that importing `capabilitytest` locks main to the initial thread through `init()`.

The PR merges cleanly into current master.

Optional nit: since importing this package changes the whole test binary (main is locked to the initial thread in `init()`), it may be worth saying so in the package doc, e.g. "Importing this package reserves the initial thread for main."

3. Optional nit: mention that this mirrors Linux's `eventpoll_release_file()`, which also drops `file->f_lock` before taking `ep->mtx`.

The PR is based on a recent master and neither touched file has changed since, so I expect no conflicts.

source.title: Check locking of file epoll registrations
source.body:
Check locking of file epoll registrations

FileDescription keeps a reverse index of epoll registrations so that the
last close can remove the file from every interested epoll instance.
Add a checklocks annotation for the mutex that protects the index.

Last close detaches the index under epollMu and then drops the mutex
before taking interestMu. Registration and deletion acquire those locks
in the opposite order.

source.title: Benchmark complete kernel state files
source.body:
Benchmark complete kernel state files

The Encode benchmark discarded each write from state.Save. It measured the
kernel object graph but omitted the statefile writer, the separately saved
CPUID and the final flush used by a split checkpoint.

Encode those objects into a reusable in-memory buffer using the input
checkpoint's metadata and compression. Include writer creation and close
in the measurement, then decode the result outside the timer so an
incomplete file cannot produce a successful measurement. Keep host file
descriptor setup and cleanup outside both benchmark timers, including on
failure.

The pages and their metadata remain separate; this measures no disk I/O.
Report the complete encoded state-file size instead of the kernel-only
byte count.

Related to #16216.

prs.title: Roll back failed epoll registrations
prs.head: 9f6054c77876e2e36acce5c3fed7d81ad3c9e5c9

items.body:
LGTM. The fix is small and correct: on `EventRegister` failure, `AddInterest` now cleans up through `removeLocked`. This removes both the orphaned interest (`EEXIST` on retry) and any ready-list entry queued by an early notification, mirroring Linux `fs/eventpoll.c:ep_insert()` (`ep_remove_safe()`). All fallible in-tree `EventRegister` implementations unregister their waiter before returning an error, the `interestMu -> readyMu` lock order is unchanged, and the unit test covers both symptoms.

Notes:
- This supersedes #13245, which only reorders the map insert and misses the queued-event case; please close #13245 when this lands.
- Possible follow-up (out of scope here): `ModifyInterest` has a similar pre-existing issue when re-registration fails.

**Security:** No security concerns. The change only adds Sentry-internal cleanup through `removeLocked` on `EPOLL_CTL_ADD` failure, with no new host syscalls, seccomp changes, or host-FD handling, and closes a pre-existing in-sandbox SelfDoS where repeated failed `EPOLL_CTL_ADD` calls (e.g. on an unconnected `/dev/fuse`) pinned orphaned interests.

source.title: epoll: avoid orphaned interest on EventRegister failure
source.body:
## Problem

`EpollInstance.AddInterest` inserts the new `epollInterest` into `ep.interest` before registering with the file, and adds it to `file.epolls` only after registration succeeds:

```go
ep.interest[key] = epi
wmask := waiter.EventMaskFromLinux(mask)
epi.waiter.Init(epi, wmask)
if err := file.EventRegister(&epi.waiter); err != nil {
	return err
}
...
file.epolls[epi] = struct{}{}
```

If `file.EventRegister` fails, `AddInterest` returns with `epi` in `ep.interest` but never in `file.epolls`.

The interest-removal paths rely on `ep.interest` and `file.epolls` staying in sync: `EpollInstance.Release` walks `ep.interest`, and the `FileDescription.DecRef` path walks `file.epolls`. An entry present in `ep.interest` but not `file.epolls` is orphaned, and it keeps the target `*FileDescription` reachable past its own release.

`EventRegister` fails deterministically for an unprivileged caller. For example, `epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_ADD)` on an opened-but-unmounted `/dev/fuse` FD reaches `fuse.DeviceFD.EventRegister`, which returns `EPERM` when the device is not connected.

## Change

Move `ep.interest[key] = epi` to after `EventRegister` succeeds. `epi` is then added to `ep.interest` and `file.epolls` only on the success path, with no fallible call between the two inserts, so a failed registration leaves nothing behind. A short comment records the ordering requirement.

## Scope

Hardening. A bounded per-`epoll_ctl` leak plus a stale `*FileDescription` reference, reachable by an unprivileged process.

source.title: Roll back failed epoll registrations
source.body:
Roll back failed epoll registrations

EPOLL_CTL_ADD inserted an interest before registering its waiter.
Ievgen Bondarenko reported that a registration error left that interest
in the map [1]. Retrying the add then returned EEXIST. A file can also
notify its waiter before returning an error, leaving a readable event
that epoll_wait can deliver for a registration that never succeeded.

Use the EPOLL_CTL_DEL removal path to discard both the interest and
any queued event. Exercise both cases with a file that signals
readability and then returns ENOSPC from registration.

[1]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/13245

Reported-by: Ievgen Bondarenko <sactransport2000@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: Ievgen Bondarenko <sactransport2000@gmail.com>

items.body:
LGTM. This is a clean, self-contained checklocks conversion:

1. All accesses to `Inotify.{events,scratch}` (`evMu`), `Inotify.{nextWatchMinusOne,watches}` (`mu`), and `Watches.ws` (`mu`), as well as callers of `newWatchLocked` and `nextWatchIDLocked`, hold the required locks, and generated stateify methods already carry `+checklocksignore`.
2. Updating the `evMu` doc comment to cover `scratch` fixes the prior mismatch with `scratch`'s own comment, and keeping `evMu` separate from `mu` preserves the `Inotify.mu -> Watches.mu -> Inotify.evMu` lock order (mirroring Linux's `fsnotify_group::mark_mutex` vs `notification_lock` split).
3. The PR applies cleanly on current `master` (`pkg/sentry/vfs/inotify.go` is unchanged upstream).

Check inotify locking contracts

Inotify documented the locks protecting its event queue, serialization
scratch buffer, and watch state without making those requirements
checkable. Add field guards and preconditions for the helpers called
while allocating and registering watches.

Keep the separate event lock: notifications can arrive while a watch
collection is locked, so using the instance mutex there would invert
the established lock order.

prs.title: Build the runsc sidecars with the C toolchain
prs.head: e482579e11a4e098f069bdeb4c66677b36bc93ff

items.body:
Thanks for cleaning up the duplicated `genrule`s! Building the three freestanding C sidecars through `cc_binary` works cleanly with `@coral_crosstool`, and `fdparking_test`, `prewarmer_single_page_test`, and `procumounter_test` all pass locally.

A few changes are needed so this also builds cleanly on `buildkite/internal` (note that PR #14056 originally used `cc_binary` for `prewarmer` and had to switch to a `genrule` in `0bb1666bb` because of internal C++ toolchain defaults):

1. **Disable `tcmalloc` in `cc_binary`**: `//tools:defs.bzl`'s `cc_binary` wrapper defaults `tcmalloc = False` in `tools/bazeldefs/cc.bzl`, but defaults `tcmalloc = True` internally, which links an `alwayslink` C++ allocator into these `-nostdlib` binaries unless `tcmalloc = False` is passed.
2. **Disable internal C++ toolchain runtime/sanitizer features**: `features = ["-coverage", "-default_link_flags", "-pie"]` covers `@coral_crosstool`, where `-lstdc++` and `-lm` come from `default_link_flags`. Internally, `-lm`/`-latomic`, `-lpthread`, C++ `-u` symbol roots + default linker scripts, and alloc-token flags come from `-default_linker_libraries`, `-use_pthread`, `-static_linking_mode`, `-heap_partitioning`, and `-use_header_modules` (and sanitizer builds also inject linker `-fsanitize=...` flags and `--custom_malloc`, which `copts = ["-fno-sanitize=all"]` does not strip—similar to why `runsc` uses `noasan = True` in `runsc/BUILD`).
3. **`link_extra_lib = None` is a no-op**: Passing `None` to a Starlark rule attribute falls back to the attribute default, and `@rules_cc//cc:cc_binary.bzl` still appends `@rules_cc//:link_extra_lib` to `deps`. Either remove the line or pass an explicit empty `cc_library` target.
4. **Commit message / PR description nit**: The description says *"Keep the public target names and filenames used to embed the binaries in runsc."* The sidecars are no longer embedded in `runsc`—they are shipped alongside `runsc` under `gvisor-bin/` via `tools/release.bzl` (as `runsc/sidecar.bzl:1` notes), while the `out` paths in the build tree are used by `testutil.FindFile` in the sidecar tests.

---

`features = ["-coverage", "-default_link_flags", "-pie"]` only suppresses the default libraries in `@coral_crosstool` (where `-lstdc++` and `-lm` live in `default_link_flags`). In the internal C++ toolchain (`buildkite/internal`), `default_link_flags` instead carries `-nostdlib++`, while `-lm`/`-latomic`, `-lpthread`, C++ runtime `-u` roots + default linker scripts, alloc-token flags, and header modules come from separate default-enabled features—please also include `"-default_linker_libraries"`, `"-heap_partitioning"`, `"-static_linking_mode"`, `"-use_header_modules"`, and `"-use_pthread"` (toolchains ignore negative features they don't define).

Also note that `copts = ["-fno-sanitize=all"]` only applies to compile actions: under sanitizer configs, toolchain features still pass `-fsanitize=...` / `-fsanitize-link-c++-runtime` to the linker (and `--custom_malloc` overrides `malloc`), which fails under `-nostdlib`. If `buildkite/internal` exercises these targets under sanitizers, `cc_binary` in `//tools:defs.bzl` may need a `noasan = True` transition analogous to `go_binary` in `runsc/BUILD` (this is why `prewarmer` was switched from `cc_binary` to `genrule` in `0bb1666bb`).

I disabled the hosted linker features you listed and passed `-fno-sanitize=all` to the link as well as the compile. The public GNU and patched Clang link checks passed; I couldn’t run the internal toolchain. [e482579e1](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/e482579e1)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

`link_extra_lib = None` is a no-op here: passing `None` to a Starlark rule attribute falls back to its default target (despite a stale `rules_cc` docstring from native `cc_binary`), and `@rules_cc//cc:cc_binary.bzl` also unconditionally appends `@rules_cc//:link_extra_lib` to `deps` (`bazel cquery --output=build //runsc/fdparking:runsc-fd-parking` still shows `deps = ["@rules_cc//:link_extra_lib"]`). Either remove this line or point `link_extra_lib` at an explicit empty `cc_library` target.

Removed `link_extra_lib = None`. It didn’t change what `cc_binary` links.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Please pass `tcmalloc = False` here. `//tools:defs.bzl`'s `cc_binary` wrapper defaults `tcmalloc = False` in `tools/bazeldefs/cc.bzl`, but defaults `tcmalloc = True` internally (`buildkite/internal`), which links an `alwayslink = 1` C++ allocator into the binary and fails under `-nostdlib`.

Set `tcmalloc = False` on all three sidecars. The transition also selects Bazel’s empty allocator so a caller’s `--custom_malloc` cannot pull one back in.

source.title: Use the official server images in port-forward tests
source.body:
Use the official server images in port-forward tests

The Nginx and Redis test images install net-tools so the port-forward
tests can look for a listening socket. Poll the service itself instead:
wait for Nginx to return HTTP 200 and for Redis to reply PONG before
starting the forwarder. Both probes run inside the server container
with clients already present in the official images.

Pull the pinned Nginx 1.31.7 and Redis 7.0.12 images through the shared
Docker Hub mirror configuration. Bazel exports the requested Linux
architecture under the existing basic/nginx and basic/redis Make names.
This removes both Dockerfiles and their apt dependencies.

prs.title: pkg/state: add value and composite decoding to graph decoder (16/21)
prs.head: 3dd75fc57e6b26ab5b4d8378a7c66959c7f3b9f6

items.body:
A named map and its underlying map can refer to the same storage:

```go
type namedMap map[int]int
plain := map[int]int{1: 7}
named := namedMap(plain)
```

If two fields hold these views, `mapTarget` assigns them the same target
during Save, but `mapRef` rejects the second type during Load. I tried
the public Save/Load calls on the [integrated branch](https://github.com/manninglucas/gvisor/commit/8c93a8892c82c359fde47860db9af205c4d2015d):
[Save succeeds and Load fails](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/890ac53d-ef37-4d4d-8108-56e214145f3d).
The [legacy codec rejects this earlier, during Save](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/ebfc042e-c1c1-4d38-988d-9a2d652aa694).

Would you use the key and element types to check whether the views can
share the restored object? [That change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/compare/c397067e24d51f19438677832f8b1f05e7f5bcf5...d4d37d21a86a2bab7e8faef555720ae94ed2cda7)
[passes the regression](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/a65f9eed-848b-41d3-9549-1fed01490cfe):
writing through one restored field and deleting through the other both
work, and a third map with the same original contents stays independent.
If different map types are meant to be unsupported, Save should reject
the second view before it returns a checkpoint.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

@parth-opensrc this rejects two valid, partially overlapping slice views when the element size is three bytes and the lower-address view is discovered first. For example:

```go
var buf [4][3]byte
views := [][][3]byte{buf[0:3:3], buf[1:4:4]}
```

Here `co.addr` is three bytes below `lo`. Their difference wraps in `uintptr`; on AMD64 the resulting value has remainder 1 modulo 3. [Save fails with this order](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/a43efe4d-8466-4824-a4a4-cf5cfdab9fe7), but succeeds when the two views are reversed. Four-byte elements pass in either order, which is why a power-of-two fixture misses it.

[Comparing the two address residues](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/32f19f8c8b2bcc074077d67915edaecc96d87650) avoids underflow. [With that change](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/76bbe067-d8b8-4d00-9be6-a5fd60553867), Save and Load preserve shared addresses and writes through both views. Those runs used the integrated rewrite; this split has the same alignment check.

Investigated by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

@parth-opensrc `SetMapIndex` copies the value here, before the queued
callback in `decodeInterface` updates its data word. I reproduced this
with a `map[uint8]any` holding a one-pointer struct. Its load hook ran
once and set the pointer, but the map entry still contained nil. Restoring
the same value directly into an interface, or storing a pointer to the
struct in the map, preserved the pointer.

[The reproduction and original runs](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/57515e448870c7326844c3b4d761bc33f56fc730/.github/qualification/graph-map-word/evidence.md)
exercise this PR's decoder components. [Queuing insertion after the
entry's callbacks](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/eb5036b67218924be2e8925f578eefe956525c0d)
also preserves the values when two maps are decoded before either queue
drains. The queued insertion needs to retain the map itself because
`ds.mapPtr` is reused.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

prs.title: Avoid closing a registered mount promise waiter
prs.head: 8d9ce8738115e23dec693545967f2c21124df6df

items.body:
LGTM. Replacing `close(ch)` with `e.NotifyEvent(waiter.EventOut)` cleanly fixes the `send on closed channel` panic when `maybeBlockOnMountPromise` observes `mp.resolved` after registering `&e` but before `maybeResolveMountPromise` finishes `mp.wq.Notify(waiter.EventOut)`. Ordering with `mp.wq.mu` prevents lost wakeups, and duplicate non-blocking notifications on the capacity-1 channel are safe.

Minor, non-blocking notes:

source.title: Avoid closing a registered mount promise waiter
source.body:
Avoid closing a registered mount promise waiter

A lookup that registers while a mount promise is being resolved may see
that the mount is ready before the resolver broadcasts. If the lookup
closes its waiter channel at that point, the broadcast sends to the
closed channel and panics.

Notify the reader through its existing waiter entry instead. The lookup
still wakes when it registers after the broadcast, and a second
notification while it is still registered is safe.

A controlled VFS test [1] reproduced the panic on the original code.
With the fix, the lookup returned the newly mounted root and left no
waiter registered. The original VFS suite and both Nogo target
architectures also passed. The run retains the intentional stock
failure.

[1]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/fef76221-1149-4f30-be7b-a46532518fdd

source.title: Keep the congestion window when probing a closed receive window
source.body:
Keep the congestion window when probing a closed receive window

When a peer advertises a zero receive window after acknowledging all
sent data, netstack enters loss recovery while probing a write it has
not yet sent. Send the probe without reducing the congestion window.
Keep the existing timeout and recovery behavior for unacknowledged data.

In the matched control [1], Linux passed and netstack reported loss with
a congestion window of one packet. With the fix [2], both passed the
same wire test and delivered the queued write when the window reopened.
The existing retransmission, probe-backoff and user-timeout checks also
passed.

source.title: tcp: send new data as the loss probe when the congestion window is full
source.body:
`probeTimerExpired` sends a previously unsent segment as the loss probe only while `Outstanding < SndCwnd`. After a tail loss the congestion window is usually full, so the probe is a retransmission instead. RACK treats the SACK of a retransmission as ambiguous and can ignore it: because of the TSecr check, or because the probe's RTT sample is below the connection's minimum RTT. Then only the RTO recovers the tail.

RFC 8985, section 7.3, says that the probe SHOULD be a previously unsent segment if one exists and the receive window allows, and that FlightSize can then exceed the congestion window by one packet until the next ACK. Before sending any probe, the sender MUST check that "there is no other previous loss probe still in flight", so that "the sender has at most one additional packet in flight beyond the congestion window limit"; `TLP.end_seq` records both kinds of probe. Section 9.3 calls this the one way RACK-TLP modulates congestion control: "one outstanding loss probe can be sent even if the congestion window is fully used". Linux does the same: `tcp_send_loss_probe` skips the probe while an earlier one is unacknowledged (`tlp_high_seq`) and, when unsent data fits the receive window (`tcp_snd_wnd_test`), calls `tcp_write_xmit` with `push_one == 2` and Nagle off, which forces out one packet past a full congestion window.

This change lets the probe send new data while `Outstanding <= SndCwnd`, so it goes at most one segment past the window, and records a new-data probe as gVisor already records a retransmitted one (`tlpRxtOut`). Without that record, a write while the probe is out could schedule the probe timer again, send a second probe and put a second packet past the window. With it, until a probe of either kind is cumulatively acknowledged (section 7.4) or the RTO fires, no probe timer is scheduled, so no second probe goes out, as section 7.3 requires. An ACK of data not yet sent is not acceptable (RFC 9293, section 3.10.7.4) and does not end the probe. `maybeSendSegment` still checks the receive window, and the probe still counts in `Outstanding`. When there is no new data, or the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds it back, the probe is a retransmission, as before.

Linux also skips the probe while `tlp_high_seq` is set, but it keeps the RTO's earlier deadline, and a write that sends nothing does not restart its probe timer. In gVisor such a write scheduled the probe timer again, and scheduling it disables the retransmission timer, so writes while a probe was out, retransmitted or new, delayed the RTO for as long as they continued. Now that no probe timer is scheduled while a probe is out, the RTO keeps its deadline.

#16659 is complementary: it lets RACK use the SACK of a probe that has to be a retransmission (at the end of a transfer, or when the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds new data back), unless the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT. This change avoids the ambiguity whenever there is new data that the receive window, Nagle and `TCP_CORK` let the probe send.

#16596 also changes the loss probe code: it changes how the ACK of a retransmitted probe ends the TLP episode. This change keeps a probe that sends new data in its own state, but the two changes touch the same lines in `rack.go`, so whichever merges second needs a rebase.

## Test

`TestRACKTLPSendsNewData` fills the initial congestion window and loses all of it with more data queued, then checks that the probe is the next new segment and that nothing is retransmitted. It then writes more data while the probe is unacknowledged and checks that no second probe goes out: the next packet is the RTO's retransmission of the first segment. Without this change, the first probe retransmits the last segment, and the test fails. If the new-data probe is not recorded, the write schedules the probe timer again, a retransmission goes out as a second probe, and the test fails too. `TestRACKTLPLostProbeRTO` repeats the lost probe on a manual clock and checks the RTO's deadline: with no ACK, with writes every 10 ms, with a duplicate ACK, with an ACK of data not yet sent, and with writes after a retransmitted probe, the next data is the RTO's retransmission of the first segment, one RTO after the probe. Without this change, the last case fails as well: the writes delay the RTO. The other TLP tests (`TestRACKTLPRecovery`, `TestRACKTLPFallbackRTO`, `TestNoTLPRecoveryOnDSACK`, `TestNoTLPOnSACK`, `TestRACKOnePacketTailLoss`) pass.

There is no packetimpact test for this yet. One in `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go`, with the window full and data queued, could check against Linux that the probe is new data; I can add it if you'd like. The existing packetimpact TLP tests send each segment before the probe timer fires, so the probe is still a retransmission there.

All tests under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` pass with this change, alone and with #16659. I ran them on this PR's base `f4c82a02` with `bazel test` on Linux arm64 (Bazel 8.8.1, all 25 targets, including the nogo checks), and with `go test` on the `go` branch export on macOS, where `pkg/test/testutil` does not build, so I cut it down to the `Poll` helpers these tests use. The first version of this change also passed on master `4777ee78` and `05154faa`. gVisor's checklocks analyzer (`go vet -vettool`) reports the same findings for the TCP package with this change as without it. I could not run `make lint`; I'm happy to fix anything presubmit finds.

## Measurements

These measurements are from the first version of this change. The revision changes only when the probe timer is scheduled while a probe is out, and how an ACK of data not yet sent is treated, and a paired rerun with both versions found the same RTO counts and fetch times within 1% (`results/2026-10-30/` in the reproduction).

Two gVisor stacks over an emulated path with a 3 ms RTT, plus up to 0.4 ms of seeded jitter that never reorders packets, and 80 Mbit/s toward the client. The sender is set up as Tailscale sets up its netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO). After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, loses everything after its first 1000 packets until the sender pauses for 3 ms; the loss probe and everything after it arrive. Each trial is a new connection, on gVisor master `4777ee78` with #15432 and #16081, which fix the stall that otherwise follows the RTO (tailscale/tailscale#21946). Reproduction and raw output: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.31–0.59 s, median 0.55 s | 2 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.33–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 24 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 | 24 | 0.32–0.55 s, median 0.34 s | 22 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 + this change | 24 | 0.30–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 24 of 24 |

On master + #15432 + #16081, the probe is a retransmission, RACK's TSecr check discards its SACK, and 22 of 24 trials wait for the RTO. In the 2 that don't, the burst ended mid-flight and later data was SACKed, so recovery did not need the probe. #16659 lets RACK use the probe's SACK, except when the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT (2 of 24 here). With this change, the probe is the next new segment, its SACK starts SACK recovery at once, and no trial waits for the RTO. Linux is not in this table: with the same drop rule, its burst usually ended mid-flight, so later data arrived and it seldom needed the probe. In 2 of its 32 trials (a 24-trial run and an 8-trial run), it lost the whole tail and recovered from the probe without an RTO (0.38 and 0.39 s).

With the gVisor that Tailscale v1.104.2 pins (`a6f909f08a72`), eight trials per row:

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 | 8 | 0.33–0.58 s, median 0.54 s | 1 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.30–0.35 s, median 0.34 s | 8 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + #16659 + this change | 8 | 0.30–0.36 s, median 0.34 s | 8 of 8 |

At the end of a transfer there is no new data for the probe, so this change does not act there.

With real tailscaled, the effect holds. Through two `tailscaled` v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), with a Linux kernel TCP client and with #15432 and #16081 on the pinned gVisor, 5 of 8 fetches with a delivered loss probe still waited for an RTO (0.35–0.68 s, median 0.62 s); with this change and #16659 as well, none did (0.36–0.47 s, median 0.38 s). That run had both changes together, not each alone.

## Benchmarks

No benchmark in `test/benchmarks` covers loss recovery, so these come from the reproduction's `run-paired-benchmarks.sh`: each sample is one measured fetch on a new connection, 24 per scenario and build. Trial i of each build used jitter seed i, and the builds took turns trial by trial, so drift in the machine's timing affects them alike. `results-to-benchfmt.py` turns the fetches into benchmark lines; `rtos/op` is the fetch's RTO count from gVisor's own counter. `TailLostProbeArrives` is the scenario of the first table; `EndOfTransferTailLost` loses the last 4 packets of a 12-packet response; `TailAndProbeLost` loses the loss probe too, so recovery starts with an RTO either way; `HoleMidFlight` loses 16 packets mid-flight while later ones arrive. Raw output: `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-probe-fix.txt`.

```
$ benchstat "#15432+#16081=master-pr15432-16081.txt" "+this change=master-pr15432-16081-tlpnew.txt"
goos: linux
pkg: netstack-rack-repro
                      │ #15432+#16081 │            +this change             │
                      │    sec/op     │   sec/op     vs base                │
TailLostProbeArrives      549.0m ± 1%   335.0m ± 1%  -38.98% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost     221.0m ± 0%   221.0m ± 0%        ~ (p=0.969 n=24)
TailAndProbeLost          552.5m ± 1%   544.0m ± 1%   -1.54% (p=0.008 n=24)
HoleMidFlight             313.0m ± 1%   312.5m ± 2%        ~ (p=0.678 n=24)
geomean                   380.6m        334.9m       -11.99%

                      │ #15432+#16081 │              +this change               │
                      │    rtos/op    │  rtos/op    vs base                     │
TailLostProbeArrives     1.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%  -100.00% (p=0.000 n=24)
EndOfTransferTailLost    1.000 ± 0%     1.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
TailAndProbeLost         1.000 ± 0%     1.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
HoleMidFlight            0.000 ± 0%     0.000 ± 0%         ~ (p=1.000 n=24) ¹
geomean                             ²               ?                       ² ³
¹ all samples are equal
² summaries must be >0 to compute geomean
³ ratios must be >0 to compute geomean
```

At the end of a transfer there is no new data for the probe, and benchstat finds no difference. In `TailAndProbeLost` the probe is lost as well, and every trial with and without this change recovers through one RTO, with no fast retransmit or SACK recovery; I have not found a mechanism for the 1.5% difference there. With four scenarios compared, a p of 0.008 is weak evidence, and separate, unpaired 24-trial runs found no difference (p=0.223; `results/2026-10-28/benchstat-probe-fix-unpaired.txt`), so I do not read it as an effect of this change.

On top of #16659 (`results/2026-10-28/benchstat-paired-all.txt`), benchstat finds no significant difference in any scenario: in these runs the TSecr fix alone already recovered all 24 `TailLostProbeArrives` trials without an RTO (19 from the probe's SACK; in the other 5 the burst ended mid-flight). In the run in the first table it missed 2 of 24; in instrumented runs of that build, every such miss was a probe whose RTT sample fell below the minimum RTT. With this change the probe is new data, and RACK applies neither of its tests for retransmitted segments to it.

source.title: tcp: let RACK use the SACK of a retransmission when timestamps are on
source.body:
`rackControl.update` skips an ACK of a retransmitted segment when the ACK's TSecr is older than the retransmission. That follows RFC 8985, section 6.2, step 2: ignore a retransmitted segment if the ACK's TSecr "indicates the ACK was not acknowledging the last retransmission of the segment". But for an ACK that SACKs a retransmission above a hole, TSecr cannot indicate that. RFC 7323, section 4.3: "An `<ACK>` for an out-of-order segment SHOULD, therefore, contain the timestamp from the most recent segment that advanced RCV.NXT." So such an ACK echoes an earlier segment's timestamp even when the retransmission did arrive, and RACK ignores it.

A common case is a tail loss probe. After a tail loss, the probe is often a retransmission from the tail, and the receiver SACKs it, but RACK ignores that SACK, does not mark the lost tail, and the sender waits for the RTO.

With timestamps on, RFC 8985's pseudocode for this step, which applies the TSecr test to SACKed segments too, rules out its own example. In Figure 1, the SACK of the TLP retransmission of P3 is what lets RACK mark P1 and P2 lost (event 5b), and the SACK of the retransmitted P2 is what lets it mark P1's retransmission lost (event 7a). With a receiver that follows RFC 7323, both ACKs echo P0's timestamp.

This change applies the TSecr test unless SACK blocks cover the whole segment: a cumulative ACK's echoed timestamp does identify the transmission, and a SACK that ends partway through the segment does not show that the rest of it arrived. For a retransmission that is SACKed in full, it keeps only the minimum RTT test. Linux makes the same split: `tcp_clean_rtx_queue` applies its TSecr test (`tcp_skb_spurious_retrans`) to cumulatively acknowledged segments, and `tcp_sacktag_one` passes SACKed ones to `tcp_rack_advance`, which checks only the minimum RTT; `tcp_match_skb_to_sack` tags a packet as SACKed only when a SACK block covers all of it. What this gives up: the SACK of a delayed original that arrives at least the minimum RTT after the retransmission now counts as delivery of the retransmission. gVisor already accepts that without timestamps, and Linux accepts it with them. The change applies to every retransmission that is SACKed in full, not only the probe.

#16660 is complementary: it sends new data as the probe when there is some, even with the congestion window full, so that its SACK is not ambiguous. The probe still has to be a retransmission at the end of a transfer, as in the test below, or when the receive window, Nagle or `TCP_CORK` holds new data back. There this change is what lets RACK act on it, unless the probe's RTT sample is below the minimum RTT (see Measurements).

#16600 changes the same TSecr comparison so that it works across a wrap of the timestamp clock. The two changes are separate but touch adjacent lines in `rack.go`, so whichever merges second needs a small rebase.

## Test

`TestRACKTLPRecoveryWithTimestamps` follows `TestRACKTLPRecovery`, with ACKs that carry timestamps the way a receiver sends them: the SACK of the probe echoes the timestamp of segment 5, the last in-order segment. Without this change, segment 6 is retransmitted only by the RTO, and the test fails; with it, segments 6 and 7 are retransmitted without an RTO. A second case SACKs only the first half of the probe: RACK must not use that SACK, and the RTO retransmits segment 6. It passes without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is skipped for a partial SACK. `TestRACKTLPRecovery` passes either way, because its ACKs carry no timestamps.

`TestRACKCumulativeAckWithOlderTSecr` covers the TSecr test that this change keeps: an ACK that cumulatively acknowledges a retransmitted segment and echoes the original's timestamp gives RACK no sample. It passes with and without this change, and fails if the TSecr test is removed.

There is no packetimpact test for this yet. One in `test/packetimpact/tests/tcp_rack_test.go` could check the same case against Linux; I can add it if you'd like.

All tests under `pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` pass with this change, alone and with #16660. I ran them on this PR's base `f4c82a02` with `bazel test` on Linux arm64 (Bazel 8.8.1, all 25 targets, including the nogo checks), and with `go test` on the `go` branch export on macOS, where `pkg/test/testutil` does not build, so I cut it down to the `Poll` helpers these tests use. The first version of this change also passed on master `4777ee78` and `05154faa`. gVisor's checklocks analyzer (`go vet -vettool`) reports the same findings for the TCP package with this change as without it. I could not run `make lint`; I'm happy to fix anything presubmit finds.

## Measurements

These measurements are from the first version of this change. The revision changes only how RACK treats a SACK that does not cover a whole retransmitted segment, and a paired rerun with both versions found no significant difference between them (`results/2026-10-30/` in the reproduction).

Two gVisor stacks over an emulated path with a 3 ms RTT, plus up to 0.4 ms of seeded jitter that never reorders packets, and 80 Mbit/s toward the client. The sender is set up as Tailscale sets up its netstack (CUBIC, SACK, RACK, host GSO). After two loss-free warm-up fetches on each connection, each measured 2.8 MB response, sent after 3 s of idle time, loses everything after its first 1000 packets until the sender pauses for 3 ms; the loss probe and everything after it arrive. Each trial is a new connection. `a6f909f08a72` is the gVisor that Tailscale v1.104.2 pins. Reproduction and raw output: https://github.com/adios-404/netstack-rack-repro.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.31–0.59 s, median 0.55 s | 2 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.32–0.55 s, median 0.34 s | 22 of 24 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 | 8 | 0.33–0.58 s, median 0.54 s | 1 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.32–0.54 s, median 0.33 s | 7 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 | 8 | 0.53–0.55 s, median 0.54 s | 0 of 8 |
| `a6f909f08a72` + #16081 + this change | 8 | 0.54–0.58 s, median 0.56 s | 0 of 8 |

In the two trials without an RTO before this change, the burst ended mid-flight and later data was SACKed, so recovery did not need the probe. With this change, 22 of 24 trials recovered without an RTO. In runs of a build that logs each RACK decision (`run-rack-decisions.sh` in the reproduction; master + #15432 + #16081 + this change, 48 trials, two jitter seeds), 37 trials recovered from the probe's SACK, 7 did not need the probe because the burst ended mid-flight, and in the 4 that waited for the RTO, step 2's other test had rejected the probe's sample: its RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.14 ms.

With #16660, the probe here is new data, as Linux sends it (`tcp_send_loss_probe`), and all 24 trials recover without an RTO. Linux is not in this table: with the same drop rule, its burst usually ended mid-flight, so later data arrived and it seldom needed the probe. In 2 of its 32 trials (a 24-trial run and an 8-trial run), it lost the whole tail and recovered from the probe without an RTO.

With a flight this large, recovery from the probe's SACK also needs #15432: without it, the recovery this change starts stalls on the pipe overcount until the RTO, as the last two rows show; see #15432 and tailscale/tailscale#21946.

At the end of a transfer the probe has to be a retransmission, because there is no new data to send, so #16660 cannot help there. In the reproduction's end-of-transfer scenario, a 14,400-byte response (12 packets) loses its last 4 packets, and the probe arrives. The Linux row runs Linux kernel TCP as the sender, over a TUN device through the same path, to the same gVisor client.

| sender | trials | fetch time | trials without an RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| master | 24 | 0.22–0.23 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 14 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 | 24 | 0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 0 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.22 s | 5 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081 + this change + #16660 | 24 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 16 of 24 |
| Linux 6.18 kernel TCP, CUBIC | 24 | 0.03–0.24 s, median 0.03 s | 20 of 24 |
| master + #15432 + #16081, client without timestamps | 8 | 0.02–0.22 s, median 0.02 s | 5 of 8 |

The count varies more from run to run than between builds. With jitter seed 1 throughout, master + #15432 + #16081 + this change recovered without an RTO in 5 of 24 trials in the run above, and an instrumented copy of it in 11 of 24; with a seed of its own for each trial, it recovered in 15 of 24 in the benchmark runs below. In instrumented runs with three jitter seeds, master + this change recovered in 12, 18 and 12 of 24 trials, and master + #15432 + #16081 + this change in 11, 15 and 15 of 24 (42 and 41 of 72). So the differences between the rows with this change above look like run-to-run variation, not differences between the builds. #16660 does not change the probe here, because there is no unsent data. In every instrumented trial that waited for the RTO, RACK had rejected the probe's sample with step 2's other test: the probe's RTT was below the connection's minimum RTT, by at most 0.25 ms. On this path that test rejected 61 of the 144 probe samples, and 141 of the 144 probe RTTs were within 0.4 ms of the minimum, the range of the jitter, so it is close to a coin toss. Linux applies the same comparison in `tcp_rack_advance`, but against `tcp_min_rtt`, which also takes the RTT of the handshake (`tcp_synack_rtt_meas`). The handshake's small packets cross the 80 Mbit/s link about 0.12 ms faster than a full segment, while gVisor's RACK minimum comes only from RACK's own samples of data segments; that may be why Linux recovered in 20 of 24. Without client timestamps, where the TSecr test does not apply, the result is similar: 5 of 8 above, and 38 of 72 in instrumented runs, with the same minimum-RTT rejections.

Related: google/gvisor#15432 and google/gvisor#16081 fix the stall in tailscale/tailscale#21946. With them, when the loss probe gets through mid-transfer, this change leaves 22 of 24 trials without an RTO, against 2 of 24 without it, where the burst ended early (24 of 24 against 3 of 24 in the benchmark runs below). At the end of a transfer, it leaves 41 of 72 instrumented trials without an RTO (15 of 24 in the benchmark runs); in the rest, RACK's minimum RTT test rejects the probe's sample.

With real tailscaled, the effect holds. Through two `tailscaled` v1.104.2 nodes over the same emulated path (`e2e/` in the reproduction), with a Linux kernel TCP client and with #15432 and #16081 on the pinned gVisor, 5 of 8 fetches with a delivered loss probe still waited for an RTO (0.35–0.68 s, median 0.62 s); with this change and #16660 as well, none did (0.36–0.47 s, median 0.38 s). That run had both changes together, not each alone.

## Benchmarks

No benchmark in `test/benchmarks` covers loss recovery, so these come from the reproduction's `run-paired-benchmarks.sh`: each sample is one measured fetch on a new connection, 24 per scenario and build. Trial i of each build used jitter seed i, and the builds took turns trial by trial, so drift in the machine's timing affects them alike. `results-to-benchfmt.py` turns the fetches into benchmark lines; `rtos/op` is the fetch's RTO count from gVisor's own counter. `TailLostProbeArrives` is the scenario of the first table; `EndOfTransferTailLost` loses the last 4 packets of a 12-packet response; `TailAndProbeLost` loses the loss probe too, so recovery starts with an RTO either way; `HoleMidFlight` loses 16 packets mid-flight while later ones arrive. With a jitter seed of its own for each trial, 15 of 24 end-of-transfer trials recovered without an RTO with this change, against 5 of 24 in the run in the table above. items.body:
Nice catch and clean test cleanup (especially moving the `t.Fatalf` assertions out of the probe callback goroutine). Two small follow-ups on the guard and test cases:

1. **Also require `rcvdSeg.parsedOptions.TSEcr != 0` (`pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/snd.go:1745`):** Per RFC 7323 §3.2, `TSecr == 0` indicates an invalid/unset echo reply. If a connection negotiated timestamps (`SendTSOk == true`) and receives an ACK carrying a TS option with `TSEcr == 0` (e.g., a peer without a valid `TS.Recent` yet or a middlebox zeroing `TSecr`), `detectSpuriousRecovery` will still compare `0 < s.retransmitTS` and count a spurious recovery. Linux's `tcp_tsopt_ecr_before()` (`net/ipv4/tcp_input.c`) and gVisor's other `TSEcr` checks (`snd.go:1668`, `connect.go:684`, `rack.go:103`) all require a non-zero `TSEcr`.
2. **Exercise `SendTSOk == true` without a valid ACK echo in `TestDetectSpuriousRecoveryWithRTO`:** Both `SendTSOk` and `parsedOptions.TS` are currently `true` in `"timestamps"` and `false` in `"no_timestamps"`, so removing `&& rcvdSeg.parsedOptions.TS` would still pass the test. Adding subcases where timestamps are negotiated (`TS: true`) and the injected ACK omits `TCPOpts` (and/or sends `TSEcr == 0`) would cover each condition directly.

source.title: Require a usable TCP timestamp echo for Eifel detection
source.body:
Require a usable TCP timestamp echo for Eifel detection

An ACK without a usable timestamp echo cannot identify whether the peer
acknowledged the first transmission or its retransmission. Without this
check, gVisor can count an RTO recovery as spurious even though the ACK
contains no evidence of that.

Require TCP timestamps to be negotiated, the ACK to carry the option,
and the echo to be nonzero before running Eifel's timestamp comparison.
Linux requires a nonzero TSEcr for this comparison [1].

Exercise an advancing ACK after a real retransmission in four cases:
an echo from before retransmission, no timestamp negotiation, a
negotiated timestamp missing from the ACK, and a negotiated timestamp
with a zero echo. Only the first case may count the recovery as
spurious.

The prior sender [2] increments both recovery counters for the zero echo.
The corrected sender [3] passes all four cases.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L2346-L2349
[2]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/0f75db78-7487-4e84-92c6-083d49ed8e59
[3]: https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/88347058-c72a-4db0-b413-96881acd6efc

source.title: Saturate the RACK reordering window multiplier
source.body:
Saturate the RACK reordering window multiplier

A duplicate SACK can increase the time RACK allows for packet
reordering. The multiplier starts at one and is stored in a byte. Once
it reaches 255, another eligible duplicate report wraps it to zero,
eliminating the reordering allowance instead of retaining its maximum.

Saturate the multiplier while continuing to update the DSACK round and
refresh its persistence. The test checks each of 256 eligible rounds,
including the RTT-capped window at and beyond the boundary.

Linux also caps the multiplier at 255:
https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.18/net/ipv4/tcp_recovery.c#L187

source.title: Register file lock waiters under the lock-set mutex
source.body:
Register file lock waiters under the lock-set mutex

A blocking flock or fcntl must register its waiter before releasing
the mutex, or a concurrent unlock can go unnoticed. LockRegion relied
on a waiter callback to release its mutex, hiding the lock transfer
from checklocks and requiring two exemptions.

Register directly with the wait queue, release the mutex, and block on
the registered channel. This keeps registration atomic with the failed
lock attempt and lets checklocks verify both sides of the wait.

source.title: Give the oldest SACK retransmission a full timeout
source.body:
Give the oldest SACK retransmission a full timeout

When selective acknowledgments identify a missing segment, TCP can
retransmit it before its timeout expires. A successful repair leaves the
old timer running. With a three-second timeout, the sender retransmits
the same 500 bytes twice only 1.5 seconds apart.

Restart the timer after a successful repair of the oldest outstanding
data. Leave that deadline alone when repairing a later hole, so that
repeated repairs cannot indefinitely postpone a timeout. A failed send
keeps the existing retry timer or starts one if needed.

The regression sends nine segments and keeps the cumulative ACK fixed
while reporting two separate holes. It checks that the next timeout
falls exactly one retransmission interval after the repair of the oldest
segment.

prs.title: overlay: retain the backing file selected for close
prs.head: 0bb7564e8121a48bcaa58ad268dd3a7ffdac691c

items.body: @ayushr2 can you nominate someone to import this?

I'm a bit confused by this. Why can't this race happen before the `fd.mu.Lock()` on line 123? We're not doing anything in this critical section which makes the mentioned race only possible after the `fd.mu.Unlock()` below.

Note that pkg/sentry/syscalls/linux/sys_file.go:Close() calls `OnClose()` with a ref on `fd` which is not released until `OnClose()` returns.

How did you hit this race? The unit test added below may not be representative of how the sentry uses these VFS objects.

If the copy-up finishes before line 123, close takes the mutex and selects the new file. The reference held by the close syscall keeps the **overlay** file description alive. After close selects its lower file and unlocks at line 132, another thread can still use a dup of that description to replace the cached file and release the lower file’s last reference. [Close syscall](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/03e72471a/pkg/sentry/syscalls/linux/sys_file.go#L541-L554) · [Cache replacement](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/03e72471a/pkg/sentry/fsimpl/overlay/regular_file.go#L75-L98)

I tried this with two guest threads, one open file, and a real FUSE server. I paused close just after it released the overlay mutex and let `fchmod(dup)` complete. On stock gVisor the server saw `RELEASE(1)`, then `FLUSH(1)` for the same handle, and the guest’s close returned `EBADF`. With the backing reference held, the server got `FLUSH(1)` before `RELEASE(1)` and close succeeded. [Stock trace](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/910bfa68-aa50-49e8-9658-3a5cc5cd1a68) · [Fixed trace](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/b14cd43e-2399-46fc-91d6-15cd915e3f4c)

The old test comment about waiting for the FUSE server was imprecise. Once FUSE has taken the inode lock to send FLUSH, copy-up’s seek waits for it. The test pauses at callback entry, before the backing file has done any work. I’ve corrected that comment.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
I see, can we drop the unit test here. LGTM otherwise.

Dropped the Go unit test and its BUILD target. The guest test remains linked in the description. On stock gVisor, close returned EBADF after the FUSE server released the lower handle before flushing it. With the reference held, close succeeded. Native Linux also completed close and fchmod successfully.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
