source.title: Keep FUSE device watches attached after connection abort
source.body:
Keep FUSE device watches attached after connection abort

Linux accepts an epoll watch on an aborted FUSE connection and reports
EPOLLERR. gVisor instead returned EPERM from ADD, and DEL left earlier
waiters on the connection's queue.

Register and unregister against the attached connection even after it
aborts. A second mount of the same descriptor must keep the original
connection and its queue, just as Linux looks up the existing superblock
by connection [1]. Only the first mount sends FUSE_INIT.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/fs/fuse/inode.c#L1874

source.title: Count selectively acknowledged TCP packets on their transmit boundaries
source.body:
TCP can report a negative count of packets the peer selectively
acknowledged. Send eight packets in one GSO entry, SACK packet 3,
cumulatively ACK 100 bytes, SACK packets 6–8 to enter recovery, then ACK
the flight. Linux reports 1, 1, 4, 0 [1]. Stock gVisor reports 0, 0, 0,
−3. With RACK enabled, one packet trace [2] waited for the 25 ms
reordering window instead of retransmitting immediately.

Record the MSS and sequence origin at transmission. A cumulative ACK can
trim a queue entry, recovery can split it, and the path MTU can fall
without changing which bytes were sent together. Credit a packet only
when all its bytes have been acknowledged. The queue entry containing
its last byte owns the credit. A timeout or restore clears the count
along with the scoreboard.

Track RACK’s delivery observation separately from this count. A peer may
discard previously SACKed data, so the sender must be able to retransmit
it after a timeout. Repeating the same SACK for an original transmission
gives RACK no new delivery to observe. Keep that observation across
timeout and restore. Clear it when the segment is successfully sent
again.

The related #14101 corrects the flight estimate (Outstanding). Both
changes visit incoming SACKs. #14101 can use the credit change here to
identify newly acknowledged packets without a second queue scan.

The corrected wire test [3] matches Linux’s four counts. After a path
MTU reduction [4], Linux still counted a packet once while
retransmitting the preceding hole with a smaller MSS. Restoring a live
socket [5] dropped the count, credited the peer’s repeated SACK once,
and returned to zero after a full ACK. At 7d7f55233 all 79 package and
packet cases passed [6], along with both owning analyzers on AMD64 and
ARM64. Stock failed the nine new wire cases.

The new timeout case reports false reordering on 7d7f55233. Linux and
f96afe457 leave TCP_INFO.ReordSeen clear. With #16738 included, the
sender still retransmits a previously SACKed segment after the receiver
discards it and detects genuine reordering. On live restore, replaying
an earlier SACK restores packet credit once and leaves the flag clear.
The TCP, RACK, SACK and packetimpact suites passed [8].

Skip unchanged SACK ranges. When new bytes join a stored range, search
at most one transmitted packet’s length beyond the new bytes. Eight
paired runs on one AMD64 CPU [7] measured one SACK walk, RACK window
update and loss scan per operation. Four timings changed significantly.

```text
                                              │ stock.bench  │          candidate.bench           │
                                              │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
RACKSparseCoverage/ordinary-128/duplicate        2.173µ ± 1%   1.796µ ± 1%  -17.37% (p=0.000 n=8)
RACKSparseCoverage/ordinary-128/new              2.172µ ± 0%   2.067µ ± 0%   -4.83% (p=0.000 n=8)
RACKSparseCoverage/tail-4096/duplicate          108.66µ ± 5%   83.11µ ± 6%  -23.52% (p=0.000 n=8)
RACKSparseCoverage/partial-GSO-4096/duplicate    284.0µ ± 1%   257.0µ ± 1%   -9.52% (p=0.000 n=8)
```

The fixture uses 32-byte packets. Each GSO entry contains eight packets.
The partial-GSO fixture starts with 60 disjoint SACK ranges. All six
workloads fell from two allocations (32 bytes) per operation to zero.
The TCP segment remains 248 bytes on AMD64. These timings measure ACK
processing.

[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/40996472066/artifacts/12952002021

prs.head: dd1bbf30e4f345371b487ecec00361f99a95f907

items.body: I also checked the two findings outside the diff. Both are in the existing production code: a missing file can stop the scan for that group, and Close does not wait for the startup scan. I left those out of this test-only PR. The test waits for scanning to finish before closing each cache. Those production issues need separate fixes and tests.

Reworks the filecache concurrent-scan test so it builds one fixture in the current layout and reuses it across trials. The test now covers the in-place scan's "already in the LRU, so don't evict" check instead of the legacy migration branch. No blocking bugs were found.

### Additional findings (lines outside the diff)
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/filecache/filecache.go:521` — Pre-existing, not introduced by this PR: if a file disappears while the scan is running, the scan stops for the rest of that group.
- Sequence: `AddFile(k)` runs before the scan reaches `k`, then `DeleteFile(k)` or a size eviction unlinks the file. When the scan reaches `k`, `os.Stat` returns `NotFound`.
- Only `InvalidArgument` is tolerated (line 514), so `WalkDir` aborts.
- Every remaining file in that group stays on disk but never enters the LRU, so it is never evicted. #7924 removed the earlier `NotFound` tolerance.

The reworked test does one `AddFile` per trial, so it can't hit this.
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/filecache/filecache.go:270` — Pre-existing, not introduced by this PR: `Close` doesn't wait for the scan, because the scan starts with a bare `go c.scanDir()` instead of `c.wg.Go`. That is why the test's deferred cleanup at `filecache_test.go:689` has to call `WaitForDirectoryScanToComplete()` itself. In production, a scan or migration that is still running can write after `Close` has synced and removed `boot_id`.

**[Re-run review](https://app.buildbuddy.io/workflows/run?action_name=Code+review&branch=sluongng%2Ffilecache-scan-fixture&env_preset=AGENT_REVIEW&repo_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fbuildbuddy-io%2Fbuildbuddy)**

<sub>Reviewed with [`bb agent review`](https://www.buildbuddy.io/docs/cli-commands#bb-agent-review) on BuildBuddy Workflows</sub>

No test now runs the legacy migration at the same time as `AddFile`. The old fixture was the only one that did, through the migration branch at `filecache.go:778-797` (`Remove(k)`, link the legacy path, unlink it). `TestFileCacheEvictionAfterSubdirPrefixing` and `TestFileCacheEvictionAfterStartupScan` both call `WaitForDirectoryScanToComplete()` before `AddFile`. So "leaving legacy migration coverage in its existing tests" covers migration alone, not migration during a concurrent add. Upgraded executors still on the flat layout run exactly that path at startup. Consider keeping a legacy fixture with a small trial count (for example, 5–10), or adding a separate small test for it.

Good catch. I kept 100 current-layout trials and added five old-layout migration trials. Each migration trial gets a fresh cache directory and adds a file while the startup scan runs. All 100 files are still checked in every trial.

The re-added file is a weaker check than before:
- `sourcePaths[i]` is the same inode that is already in the cache. `ANON` uses `Clone`, which uses `FastCopy`, which is `os.Link` on Linux.
- If the scan hasn't reached `k` yet, `l.Remove(k)` does nothing and `cloneOrLink` treats `EEXIST` as success (`FastCopy` in `fastcopy_linux.go`). The re-add is then a complete no-op.
- The old test re-added a separate `action.output` file, and neither version checks file contents.

Writing a fresh copy each trial is cheap: one file, compared with the 100 the old version wrote.

Fixed. Each trial now writes a fresh source file before starting the cache, then re-adds that file. It no longer reuses the inode already in the cache. The test also checks the contents of the linked re-added file.

This may not fix the Windows timeout. Each trial still links 100 files with `FastLinkFile`, which is a `CopyFileW` on Windows. The next `NewFileCache` then deletes all 100 with `os.RemoveAll(TempDir())`, for about 10k copies and 10k deletes in total. The change removes about 100 writes and 100 migration copy-and-unlink operations per trial, roughly half the I/O. As the description says, Windows CI needs to confirm this fits the `size = "small"` budget.

Agreed. The first revision passed the Windows executor CI job with the existing budget. That is one passing run, not proof that the flake is gone. The updated test keeps all link checks and needs a new Windows CI result. I have not changed any timeout or wait budget.

Nit: `for i := range n` (line 702) shadows the re-added `i` from line 695 (this predates the PR). Also, every trial now shares one `filecacheRoot`, so the failure message should say which node was re-added. Renaming the outer variable (for example, to `readded`) and including it in the message fixes both.
Fixed. The variable is now named `readded`, and link failures include both the trial number and the re-added node.

Low confidence: nothing forces `AddFile` to overlap the scan, and that was true before too. The in-place scan no longer copies files while holding the lock, so it is much shorter. More trials may now run entirely before or after the scan and never exercise the race, and the test can't report how many trials actually overlapped.

Agreed: overlap still depends on timing. I made that clear in the test and PR description and kept a few migration trials. The existing test API has no way to pause the scan at the relevant point. I left a new scan hook out of this test-only fix rather than adding sleeps or claiming that overlap is guaranteed.

source.title: Enable vhost-net in x86 guest kernels
source.body:
The x86 guest configs disabled vhost-net, so the guest could not provide `/dev/vhost-net` to nested userspace network backends (#13604). This enables `CONFIG_VHOST_NET`, plus the `CONFIG_VHOST` and `CONFIG_VHOST_IOTLB` options it selects, in the 5.15 and 6.18 configs, and rebuilds both kernels.

This supersedes #13803, which targeted the 6.1 config that #13812 replaced with 6.18.

Rebuilding 5.15 changes the default guest kernel digest, so existing x86_64 VM snapshots are invalidated on the next executor rollout.

prs.title: Enable vhost-net in x86 guest kernels
prs.head: 1c8ea1521a8b39fb5e39346367c605ea51706f4b

items.body: hey @bduffany, has this run into a problem?
would be neat to fold https://github.com/buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy/pull/13938 into the same kernel update if possible and convenient

Turns on `CONFIG_VHOST_NET` (along with `CONFIG_VHOST` and `CONFIG_VHOST_IOTLB`) in the x86_64 5.15 and 6.18 guest kernel configs, and updates `deps.bzl` to point at the rebuilt kernel binaries.

### Additional findings (lines outside the diff)
- `enterprise/server/cmd/goinit/main.go:241` — `/dev/vhost-net` stays root-only (0600). goinit relaxes `/dev/net/tun` and `/dev/fuse` to 0666 because the guest has no udev. On a normal distro, udev also makes `/dev/vhost-net` 0666, but it isn't added to this list. As a result, rootless Podman/QEMU, or any action running as a non-root user, gets EACCES when opening it, and only root in the guest benefits from this change. Consider adding `/dev/vhost-net` here.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/BUILD:10` — The default 5.15 kernel is built from the bare `v5.15` tag (5.15.0). This target has no `git_tag`, so the build uses tag `v5.15`. This PR now compiles the vhost/vhost_net driver into every x86_64 guest without the later 5.15.y fixes, such as the iotlb hung-thread fix and the vhost_net ubuf refcount fix. `rebuild.sh:48` already recommends pinning a point release, as the 6.18 target does with `v6.18.57`.
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/containers/firecracker/firecracker_test.go:418` — No test checks that `/dev/vhost-net` exists. `TestFirecrackerRunSimple` already runs `stat` on `/dev/fuse` and `/dev/net/tun`. Adding `/dev/vhost-net` to the amd64 branch would catch a kernel uploaded from the wrong config, or a later config edit that drops VHOST_NET. The new sha256 values in `deps.bzl` only show the file matches what was uploaded, not which config it was built from.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/microvm-kernel-aarch64-v5.10.config:2135` — arm64 is still `# CONFIG_VHOST_NET is not set`, with no TODO, so the fix for #13604 only covers x86_64. TUN is already tracked with a TODO in the test; this should be tracked the same way.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/rebuild.sh:83` — The build can't be reproduced to check the new hashes. `KBUILD_BUILD_TIMESTAMP`, `KBUILD_BUILD_USER` and `KBUILD_BUILD_HOST` are never pinned, so a reviewer can't rebuild and confirm that `10b243f5…` and `4c27704a…` came from these configs. This problem predates the PR, but it matters most when a PR's whole change is a new hash.

**[Re-run review](https://app.buildbuddy.io/workflows/run?action_name=Code+review&branch=guest-kernel-vhost-net&env_preset=AGENT_REVIEW&repo_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fbuildbuddy-io%2Fbuildbuddy)**

<sub>Reviewed with [`bb agent review`](https://www.buildbuddy.io/docs/cli-commands#bb-agent-review) on BuildBuddy Workflows</sub>

This config is missing `CONFIG_VHOST_TASK=y`. In kernels 6.4 and later, enabling `VHOST` automatically turns on `VHOST_TASK` too. `rebuild.sh:75` runs `make olddefconfig`, so the kernel that was actually built has it, but the checked-in file doesn't. The new header line also says VHOST_NET only pulls in VHOST and VHOST_IOTLB, which is wrong for 6.18. If someone compares this file with the guest's `/proc/config.gz`, they'll see a difference that shouldn't be there.

This will invalidate every x86_64 VM snapshot. The 5.15 kernel digest is part of every x86_64 snapshot key, so on rollout all recycled runners and CI workflows will cold-boot. Any kernel change has that cost, but it's worth deciding on purpose. Options are shipping in 6.18 only for now, or bundling this with the next 5.15 rebuild that's needed anyway.

Heads-up: vhost worker threads behave differently on 6.18 than on 5.15. `CONFIG_VHOST_ENABLE_FORK_OWNER_CONTROL` is unset, and that now matters because VHOST is built in. On 6.18 the worker threads always run in the owner's thread group and count against its pids/`RLIMIT_NPROC` limits; on 5.15 they're separate kernel threads. Mostly relevant for anyone comparing the two kernels in the upgrade experiment.

prs.title: Select Firecracker guest kernel versions
prs.head: 8c704d5324518b02f430a3f5f0f9388549c65eab

items.body:
The context is in the referenced ticket: we want the kernel version to be an explicit property of the execution environment because gvisor's test suite tests the behavior of the host kernel in order to compare it to gvisor's behavior.

Without an execution property we get incorrect test result caching.

@tamird got it, thanks for clarifying. I agree that for tests that explicitly exercise kernel behavior, changing the guest kernel without changing the action cache key is a correctness problem. We'll need to discuss this internally and reach consensus on what kernel-selection API and support policy we can commit to, including how we handle updates and retire older versions. I understand why an explicit execution property would be useful here; we need to work through those support implications before committing to it.
@bduffany makes sense, thanks!

Currently we can switch kernel versions without breaking people (we have a process for ramping this up via experiment, carefully monitoring errors, and working w/ people to address breakages), but this property would lock it in as a public API that we have to support, which I'm not sure we can commit to right now.

If you give a bit more context for why you need to opt in to 5.15, I think we could consider some alternatives here. FWIW, v5.15 is EOL in December of this year

source.title: Send SNI in the Node.js CA certificate test
source.body:
The Node.js CA interaction test connects to www.nodejs.org without
sending a TLS server name. The endpoint can return its default nodejs.org
certificate, which does not cover www.nodejs.org, so hostname verification
fails before the test checks the supplied CA behavior.

Apply the correction proposed in [nodejs/node#66835][upstream] to the
runtime image. Send www.nodejs.org as the server name while preserving the
hostname, certificate verification, and all CA assertions. Include the
patched test in the existing image syntax checks.

The fresh source image and complete declared gVisor Node.js runtime profile
passed in both filesystem modes: 160 runtime shards and 7,898 inner tests.
This qualification used the source-image integration branch and retains
the profile's existing exclusions. The earlier focused affected-partition
run also passed. Upstream Node metadata checks have passed; these gVisor
results do not establish a full upstream Node source-suite result.

Assisted by OpenAI Codex.

[upstream]: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/66835

## 2026-10-28, Version 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 (Alpha), @RafaelGSS

### Notable Changes

#### V8 15.6

The V8 engine is updated to version 15.6.75.13, up from 14.6 in Node.js 26. Highlights:

* New language features enabled by default: `Math.sumPrecise()`, `Intl.Locale.prototype.variants`, `Iterator.prototype.join()`, `Iterator.prototype.includes()`, `Iterator.zip()` and `Iterator.zipKeyed()`.
* Experimental features behind flags: `import defer` (`--js-defer-import-eval`), Immutable `ArrayBuffer` (`--js-immutable-arraybuffer`) and RegExp buffer boundaries (`--js-regexp-buffer-boundaries`).
* Memory: when `--max-old-space-size` is not set, the default heap size limit is now half of the physical memory clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB, and memory held by `Buffer` and `ArrayBuffer` instances now counts toward the heap limit. Applications that relied on the previous defaults should set `--max-old-space-size` explicitly.
* Serialization: `v8.serialize()`, `structuredClone()` and `postMessage()` use a new format that older Node.js releases cannot read. `v8.cachedDataVersionTag()` and the compile cache also change on every Node.js patch of V8, not only on V8 version changes.
* Observable behavior changes: `Math` methods now use LLVM's libm and may differ in the last bit; `Math.random()` sequences change for a given `--random-seed`; `error.stack` is no longer looked up through the prototype chain; `await` incurs fewer microtasks; `Array.prototype.sort()` uses PowerSort for large arrays and remains stable.
* Heap snapshots include internal objects, numeric values and full script sources. Taking one takes about twice as long and the file is about twice as large.
* WebAssembly: asm.js is no longer compiled to WebAssembly, and the `--experimental-wasm-<name>` flags are renamed `--wasm-<name>`.

A more complete list of notable V8 changes between 14.6 and 15.6 will be shared soon.

source.title: Select Linux UAPI headers independently
source.body:
Use Linux 6.18 UAPI headers for targets without an explicit kernel
version constraint. The glibc 2.28 default otherwise selects Linux 4.19
headers, which lack declarations such as `NFT_MSG_DESTROYTABLE` used by
gVisor's netfilter syscall tests.

The header choice applies to both glibc and musl without changing the
target libc or execution platform. Explicit kernel constraints still
take precedence. Projects that do not set a default keep the existing
libc-based selection.

[The upstream implementation][1] landed after hermetic-llvm 0.8.26.
gVisor pins 0.8.24, so this change carries the interface as a patch to
that release. Updating to a BCR version with the interface removes the
need for the local patch.

[1]: https://github.com/hermeticbuild/hermetic-llvm/commit/3dd710dd9cb57adc0a8baf4220f5bc1e38ebd9bc

prs.title: Add an opt-in native POSIX test wrapper
prs.head: b9d613ad6ba7e5bd73b88ca498bf3ecf7f13c699

items.body: What's the benefit of doing this?

> What's the benefit of doing this?

The bash one requires certain tools be present in the executor, a requirement not satisfied by systems trying to do true hermetic execution.

It also aligns posix more closely with windows, which already uses the native binary

Which tools are problematic? Can we instead try to align the shell wrapper to the POSIX spec?

I think if we're going to do this, we need a better cross-platform story. As this PR stands, the choice of test wrapper is AFAICT host-dependent, so cross-platform execution won't work (e.g. Bazel running on macOS with remote execution on Linux) which is a capability regression in comparison with the shell implementation.

> Which tools are problematic?

test-setup.sh requires Bash and executor utilities including ps/pgrep, stat, file, and zip

> Can we instead try to align the shell wrapper to the POSIX spec?

We could, but it would still require a shell and is actually a bit of a crutch, more on that below.

> I think if we're going to do this, we need a better cross-platform story. As this PR stands, the choice of test wrapper is AFAICT host-dependent, so cross-platform execution won't work (e.g. Bazel running on macOS with remote execution on Linux) which is a capability regression in comparison with the shell implementation.

Are you sure about this? I'm certainly no expert in this code, but what you write doesn't match my understanding of what is happening or my testing (Using [actiond](https://github.com/hermeticbuild/actiond/) on a Mac host). The wrapper dependency is configured for the test execution platform. [native_posix_test_wrapper_binary](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/b9d613ad6ba7e5bd73b88ca498bf3ecf7f13c699/tools/test/BUILD.tools#L159-L180) reuses the embedded binary when that platform matches the host constraints and otherwise builds the wrapper for the selected platform. This follows the host-prebuilt/source-built pattern Fabian introduced for [zipper and Windows launcher tooling in #26019](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/pull/26019). Unifying this pattern is a Good Thing precisely because POSIX doesn't really help on Windows, hence my comments earlier about relying on POSIX compatibility to mask the confusion between host/exec being a crutch.

> Are you sure about this? I'm certainly no expert in this code, but what you write doesn't match my understanding of what is happening or my testing (Using [actiond](https://github.com/hermeticbuild/actiond/) on a Mac host). The wrapper dependency is configured for the test execution platform. [native_posix_test_wrapper_binary](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/b9d613ad6ba7e5bd73b88ca498bf3ecf7f13c699/tools/test/BUILD.tools#L159-L180) reuses the embedded binary when that platform matches the host constraints and otherwise builds the wrapper for the selected platform. This follows the host-prebuilt/source-built pattern Fabian introduced for [zipper and Windows launcher tooling in #26019](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/pull/26019). Unifying this pattern is a Good Thing precisely because POSIX doesn't really help on Windows, hence my comments earlier about relying on POSIX compatibility to mask the confusion between host/exec being a crutch.

Fair enough - I didn't realize there was a fallback to compilation. But then there's a different unfortunate consequence: you can no longer run tests across platforms without setting up a cross-compilation C++ toolchain.

I think getting rid of the bash (ps/stat/file/zip) dependencies on executors is a win not only for minimal containers / micro VMs, and the watchdog in `tw.cc` looks cleaner than the `ps` polling loop in `test-setup.sh`.

Unfortunately, the cross-platform concern is real: a Mac user running tests against Linux RBE on a pure Java or Go project suddenly requires a exec-platform C++-toolchain just to compile the test wrapper. It will break their build unless they configured a cross-compiler.

@fmeum mentioned on #19587 for zipper and the Windows launcher that might help long term: moving these tools into a dedicated module/toolchain that distributes multi-arch prebuilts (like buildozer or remote_java_tools) with source compilation only as a fallback for untiered platforms - cc @meteorcloudy.

I am not thrilled by maintaining three different things (`tw.cc` for two platforms and `test-setup.sh`), but iff we have a credible plan to get rid of the shell thing completely, I could be convinced that using `test-setup.sh` is a valid fallback option in case there is no C++ toolchain available.

In any case, we should make sure we are not breaking things like coverage by a change like this.

If we go through the setup for this separate module (or repos referenced by `bazel_tools`), we could drop `test-setup.sh` entirely if we assume that platforms without prebuilts are targeted by some C++ toolchain.
I'm not a huge golang proponent but if there are concerns about C++ toolchain stuff maybe using that for easier cross compilation would solve that?

items.body:
Thanks for your pull request! It looks like this may be your first contribution to a Google open source project. Before we can look at your pull request, you'll need to sign a Contributor License Agreement (CLA).

View this [failed invocation](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15325/checks?check_run_id=111995961751) of the CLA check for more information.

For the most up to date status, view the checks section at the bottom of the pull request.
Can you post benchmark results?

@EtiennePerot Benchmarks of `3cd9a5d9` against its parent `97e8e896` on this machine (Ryzen 3 5300U, powersave, clocks moving between about 1.5 and 3.9 GHz).

The harness is the in-process e2e channel endpoint, not `//test/benchmarks/tcp`. The sender injects segments and stays inside the latest advertised window. It reads when the window closes, on 3 duplicate ACKs, or after 200ms with no ACK, then retransmits from the oldest unacknowledged byte. Numbers are medians.

Steady state, application keeps up, 512 KiB receive buffer, no dropped segments. Pipelined 1448 B was 160–227 MiB/s on parent and 185–253 MiB/s on this PR (25,600 segments). Stop-and-wait 1 B was 9.9–10.7 µs/segment on parent and 9.3–10.4 µs/segment on this PR (8,000 segments). The spread from the CPU clock is larger than the difference between the two commits, including 536 B and 64 B. I don't see a steady-state regression in this setup.

Small segments into a 64 KiB receive buffer (the `32<<10` test-helper value; the helper doubles it), scale 1, 2 second run. The sender fills the window before the application reads. That is the exhaustion case from #15144.

| payload | parent | this PR | parent drops / silence timeouts | this PR drops / silence timeouts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1448 B | 5.8 MiB/s | 6.2 MiB/s | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| 536 B | 3.8 MiB/s | 5.7 MiB/s | 480 / 1 | 4 / 0 |
| 100 B | 0.047 MiB/s | 1.9 MiB/s | ~2000 / 9 | 30 / 0 |
| 1 B | 642 B in 2s | 66 KB in 2s | ~194k / 5 | ~3400 / 0 |

On parent, 1 B and 100 B segments fill segment memory while the advertised window is still open. The rest of that window is dropped with no ACK, and the sender waits out the silence timer. This PR ACKs those rejects at the current receive sequence (without accepting the payload) and, once the segment cost has been learned, reopens a window sized for that cost, so the transfer keeps moving. The initial window is not shrunk, so a 1 B burst can still overshoot and drop; those drops no longer stall the sender for the silence timeout.

Could we bound the work queued to send these ACKs? Your 536-byte
benchmark shows why acknowledging rejected data matters (480 drops on
the parent, 4 here). The part that worries me is keeping a queue entry
for *every* rejected segment until the TCP worker can run.

I [repeated the same 4 KiB data segment while holding off dequeue](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/1343dc381c63c720ab2d12f24371d04a959acfbe).
With a 4,096-byte receive budget, the endpoint charged 4,724 bytes
after one packet, 24,820 after 33, and 165,492 after 257. Draining the
queue returned the charge to zero. [Run and original test output](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/6677d109-c3a7-4693-b395-38036ea6102a).

Could repeated rejects share a pending ACK for the same receive state,
or otherwise have a bounded queue? That would keep the memory cost
bounded when the peer is faster than the worker, while preserving the
progress in your small-segment benchmark.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

I also ran `bazel test //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` (Bazel 8.8.1, Linux arm64): all 25 targets, including the nogo checks, pass at this PR's head, on its base `f4c82a02`, and with #16660 applied on top.
Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

This correctly advances RACK for a fully SACKed retransmission. Could we also cover a SACK that ends partway through the retransmitted segment? With the cumulative ACK at 10, I retransmitted bytes [30,40) and SACKed only [30,35). On this head RACK advanced its end sequence to 40, exactly as it did for a full [30,40) SACK. The peer hasn't reported delivery of [35,40); using 40 as the reference can affect loss detection for other segments.

[The two packet cases](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/cafedc99567fcc65ac3d96163a255ec144c628dc) ran on the [base](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/fe22e38d-f3eb-4be8-9e3d-8a0374d3de73) and [this head](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/0573285e-2d37-4da4-b544-582e3be50230). Can we credit only bytes the peer SACKed, or build on the whole-segment check in #15634?

Thanks, you're right: on that head a SACK of [30,35) moved RACK's end sequence to 40, the same as a SACK of all of [30,40). I've amended the commit so that the TSecr test is skipped only when the scoreboard shows the whole retransmitted segment SACKed (`IsSACKED(seg.sackBlock())`; `handleRcvdSegment` inserts this ACK's blocks before `walkSACK` calls `update`). A SACK that ends partway through the segment keeps the TSecr test, as on the base, so with an older echo RACK takes no sample from it. Linux also tags a packet as SACKed only when a SACK block covers all of it (`tcp_match_skb_to_sack`).

I didn't try to credit only the SACKed bytes: RACK can use part of a segment only once the segment is split at the SACK boundary, which is what #15634 does, at MSS boundaries. On top of #15634, `walkSACK` passes `update` only segments that are SACKed whole, so this check would hold for every SACKed segment there.

With your two cases on the new head, RACK's end sequence stays at 10 for [30,35) and moves to 40 for [30,40). `TestRACKTLPRecoveryWithTimestamps` now also SACKs only the first half of the probe: RACK takes no sample, and the RTO retransmits segment 6. That case passes on the base and fails on the previous head. All 25 `//pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` targets still pass with Bazel on Linux arm64, alone and with #16660.

I also ran `bazel test //pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/...` (Bazel 8.8.1, Linux arm64): all 25 targets, including the nogo checks, pass at this PR's head, on its base `f4c82a02`, and with #16659 applied on top.
Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Could the pending-probe check run before schedulePTO disables the retransmission timer? With a three-second RTO and no further ACKs, queuing ten bytes every 10 ms for three seconds kept even the original retransmission from appearing by six seconds. Those writes put nothing on the wire. With no writes, the same socket retransmitted the oldest bytes at exactly three seconds. I'd check that original deadline alongside the absence of a second probe.

Thanks, I reproduced it: on that head, writes every 10 ms kept the RTO from firing for as long as they lasted, and a single duplicate ACK moved it one PTO later. The check now runs in `shouldSchedulePTO`: while a probe of either kind is out, no PTO is scheduled, so writes and ACKs leave the retransmission timer armed with the deadline it got when the probe went out. `probeTimerExpired` no longer needs its early return, since the probe timer can't be armed while a probe is out. On the base, writes delayed the RTO the same way while a retransmitted probe was out; this fixes that case too.

`TestRACKTLPLostProbeRTO` checks this on a manual clock. With no ACK, writes every 10 ms, a duplicate ACK, an ACK beyond SND.NXT, and writes after a retransmitted probe, the next data is the RTO's retransmission of the first segment, one RTO after the probe, with one timeout. Your four cases pass too: in each, the oldest bytes go out exactly 3 s after the probe.

An ACK beyond SND.NXT can also end the probe episode. After a new-data probe covering [120,130), an ACK for 131 caused [120,130) to go out again 60 ms later, with no intervening timeout. A duplicate ACK at the old frontier didn't do that. Can we clear the episode only after validating an ACK that covers the probe? [Reproducer](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/6fe5e54b8e7def448890ef77b1de9a2692817d04) and [results for both cases and controls](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/5f626fb7-5e25-4f65-914b-77f423c1f08d).

Thanks, reproduced as well: an ACK one byte past the probe ended the episode, and the probe went out again one PTO later. The new-data probe now ends only on an ACK at or below SND.NXT; an ACK of data not yet sent is not acceptable (RFC 9293, section 3.10.7.4). With the change above, that ACK also schedules no PTO, so the next data is the RTO's retransmission of the oldest bytes, on time. The "ACK of unsent data" case in `TestRACKTLPLostProbeRTO` covers it.

#16378 would drop such an ACK before the sender sees it; this check doesn't depend on it. The retransmitted-probe path (`tlpHighRxt <= ack`) still ends its episode on such an ACK, as on the base, and then also starts a congestion response. I left that to #16378, but I can add the same bound there if you'd rather have it in this PR.
